Initially created: 2025-12-06T13:37:42.367+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.

p.seg: Sīmǎ Guāng
compiled by imperial command
Later Learner Tiāntāi
The Shí clan, having followed the Prince of Jìn from Dàiběi and risen in Tàiyuán,
later also used Tàiyuán as the base to initiate their enterprise and seize the Central Plains;
Tàiyuán governed Jìnyáng,
and the Khitan subsequently named it with the designation "Jìn",
hence the state was named Jìn.
Emperor Gāozǔ, the Sagely, Cultured, Martial, Illustriously Virtuous, and Filial Emperor, First Part, Upper Section
His personal name was Jìngtáng,
surname Shí.
His father, Nièlièjī,
was originally of foreign descent,
having submitted to the Táng under the Zhūyé clan,
and followed the Zhūyé clan to settle in Yīnshān.
His surname was Shí,
but it is unknown when the surname was acquired.
The Wǔdài Huìyào states: After Jìn gained the empire,
they claimed descent from the Wèi grandee Shí Què.
First year of Tiānfú
(Bǐngshēn, 936)
In this year, the eleventh month was when the era name was changed and the accession took place.
1 Spring,
first month,
Wú's Xú Zhīgào first established the Grand Marshal's office.
Wú appointed Xú Zhīgào as Grand Marshal;
see the tenth month of winter in the previous year in the preceding scroll.
2 Dīngwèi day,
the Táng sovereign installed his son Chóngměi as Prince of Yōng.
3 Guǐchǒu day,
the Táng sovereign held a banquet for the Thousand Springs Festival.
The Táng sovereign designated his birthday as the Thousand Springs Festival.
The Wǔdài Huìyào states: The Emperor was born on the thirteenth day of the first month in the first year of Guāngqǐ of Táng.
Since the Jìn era name is used for chronology,
the Prince of Lù is referred to as the Táng sovereign.
He took leave to return to Jìnyáng.
The Emperor was drunk,
and said:
"Why not stay a while longer?
Leaving in such haste,
do you intend to rebel with Shí Láng?"
Shí Jìngtáng heard this,
and became even more fearful.
4 Third month,
Bǐngwǔ day,
appointed Hànlín Academician and Vice Minister of Rites Mǎ Yǐnsūn as Vice Director of the Secretariat and Tongpingzhangshi.
Yǐnsūn was by nature cautious and timid,
so matters in the Secretariat often became stagnant,
and he rarely received guests.
People at the time called him
"the three unopened",
referring to his mouth, seal, and gate.
5 Shí Jìngtáng gathered all his goods stored in Luòyáng and various circuits and brought them back to Jìnyáng,
claiming it was to aid military expenses,
but everyone knew he harbored different intentions.
The Táng sovereign, at night, spoke leisurely with his close ministers, saying:
The Táng sovereign enjoyed conversing with close ministers at night; see the previous year in the preceding scroll.
Cóng,
pronounced qiān róng fān.
"Shí Láng is my closest relative,
and there is no reason for suspicion;
but if rumors are not dispelled,
and by chance discord arises,
how can it be resolved?"
None replied.
Duānmíngdiàn Academician and Jǐshìzhōng Lǐ Sōng, after withdrawing, said to his colleague Lǚ Qí:
Lǐ Sōng at the time served in the palace alongside Lǚ Qí.
"We have received deep favor,
how can we act like the common crowd,
merely observing from the sidelines?
What plan should we devise?"
Qí said:
"If Hé dōng harbors rebellious designs,
they will certainly ally with the Khitan for support.
The Khitan queen mother, because Zànhuá is in China,
has repeatedly sought a marriage alliance,
but only because the search for Jícì and others has not succeeded,
that the peace has not been concluded.
Zànhuá,
was the eldest son of the Khitan ruler Ābǎojī.
His surrender is recorded in scroll 277, first year of Chángxīng of Emperor Míngzōng.
The search for Jícì is recorded in the third year.
The Khitan queen mother
refers to Empress Shùlǜ.
If we annually send ritual gifts worth over a hundred thousand strings of cash to them,
they will gladly comply.
In this way,
even if Hé dōng wishes to act arrogantly,
they will be powerless."
Sōng said:
"This is my intention as well.
However, funds and grain all come from the Three Departments,
so we should further consult Minister Zhāng about it."
They then informed Zhāng Yánlǎng,
and Yánlǎng said:
"If we follow the Academicians' plan,
not only can we control Hé dōng,
but we can also reduce border expenses by nine-tenths,
meaning a reduction of nine parts out of ten.
If the Sovereign agrees,
just assign the task to this old man,
I will gather additional funds beyond the treasury to supply it."
Another evening,
the two secretly spoke to the Emperor,
and the Emperor was greatly pleased,
praising their loyalty.
The two privately drafted a letter to the Khitan, awaiting orders.
After some time,
the Emperor informed Privy Council Academician Xuē Wényù of the plan,
and Wényù replied:
"With the Son of Heaven's dignity,
to humble oneself and serve the barbarians,
is that not disgraceful?!
Moreover,
if the barbarians follow precedent and request to marry a princess,
how can we refuse?"
Since the Táng dynasty, from Tàizōng onward, imperial clan women were made princesses and married to various foreign tribes,
called "harmony princesses";
later, the Uyghurs having rendered service to China,
even the emperor's own daughter was given in marriage.
"Entrusting safety and danger to a woman."
The Emperor's mind then changed.
Róng Yù,
a man of the Táng,
was skilled in poetry.
Hàn Yuándì married Wáng Zhāojūn to the Xiongnu,
later generations pitied her,
and competed in composing songs and poems to recount the event.
He urgently summoned Sōng and Qí to the rear tower,
in great anger,
and rebuked them, saying:
"You gentlemen all know past and present,
and wish to assist the ruler in achieving great peace;
now you devise such plans!
I have a daughter still smelling of milk,
do you wish to abandon her in the desert?
Moreover, you wish to deliver the wealth used to nurture soldiers to the barbarian court?"
Nurturing soldiers
refers to maintaining the army.
Meaning they wished to cut the wealth for maintaining the army to make peace with the barbarians.
The two were afraid,
sweating profusely,
and said:
"We, your servants, intended to exhaust our foolishness to repay the state,
not to scheme for the barbarians;
we beg Your Majesty to examine this."
They bowed in apology countless times,
but the Emperor continued to berate them.
Lǚ Qí, breathless,
ceased bowing slightly,
and the Emperor said:
"Lǚ Qí is stubborn,
does he deign to regard me as the ruler?!"
Qí said:
"We, your servants, devised an unworthy plan,
we beg Your Majesty to punish our crime;
what use is much bowing?!"
The Emperor's anger gradually subsided,
and he stopped their bowing,
bestowed each a cup of wine, and dismissed them.
Dismissed,
meaning sent them to their quarters.
Dīngsì day,
appointed Qí as Vice Censor-in-Chief,
effectively distancing him.
Lǚ Qí being favored by the Táng sovereign began in scroll 277, first year of Chángxīng of Emperor Míngzōng.
The Vice Censor-in-Chief resides in the outer court,
and cannot serve in the palace,
hence called distancing.
6 Wú's Xú Zhīgào appointed his son, Deputy Commander-in-Chief Jǐngtōng, as Grand Commandant and Deputy Marshal,
and Commander's Judge Sòng Qíqiū and Army Marshal Xú Jiè as Left and Right Marshals of the Marshal's office.
7 The Mǐn sovereign Chǎng changed the era name to Tōngwén,
installed the virtuous Lady Lǐ as Empress,
that is, Lǐ Chūnyàn.
8 The Military Commissioner of Jìngjiāng, Concurrently Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs Mǎ Xīgǎo had implemented good governance.
The Supervisor-in-Chief Péi Rénxǔ slandered him to the King of Chǔ, Xīfàn,
saying that he was winning over the hearts of the people.
Xīfàn became suspicious of him.
In summer,
the fourth month,
a general of Hàn, Sūn Déwēi, invaded the two prefectures of Méng and Guì.
Méng Prefecture
was originally Lìpǔ County of Cāngwú Commandery during the Hàn Dynasty.
In the Suí Dynasty, Lìpǔ was divided to establish Suíhuà County.
In the fourth year of the Wǔdé era of the Táng Dynasty, it was renamed Lìshān,
and Lì Prefecture was established in the county.
It was soon changed to Gōng Prefecture;
in the eighth year of the Zhēnguàn era, it was changed to Méng Prefecture,
because east of the prefecture was Méng Mountain,
and at the foot of the mountain was Méng River,
and many people there bore the surname Méng.
In the fifth year of the Xīníng era of the Sòng Dynasty, Méng Prefecture was abolished,
and Lìshān County was placed under Zhāo Prefecture.
(Xīfàn) personally led five thousand infantry and cavalry to Guì Prefecture.
Xīgǎo was afraid.
His mother, Lady Huá,
went to meet Xīfàn at Quányì Ridge.
Quányì Ridge was in Quányì County of Guì Prefecture,
which was Shǐ'ān Ridge.
She said, "Xīgǎo's governance has been ineffective,
leading to enemy troops entering our borders,
and troubling Your Highness to personally traverse dangerous and difficult terrain.
This is all my fault.
I wish to have my fief reduced,
and to serve sweeping duties in the palace,
in order to redeem Xīgǎo's crime."
Xīfàn said:
"It has been a long time since I saw Xīgǎo,
and I heard that his governance was particularly outstanding,
so I came to see him,
for no other reason."
The Hàn troops withdrew from Méng Prefecture,
and Xīgǎo was transferred to serve as the administrator of Lǎng Prefecture.
(This) laid the groundwork for Xīfàn to kill Xīgǎo.
9 Gāo Cónghuì sent an envoy to present a letter to Xú Zhīgào,
urging him to assume the imperial throne.
Gāo Cónghuì, with his meager three prefectures situated between Táng, Wú, and Shǔ,
coveted their rewards and gifts,
and declared himself a subject to whichever direction he faced.
The various states called him
"Gāo the Shameless,"
and there was a reason for it.
10 Earlier,
Shí Jìngtáng wanted to test the intentions of the Táng ruler,
and repeatedly submitted memorials pleading his own frail health,
requesting to be relieved of his military authority,
and transferred to another military command;
military authority,
referring to the position of Northern Front Commander of Cavalry and Infantry.
(He was) transferred to command Yùn Prefecture.
Fáng Gǎo, Lǐ Sōng, Lǚ Qí, and others all strenuously advised against it,
believing it was not permissible,
and the Emperor hesitated for a long time.
In the fifth month,
on the night of Gēngyín,
Lǐ Sōng was on urgent leave outside the palace.
"Qǐngjí"
means requesting leave.
The Emperor discussed matters concerning Hé Dōng with him,
and Wényù said:
"There is a proverb:
'Building a house in the middle of the road,
it will not be completed in three years.'
This matter must be decided by Your Majesty's own will;
the ministers are all concerned with their own interests,
how could they speak their minds fully!
In my view,
whether Hé Dōng is transferred or not, it will rebel,
it is only a matter of time,
it would be better to plan ahead."
Prior to this,
a diviner said that the state this year would obtain a worthy assistant,
who would devise extraordinary strategies,
and stabilize the realm.
The Emperor believed Wényù was the one,
and upon hearing his words,
was greatly pleased,
and said:
"Your words greatly clarify my thoughts,
success or failure, I have decided to act."
He immediately drafted the appointment list,
and ordered the Academy of Scholars to draft the edict.
Appointments personally written by the imperial brush and issued externally are called "chúmù,"
those submitted by the chief ministers for approval and then implemented are also called "chúmù."
On Xīnmǎo,
(the Emperor) appointed Jìngtáng as the Military Commissioner of Tiānpíng,
and appointed the Commander of the Imperial Guard Cavalry and Military Commissioner of Héyáng, Sòng Shěnqián, as the Military Commissioner of Hé Dōng.
Sòng Shěnqián had followed the Táng ruler since Fèngxiáng,
so (the Emperor) wanted to use him to replace Jìngtáng.
Upon hearing Jìngtáng's name called,
the officials of both ranks looked at each other, their faces turning pale.
"Liǎng bān"
refers to the civil and military official ranks.
On Jiǎwǔ,
(the Emperor) appointed the Military Commissioner of Jiànxióng, Zhāng Jìngdá, as the Commander of Northwestern Barbarian and Chinese Cavalry and Infantry,
to hasten Jìngtáng's departure to Yùn Prefecture.
Jìngtáng was suspicious and fearful,
and consulted with his generals and aides, saying:
"When I returned to Hé Dōng again,
His Majesty personally promised never to replace me;
(This statement by the Táng ruler was likely made at the beginning of his reign,
when Jìngtáng came to court and was sent back to his command.)
Could it be like what was said this year during the Thousand Springs Festival with the Princess?
I am not starting a rebellion,
but the court is provoking it.
How can I just wait to die on the road with my hands tied!
For now, let us submit a memorial pleading illness to observe their intentions.
If they are lenient with me,
I will serve them;
if they send troops against me,
then I will change my plans."
Judging from Jìngtáng's words here,
seeking aid from the Qìdān was a premeditated plan in his heart,
and Sāng Wéihàn's words merely coincided with his intentions.
Jìngtáng, because of his simple and straightforward nature,
did not blame him.
The Administrative Assistant of the Military Commission, Zhào Yíng of Huáyīn, urged Jìngtáng to proceed to Yùn Prefecture;
the Surveillance Assistant, Xuē Róng of Píngyáo, said:
"I am a scholar,
unfamiliar with military affairs."
The Chief Bailiff Liú Zhīyuǎn said:
"My Lord, you have long commanded troops,
and have won the hearts of the soldiers;
now you hold a strategically advantageous location,
with elite troops and strong horses.
If you raise troops and issue a proclamation,
'chēng'
means to raise.
How can you throw yourself into the tiger's mouth because of a single sheet of an appointment edict!"
The Secretary, Sāng Wéihàn of Luòyáng, said:
"When His Majesty first ascended the throne,
and you, My Lord, entered the court,
did His Majesty not know that a flood dragon cannot be released into the deep abyss?
There is an ancient saying: A fish cannot leave the deep waters,
a divine dragon that loses its power
is no different from an earthworm.
This is Heaven's will lending you a sharp weapon.
The late Emperor Míngzōng left behind affection among the people,
while the current ruler, being a son of a concubine who replaced him,
does not have the people's heartfelt support.
You, My Lord, are the beloved son-in-law of Emperor Míngzōng.
Now the current ruler treats you as a rebel,
this is not something that can be avoided by merely confessing and apologizing.
You must strive for a plan to preserve yourself.
The Qìdān
have long sworn brotherhood with Emperor Míngzōng,
and now their tribes are near Yún and Yìng.
(The Qìdān royal tent had been stationed at Nàlà Lake since the third year of the Chángxīng era of Emperor Míngzōng.)
In case of emergency,
they can be summoned in the morning and arrive by evening.
Why worry about not succeeding?"
Jìngtáng's mind was thus made up.
Earlier,
the court was suspicious of Jìngtáng,
and appointed the General of the Yǔlín Guards, Yáng Yànxún of Bǎodǐng, as the Deputy Military Commissioner of Běijīng,
(Bǎodǐng County belonged to Hézhōng Prefecture,
it was Fényīn County of the Hàn Dynasty.
In the twenty-first year of the Kāiyuán era of Emperor Xuánzōng of Táng, when sacrificing at Fényīn,
a precious tripod was obtained,
hence the name was changed.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì: In the fourth year of the Dàzhōng Xiángfú era of the Sòng Dynasty, Bǎodǐng was renamed Rónghé County,
located one hundred lǐ north of Hézhōng Prefecture.)
(Jìngtáng) also confided the situation to him.
Yànxún said:
"I do not know how many troops and provisions Hé Dōng has,
can they withstand the court?"
Those around (Jìngtáng) requested to kill Yànxún,
but Jìngtáng said:
"I alone guarantee the safety of the Deputy Commissioner,
do not speak of this anymore."
According to the Old History of the Five Dynasties, Yáng Yànxún was a deep and steady person,
and it was likely because of this that he was spared.
On the Wùxū day,
Huángfǔ Lì, the military commissioner of Zhāoyì, reported that Shí Jìngtáng had rebelled.
The two military districts of Bìng and Lù shared a border,
so he learned of the matter and reported it first.
“The Emperor is an adopted son,
and should not inherit the sacrifices,
I request that the throne be passed to Prince Xǔ.”
Prince Xǔ was Cóng Yì,
the son of Emperor Míngzōng.
The Emperor responded with an edict saying:
“You, sir, were certainly not distant from Prince È,
the events at Wèizhōu,
are known throughout the world;
it is said that Shí Jìngtáng killed all the mounted attendants of Emperor Mǐn,
and left the Emperor alone in Wèizhōu.
The event is recorded in the first year of Qīngtài in the previous scroll.
Prince È refers to Emperor Mǐn.
When Prince Lù ascended the throne,
he issued an order through the Empress Dowager demoting Emperor Mǐn to Prince È.
Who would believe it!”
On the Rényín day,
an imperial decree was issued stripping Shí Jìngtáng of his official titles and ranks.
On the Yǐsì day,
Zhāng Jìngdá was appointed as the concurrent commander of the four sides’ battle formations at Tàiyuán,
Zhāng Yànqí, the military commissioner of Héyáng, was appointed as the commander of the cavalry and infantry armies,
Ān Shěnqí, the military commissioner of Ānguó, was appointed as the commander of the cavalry army,
Xiànglǐ Jīn, the military commissioner of Bǎoyì, was appointed as the commander of the infantry army,
and Wǔ Tínghàn, the senior general of the Right Gate Guard, was appointed as the commander of the trenches and fortifications.
On the Bǐngwǔ day,
Zhāng Jìngdá was appointed as the overall commander of the four sides’ military forces at Tàiyuán,
with Yáng Guāngyuǎn, the military commissioner of Yìwǔ, as his deputy commander.
This sets the stage for Yáng Guāngyuǎn killing Zhāng Jìngdá and surrendering to Jìn.
On the Dīngwèi day,
Zhāng Jìngdá was further appointed to oversee the administrative affairs of the Tàiyuán headquarters,
and Gāo Xíngzhōu, the former military commissioner of Zhāngwǔ, was appointed as the pacification and battle formation commander for the four sides of Tàiyuán.
After Yáng Guāngyuǎn departed,
there was a mutiny in the Dìngzhōu army,
which was suppressed by the deputy general Qiānchéng Fāngtài.
The Hàn dynasty established the state of Qiānchéng,
later changed to the commandery of Lè’ān,
the Suí dynasty abolished the commandery of Lè’ān and established Qiānchéng County,
which belonged to Qīngzhōu during the Táng.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Qiānchéng County is eighty lǐ north of Qīngzhōu.
The character “乘”
is pronounced as “shèng.”
Zhāng Jìngdá led thirty thousand troops and encamped at Jìn’ānxiāng,
Jìn’ānxiāng is south of Jìnyáng City.
According to the Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ,
the Jìn’ānzhài is south of Jìncí.
On the Wùshēn day,
Jìngdá reported that Ān Shěnxìn, the commander of the northwest vanguard cavalry, had defected and fled to Jìnyáng.
Shěnxìn
was the nephew of Ān Jīnquán,
and Shí Jìngtáng had a prior relationship with him.
The Ān clan’s followers and Shí Jìngtáng were originally both from the area north of Dài.
Ān Yuánxìn, the commander of the Xióngyì army from Mǎyì,
led over six hundred of his troops to garrison Dàizhōu,
and the prefect of Dàizhōu, Zhāng Lǎng, treated him well.
Yuánxìn secretly advised Lǎng, saying:
“I observe that Lord Shí is a man of integrity,
and his undertaking is sure to succeed;
why don’t you secretly send someone to convey your intentions,
so you can preserve yourself.”
Lǎng did not agree,
and from then on they became suspicious of each other.
Yuánxìn plotted to kill Lǎng,
but did not succeed,
so he led his troops to join Shěnxìn,
and Shěnxìn then led several hundred cavalry under his command, along with Yuánxìn, to plunder Bǎijǐng and flee to Jìnyáng.
Jìngtáng said to Yuánxìn:
“What advantages or disadvantages did you see,
to abandon the strong and join the weak?”
He replied:
“Yuánxìn does not know astrology or read omens,
but judges based on human affairs.
What the Son of Heaven uses to rule the world,
nothing is more important than trust.
Now the Emperor has broken great trust with you, my lord,
even those who are close and noble cannot protect themselves,
Shí Jìngtáng is the Emperor’s son-in-law,
which can be considered close;
he holds the office of Zhōngshū Lìng,
commands armies with authority,
and controls the northern region exclusively,
which can be considered noble.
His downfall can be expected imminently,
what strength does he have!”
Jìngtáng was pleased,
and entrusted him with military affairs.
Ān Zhòngróng, the northwest patrol inspector of Zhènwǔ, garrisoned north of Dài,
according to the Xīn Wǔdài Shǐ,
Ān Zhòngróng was the border patrol commander of Zhènwǔ.
The character “帥”
is read as “shuài”;
the same applies below.
He was from Shuòzhōu.
Sòng Shěnqián was appointed as the military commissioner of Níngguó and concurrently commander of the imperial guard cavalry.
Since Shí Jìngtáng refused to be replaced,
Sòng Shěnqián was therefore given command and put in charge of the palace guard.
Shěnqián
was a deputy general when the Táng ruler was stationed at Fèngxiáng.
The military commissioner of Tiānxióng, Liú Yánghào, relied on the influence of the empress’s clan,
and became arrogant and unrestrained,
Liú Yánghào
was the younger brother of the Táng ruler’s empress.
He reduced the provisions and rewards for the officers and soldiers,
and indulged in endless feasting and drinking.
Zhāng Lìngzhāo, the deputy commander of the Pěngshèng army, took advantage of the soldiers’ resentment and anger,
and plotted to respond to Hédōng with the forces of Wèibó.
On the Guǐchǒu day before dawn,
he led his troops to attack the administrative city,
and captured it;
Yánghào escaped with his life,
and the mutinous soldiers looted extensively.
Lìngzhāo reported:
“Yánghào failed in his governance and control,
leading to the army’s mutiny;
I have already pacified the soldiers,
and temporarily taken charge of the military government,
“I have already”
the character “以”
in
should be
When Yánghào reached Luòyáng,
the Táng ruler was angry,
and ordered him exiled to a distant place;
the empress pleaded on his behalf,
and in the sixth month,
on the Gēngshēn day,
he was only stripped of his official titles and ranks,
and sent back to his private residence.
On the Xīnyǒu day,
Xú Jǐngqiān, the Grand Guardian and concurrent Chief Minister of Wú, was dismissed due to illness,
and his younger brother Jǐngsuì replaced him as Vice Director of the Chancellery and participant in administrative affairs.
On the Guǐhài day,
the Táng ruler appointed Zhāng Lìngzhāo as General of the Right Thousand Bull Guard and acting administrator of the Tiānxióng military government.
Lìngzhāo, because the mobilization of troops was not yet complete,
temporarily accepted the new appointment.
Soon an edict was issued transferring him to be the defense commissioner of Qízhōu,
but Lìngzhāo used the excuse that the soldiers detained him,
actually waiting to see the outcome of Hédōng’s situation.
The Táng ruler sent an envoy to instruct him,
but Lìngzhāo killed the envoy.
On the Jiǎxū day,

Fàn Yánguāng, the military commissioner of Xuānwǔ and concurrent Zhōngshū Lìng, was appointed as the pacification commissioner of the Tiānxióng four sides campaign and administrator of the Wèibó headquarters,
“Wèibó”
probably should be
“Wèizhōu”.
Yáng Guāngyuǎn was appointed as his deputy.
On the Bǐngzǐ day,
Lǐ Zhōu, the left-behind of the Western Capital, was appointed as the deputy pacification commissioner of the Tiānxióng four sides campaign.
Shí Jìngtáng’s sons, the senior general of the Right Guard, Chóng Yīn, and the deputy commissioner of the Imperial City, Chóng Yì, heard that Jìngtáng had raised troops,
and hid in a well among the common people.
His younger brother, the commander of Yízhōu, Jìngdé, killed his wife and daughters and fled,
but was soon captured,
and died in prison,
while his cousin, the commander of the Zhāngshèng army, Jìngwēi, committed suicide.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the Wùzǐ day,
Chóng Yīn and Chóng Yì were captured,
and executed,
along with the families that had hidden them.
On the Gēngyín day,
the King of Chǔ, Xīfàn, returned north from Guìzhōu.
He arrived in Guìzhōu in the fourth month,
and returned in the seventh month.
The character “還”
is pronounced as “xuán,”
or also as “huán.”
Sāng Qiān, the infantry commander of Yúnzhōu, reported that Yǐn Huī, the military commissioner of Yìngzhōu, had expelled Shā Yànxún, the military commissioner of Yúnzhōu,

Jìngtáng did not heed his advice.

The Khitan ruler was greatly pleased,

"My son recently dreamed that Shí Láng sent an envoy here,"

"Bǐ,"
pronounced as pí zhì fān,
means 'recently.'
This is the will of Heaven."
From this time onward,
the Liáo destroyed the Jìn,
the Jīn shattered the Sòng,
(original text missing sixteen characters.
) The present territorial extent,

Was it truly the will of Heaven!
They promised to mobilize their entire nation to come to his aid by mid-autumn.

on the day Jǐwèi,

Yáng Guāngyuǎn's plan,

Soon after, the Khitan advanced directly in,

The Emperor, hearing that the Khitan had promised Shí Jìngtáng aid by mid-autumn,

Whenever they attempted construction works,

Within Jìnyáng, the situation grew increasingly desperate by the day,
and food supplies gradually dwindled.
Had Khitan reinforcements not arrived,
Jìn could not have held out.

Yángwǔ Valley is in Guō County, Dàizhōu.

Dàizhōu Prefect Zhāng Lǎng and Xīnzhōu Prefect Dīng Shěnqí defended their walled cities and held firm,

Shěnqí
was from Míngzhōu.

unarmored,

The Táng troops advanced along the bank,

The infantry in the north were mostly killed by the Khitan,

The Khitan unleashed their troops to press the advantage,

Nearly ten thousand infantry perished,

Jìngdá and others gathered the remaining troops and defended Jìn'ān,

Jìngtáng obtained over a thousand Táng soldiers who had surrendered.
Liú Zhīyuǎn urged Jìngtáng to kill them all.
Although the Táng forces were defeated,
their numbers were still substantial.
Liú Zhīyuǎn feared the surrendered soldiers would rebel and return,

That evening,
Jìngtáng went out of the north gate,
(the north gate of Jìnyáng city)
The Khitan ruler grasped Jìngtáng's hand,
regretting they had not met sooner.
As they had not met face-to-face before this,
this was natural,
and it must also be that Shí Jìngtáng's bearing and appearance were imposing enough to command his gaze.
"The Emperor has come from afar,

The Khitan ruler said:

They did none of it,
so I was able to drive deep and far,

Once the armies clashed,
my morale was at its peak,
while theirs was just faltering.
If I did not seize this moment to strike swiftly,
(meaning he should exploit the sharpness of his newly arrived troops and use their vanguard.)

Jìngtáng greatly admired and submitted to this.
On the Rényín day,
Jǐngtáng led his troops to join the Khitan in besieging the Jìn'ān Stockade.

Zhāng Jìngdá and his troops still numbered fifty thousand men,

The Art of War states: Place them in a death ground, and they will fight to live.
If Zhāng Jìngdá and the others could have, before the encirclement was fully formed,
encouraged and instructed the officers and soldiers,
exerting their utmost strength in a desperate battle,
victory or defeat would have been uncertain.

The Táng sovereign was greatly alarmed,

Qīngshān,

"Jiū,"
is the same as
"jiū"

Referring to the troops of commanders Fàn Yánguāng, Zhào Déjūn, and Pán Huán.

Zhāng Yánlǎng wanted to use this opportunity to allow Zhào Yánshòu to be relieved of his Privy Council duties.
Zhào Yánshòu was then serving as Privy Councilor,

"Wénjì's words are correct."

Zhāng Yánlǎng and Hanlin Academician Xūchāng Hé Níng and others

If the court issued an open proclamation about this,

An open proclamation means
intending to let the Khitan know.

This was also a strategy to lift the siege.
The Emperor deeply agreed,

The Emperor's worry and dejection showed in his expression,

"Do not speak of it,

When Lǐ Sìyuán raised troops toward Luò,
Zhuāngzōng's expression showed dismay;
when Shí Jìngtáng held troops and defied orders,
the Prince of Lù said it made his heart and courage fall to the ground.
Why were they so brave facing the enemy in ordinary times,

It seems that between Zhuāngzōng and Míngzōng,
and between the Prince of Lù and the Jìn founder,
all had moved through the battlefield together,
and inwardly assessing their intelligence and strength, none greatly surpassed the others.
But seizing the moment and utilizing circumstances occasionally fell short for some,
and thus their morale faltered first.
In winter, the tenth month,
on the Rénxū day,
an edict was issued to extensively requisition horses from all military officers and the common people;
also, commoners were conscripted as soldiers,
with one conscripted man from every seven households,

Reward,
kǔ dào fān.

31. The former Prefect of Fāngzhōu, Liú Jǐngyán,
was from Yánzhōu.
He was wealthy and fond of chivalry,

His household had able-bodied men and weapons,

Yáng Hànzhāng, the Military Governor of Zhāngwǔ, governed poorly,

"I have come three thousand lǐ to aid in your difficulty,
and must achieve success.

you are truly the ruler of the Central Plains."
When the Khitan sovereign first came to aid in the difficulty,

At that time, he certainly perceived it in his immediate presence.
When they besieged Jìn'ān,

he did not merely take his demeanor and appearance,

Shí Jìngtáng probably ascended the throne wearing northern attire.
On that day,
he assumed the position of Emperor.
Examination of discrepancies: The Veritable Records of the Deposed Emperor states:

is recorded in the Táng History.

People all consider the Shí Jìn's cession of the sixteen prefectures as the beginning of the north dismantling its own defensive barriers.
I say that the various prefectures north of Yànmén,
abandoning them still left passes and strategic points that could be defended.
During the Jiàn'ān era of the Hàn, amidst turmoil,
the lands north of the Xíng Pass were abandoned,

If Yān, Jì, Shùn, and other prefectures were ceded,

the Táng ruler ordered Héyáng military commissioner Cháng Cóngjiǎn and Zhàozhōu prefect Liú Zàimíng to defend the southern city of Héyáng,
then severed the pontoon bridge,
and returned to Luòyáng.
He sent the eunuch Qín Jìmín and the imperial city commissioner Lǐ Yànshēn to kill Zhāoxìn military commissioner Lǐ Zànhuá at his residence.
Lǐ Zànhuá was
the elder brother of the Qìdān ruler,
hence they killed him.
39 On the jǐmǎo day,
the Emperor arrived at Héyáng,
Cháng Cóngjiǎn came out to surrender,
and boats were already prepared.
Although the Táng ruler had severed the river bridge,
Cháng Cóngjiǎn prepared boats to ferry the Jìn troops across.
(Note on pronunciation for 降:
hù jiāng fān.)
The Zhāngshèng army were likely those left to garrison Héyáng.
He sent them back to their original posts.

40 The Táng ruler ordered cavalry commander-in-chief Sòng Shěnqián, infantry commander-in-chief Fú Yànráo, Héyáng military commissioner Zhāng Yànqí, and Xuānhuī Southern Court commissioner Liú Yánlǎng to lead over a thousand cavalry to Báimǎ Bǎn to survey the battleground,
(This is Bái Sīmǎ Bǎn,
located north of Luòyáng.
The history text omits
the character "司"
(Note on pronunciation for 行:
xià mèng fān.)
They fled to the northern army.
(This northern army refers to the Jìn troops who came from Tàiyuán to Héyáng.)
"What place cannot be fought in,
who is willing to stand here?"
(This indicates the people's hearts were already alienated.)
On the gēngchén day,
the Táng ruler again discussed with the four generals about returning to Héyáng,
(the four generals refer to Sòng Shěnqián and the other three.)
(Note on pronunciation for 復:
fú yòu fān.)
The Emperor, concerned the Táng ruler might flee west,
sent a thousand Qìdān cavalry to block Miǎnchí.
On the xīnsì day,
the Táng ruler, along with Empress Dowager Cáo, Empress Liú, Prince Yōng Chóngměi, and Sòng Shěnqián, carrying the imperial seal, ascended the Xuánwǔ Tower and immolated themselves.
He was fifty-one years old.
Sòng Shěnqián had started the uprising with the Táng ruler at Fèngxiáng,
he was a close commander,
therefore he died with him.
(Note on pronunciation for 雍:
yú yòng fān.)
(This Empress refers to the Táng ruler's Empress Liú.)
"When the new Son of Heaven arrives,
he certainly will not live in the open,
it will later heavily burden the people's labor;
to die and leave behind resentment,
what use is that!"
So they stopped.
Wáng Shù said to the Empress Dowager:
"The situation is critical,
we should hide for now,
and wait for your brother-in-law."
(The Empress Dowager is Empress Dowager Cáo.
Brother-in-law refers to the Emperor.
The Empress is the daughter of Empress Dowager Cáo,
hence Wáng Shù told her to hide and wait for the Emperor's arrival.)
"That my descendants, women, have come to this in one day,
(Son refers to the Táng ruler;
grandson refers to Chóngměi;
wife refers to Empress Liú;
daughter refers to the Táng ruler's daughter.)
Younger sister, do your best."
Shù then hid with Prince Xǔ Cóngyì at the polo field,
and escaped harm.
That evening,
the Emperor entered Luòyáng,
and stayed at his old residence.
The Táng soldiers all removed their armor and awaited punishment,
the Emperor comforted and released them.
The Emperor ordered Liú Zhīyuǎn to take charge of the capital,
Zhīyuǎn sent the Hàn troops back to their camps,
quartered the Qìdān at Tiāngōng Temple,
the city was orderly,
no one dared violate orders.
Scholars and commoners who had fled and hidden to avoid the chaos,
returned within a few days to resume their livelihoods.
(The history records Liú Zhīyuǎn's talent and strategy.)
Earlier,
when the Emperor was in Hédōng,
he was distrusted by the Táng court,
the Vice Director of the Secretariat, concurrent Tongpingzhangshi, and administrator of the Three Departments, Zhāng Yánlǎng, did not want Hédōng to accumulate much wealth,
so he collected all finances and taxes beyond what was designated for local military use.
(Under the Táng system, the finances and taxes of each prefecture were divided into three parts:
one part for tribute to the central government,
sent to the capital for imperial use;
two parts sent to the military commissioner,
delivered to the military commissioner and observation commissioner offices;
three parts retained by the prefecture,
kept for prefectural expenses.
Later, when the empire was entirely divided among military governors,
subordinate prefectures still called their portion 'retained by the prefecture',
while the headquarters prefecture called theirs 'retained for the commissioner'.
[Note on pronunciation for 朝:
zhí yáo fān.]
[Note on pronunciation for 使:
shū lì fān.])
On the rénwǔ day,
all officials came for an audience,
only Yánlǎng was seized and handed over to the Censorate,
the rest all gave thanks for imperial grace.
(The Hàn dynasty's Féng Yǎn once said: others hate it when I curse them,
I myself desire to curse others.
When the Jìn founder first entered Luòyáng and first seized Zhāng Yánlǎng,
not only did he show pettiness to the world,
it also was not a way to encourage officials to perform their duties faithfully.
Once executed, regret would be too late.)
On the jiǎshēn day,
the imperial carriage entered the palace,
and a great amnesty was declared:
"All officials, central and local, shall not be questioned,
only the treacherous ministers Zhāng Yánlǎng, Liú Yánhào, Liú Yánlǎng, for their villainy, corruption, and baseness,
their crimes cannot be pardoned;
Vice Director of the Secretariat and Tongpingzhangshi Mǎ Yǐnsūn, Chief of Staff Fáng Hào, Xuānhuī commissioner Lǐ Zhuānměi, Hézhōng military commissioner Hán Zhāoyìn, etc.,
although holding high positions,
did not engage in flattery and compliance,
are all pardoned and removed from office;
officials, central and local, who submitted earlier,
shall be separately appointed and employed by the Secretariat-Chancellery.")
Liú Yánhào hid at Lóngmén,
(Jiǔyù Zhì: Hénán prefecture, Hénán county has a Lóngmén town.)
and hanged himself.
Liú Yánlǎng was about to flee to the southern mountains,
(The southern mountains of Luò city are the Yīyáng mountains.)
and was killed.
Zhāng Yánlǎng was beheaded;
afterwards, when selecting a Three Departments commissioner,
finding a suitable person was difficult,
the Emperor deeply regretted it.
The people of Mǐn, hearing of the Táng ruler's demise,
sighed, saying:
"The crimes of the Prince of Lù,
were not heard of throughout the land,
what then of our own ruler!"
(The history records the deep resentment of the Mǐn people towards their ruler.)
41 In the twelfth month,
on the xīnyǒu day, the first day of the month,
the Emperor went to Héyáng,
to bid farewell to Grand Minister Wēn and the Qìdān troops returning to their country.
42 He posthumously demoted the Táng ruler to commoner status.
43 On the dīnghài day,
he appointed Féng Dào concurrently as Vice Director of the Chancellery and Tongpingzhangshi.
44 Cáozhōu prefect Zhèng Ruǎn was greedy and cruel,
commander Shí Chónglì took advantage of the chaos to kill him,
(Taking advantage of the chaos means taking advantage of the chaos in the Central Plains.)
(The history records that greedy and cruel people cannot escape not only in times of order,
but also in times of chaos.)
45 On the xīnmǎo day,
he appointed the former Táng Vice Director of the Secretariat Yáo Yǐ as Minister of Justice.
46 Earlier,
Shuòfāng military commissioner Zhāng Xīchóng governed with authority and trustworthiness,
the people and foreigners loved him,
he promoted garrison farms to reduce water transport;
after five years in his post,
he requested an inward transfer,
the Táng Prince of Lù appointed him as Jìngnán military commissioner.
The Emperor, making peace with the Qìdān,
feared they might again seize Língwǔ,
(The Qìdān, having obtained Yān and Yún,
might take advantage of the situation to also seize Língwǔ.)
(Note on pronunciation for 好:
hū dào fān.)
(Note on pronunciation for 復:
fú yòu fān.)
On the guǐsì day,
he again appointed Xīchóng as Shuòfāng military commissioner.
47. Initially,
Chéngdé Jiedushi Dǒng Wēnqí was greedy and cruel,
amassing goods worth tens of thousands,
and took the Yánèi Dūyúhòu of Píngshān, Mì Qióng, as his confidant.
Píngshān County belonged to Zhènzhōu,
originally the Suí-established Fángshān County.
At the end of the Táng Tiānbǎo era,
Ān Lùshān rebelled,
Emperor Xuánzōng changed Lùquán County to Huòlù,
and Fángshān County to Píngshān.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Píngshān is 65 lǐ west of the prefecture.
Zhào Déjūn invited Dǒng Wēnqí to jointly rescue Jìn'ān,
and they both perished together.
Buried in a single pit,
but his goods were taken.
An elephant has tusks, yet they cause its body to be burned;
it is because of the treasure.
This sets the stage for Mì Qióng being killed by Fàn Yánguāng.
Yì,
read as yú jì fān.
A memorial reported a military mutiny.
48. Tóngzhōu junior officer Mén Duó killed Jiedushi Yáng Hànbīn,
burning and plundering the prefectural city.
The Hénán Guānshì Zhì states: Later Wèi changed the Chìmén clan to the Mén clan.
Also, the Tǔmén clan was changed to the Mén clan,
and the Kùmén clan was changed to the Mén clan.
Xiào,
read as hù jiào fān.
49. An edict posthumously honored Lǐ Zànhuá as Prince of Yān,
and sent an envoy to escort his coffin back to his country.
50. Zhāng Lǎng led his troops to the court.
When the Emperor first raised his cause,
Zhāng Lǎng guarded Dàizhōu,
and did not submit.
Jiàng,
read as jí liàng fān.
51. On Gēngzǐ,
appointed the Táng Zhōngshū Shìláng Lú Wénjì as Lìbù Shàngshū.
Appointed Huángchéngshǐ of Jìnyáng, Zhōu Huái, as Dàjiāngjūn and concurrently Sānsīshǐ;
Huái declined, saying:
"I know my own talent is not equal to the post;
I would rather be abandoned for avoiding duties,
than to incur guilt by presuming upon favor."
The Emperor permitted it.
52. The Emperor heard that Pínglú Jiedushi Fáng Zhīwēn had died,
and dispatched Tiānpíng Jiedushi Wáng Jiànlì to lead troops to pacify Qīngzhōu.
This was to guard against changes.
Jiàng,
read as jí liàng fān;
same below.
53. Changed Xīngtángfǔ to Guǎngjìnfǔ.
Later Táng changed Wèizhōu to Xīngtángfǔ,
when Jìn arose,
it was changed again to Guǎngjìnfǔ,
changing the prefecture name with the change of dynasty.
54. Ānyuǎn Jiedushi Lú Wénjìn heard that the Emperor had been established by the Qìdān,
and considering himself originally a Qìdān rebel general,
Lú Wénjìn fled from the Qìdān,
see scroll 275, Míngzōng Tiānchéng first year.
On Xīnchǒu,
he abandoned his garrison and fled to Wú.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Ānzhōu is 400 lǐ east to Huángzhōu,
and 360 lǐ southeast to Èzhōu.
Huáng and È were both Wú territory.
He summoned his main generals,
informed them of the reason,
and they all bowed farewell and withdrew.
55. Xú Zhīgào, considering Zhènnán Jiedushi‧Tàiwèi concurrently Zhōngshū Lìng Lǐ Déchéng, and Déshèng Jiedushi concurrently Zhōngshū Lìng Zhōu Běn to be of high prestige and standing,
wanted them to lead the masses in supporting him.
Běn said:
"I received great kindness from the Former King,
the Former King referred to by Zhōu Běn
is Yáng Xíngmì.
Shuài,
read as shuài.
I regret being unable to save the Yáng clan in their peril,
and now you want me to do this?
How can I!"
His son Hóngzuò pressured him,
and reluctantly, together with Déchéng, he led the generals to Jiāngdū to petition the Wú ruler,
extolling Zhīgào's merits and virtue,
requesting the performance of the investiture ceremony;
and also went to Jīnlíng to urge accession.
Sòng Qíqiū said to Déchéng's son Jiànxūn:
"Your honored father,
a founding meritorious minister of Tàizǔ,
Yáng Xíngmì of Wú was given the temple name Tàizǔ.
At that time, there were many strange occurrences in the Wú palace,
the Wú palace,
meaning the Jiāngdū palace.
Yāo,
read as yī yáo fān.
"Is the Wú mandate about to end!"
Those around said:
"This is Heaven's will,
not human affairs."
56. Gāolì King Wáng Jiàn used troops to defeat Xīnlú and Bǎijì,
and then all the Eastern Yi states submitted to him.
He had two capitals,
six prefectures,
nine military districts,
and one hundred and twenty commanderies.
Wáng Jiàn obtaining Gāolì is seen in scroll 271, Liáng Jūnwáng Lóngdé third year.

Tiānfú second year (Dīngyǒu, 937)
1. Spring,
first month,
Yǐmǎo,
there was a solar eclipse.
Examination of discrepancies says: The Veritable Records state:
"First month, Jiǎyín first day, Yǐmǎo solar eclipse."
The Shíguó Jìnián states:
"Shǔ, Yǐmǎo first day solar eclipse."
Probably the Jìn people changed the calendar to avoid a solar eclipse on the three dynasties' first day.
2. An edict appointed the former Běimiàn Zhāoshōu Zhǐhuīshǐ Ān Zhòngróng
This refers to the military post Ān Zhòngróng was granted during the siege of Jìnyáng,
hence called 'former'.
Zhòng,
read as zhí lóng fān.
At that time, Mì Qióng made himself Liúhòu of Chéngdé,
and Ān Zhòngróng replaced him.
Mì,
is a surname;
between Hàn and Wèi there was Nán'ān Mì Yí.
Zhòngróng went to Zhènzhōu together with the Qìdān general Zhào Sīwēn,
and Qióng dared not refuse the order.
Fearing the Qìdān.
On Bǐngchén,
Zhòngróng memorialized that he had assumed office.
This sets the stage for Ān Zhòngróng's rebellion from Chéngdé.
He was from Xíngzhōu.
3. The Qìdān made Yōuzhōu their Nánjīng.
Ōu Shǐ says: Made Yōuzhōu Yānjīng.
Considering Zhào Sīwēn being Liúshǒu,
then Nánjīng is correct.
4. Lǐ Sōng and Lǚ Qí fled and hid among the common people of Yīquē.
The Emperor, because when he first governed Hé dōng,
Sōng had been instrumental,
felt grateful to him;
Lǐ Sōng's proposal for the Emperor to govern Hé dōng
is seen in scroll 278, Táng Míngzōng Chángxīng third year.
Lǐ Sōng and Lǚ Qí proposed making peace with the Qìdān to control Hé dōng,
see last scroll, last year, third month.
On Yǐchǒu,
appointed Qí as Mìshū Jiān;
on Bǐngyín,
appointed Sōng as Bīngbù Shìláng and concurrently in charge of Hùbù.
5. Initially, when Tiānxióng Jiedushi concurrently Zhōngshū Lìng Fàn Yánguāng was still obscure,
a fortune-teller, Zhāng Shēng, told him:
"You will certainly become a general and minister."
After Yánguāng became eminent,
he trusted and valued him.
Yánguāng once dreamed a snake entered his belly from his navel,
and asked Zhāng Shēng about it.
Zhāng Shēng said:
"The snake is the dragon,
an omen of the emperor."
From then on, Yánguāng harbored improper ambitions.
The Táng Lùwáng had always been on good terms with Yánguāng,
and after Zhào Déjūn's defeat,
Yánguāng led troops from Liáozhōu back to Wèizhōu,
Zhào Déjūn's defeat seen last scroll, last year, intercalary eleventh month.
Fàn Yánguāng stationed at Liáozhōu seen last year, tenth month;
his return to Wèizhōu must also have been in the intercalary eleventh month.
Internally uneasy,
he secretly contacted Mì Qióng by letter,
wanting to join him in rebellion;
Qióng received his letter but did not reply,
and Yánguāng resented him.
When Qióng was about to go to Qí,
passing through Wèi territory,
Yánguāng wanted to silence him,
and also coveted his goods,
sent troops to intercept him at Xiàjīn,
and killed him.
This sets the stage for Fàn Yánguāng's rebellion from Wèi,
and again, for his goods causing him to be killed by Yáng Guāngyuǎn.
Xiàjīn,
ancient Shū County,
Táng Tiānbǎo first year renamed Xiàjīn,
belonged to Bèizhōu;
Sòng placed Xiàjīn under Běijīng,
250 lǐ northeast of the capital.
Xià,
read as hù yǎ fān.
On Dīngmǎo,
Yánguāng memorialized that the bandit-catching troops at Xiàjīn had mistakenly killed Qióng;
the Emperor did not inquire.
6 On the Wùyín day,
Lǐ Sōng was appointed as Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāng Shì,
serving concurrently as Shūmì Shǐ,
while Sāng Wéihàn was also appointed as Shūmì Shǐ.
At that time, the Jìn dynasty had just gained control of the realm,
and many regional military governors had not yet submitted;
even among those who had submitted,
they were restless and uneasy.
In the aftermath of war,
the state treasury was exhausted,
the common people were impoverished,
and the Khitan made endless demands.
Sāng Wéihàn advised the emperor to be sincere and let go of grievances to pacify the regional governors,
to use humble words and generous gifts to serve the Khitan,
to train soldiers and repair weapons to strengthen military preparedness,
to focus on agriculture and sericulture to fill the granaries,
and to promote trade to enrich the treasury.
Within a few years,
the Central Plains became somewhat stable.
The historical record states that Sāng Wéihàn was beneficial to the early establishment of the Shí Jìn dynasty in this way.
Jiǎ,
pronounced gǔ.
7 The crown prince of Wú, Liǎn, married the daughter of Qí Wáng Zhīgào.
Zhīgào began building the Grand Ancestral Temple and the Altars of Soil and Grain,
changing Jīnlíng to Jiāngníng Fǔ.
Previously,
Wú had designated Shēngzhōu as Jīnlíng Fǔ,
and now it was renamed again.
The main hall was called the Diàn;
he appointed Left and Right Sīmǎ Sòng Qíqiū and Xú Jiè as Left and Right Chéngxiàng,
and Mǎbù Pànguān Zhōu Zōng and Nèishū Pànguān Yīxiàn native Zhōu Tíngyù as Nèishū Shǐ.
Yī,
a county from the Hàn dynasty,
belonged to Shèzhōu in the Táng dynasty.

Yī,
Yán Shīgǔ pronounced it as Yī,

and nine infantry armies.

the ruler of Wú appointed Lú Wénjìn as Xuānwǔ Jiédù Shǐ,
with Xuānwǔ Jūn stationed in Biànzhōu,

the ruler of Wú sent Yíyáng Wáng Zǎo to the Western Capital,

Zǎo,
pronounced zǐ hào fān.
The king received the imperial edict,

10 Yuán Guàn, the Shùnhuà Jiédù Shǐ and Tóng Píngzhāng Shì, who was the younger brother of Wúyuè King Yuán Guàn, offended Yuán Guàn,
and was demoted to a commoner.
The beginning of Qián Yuán Guàn's offense is recorded in volume 278, in the fourth year of Táng Míngzōng's Chángxīng era.
Guàn,
pronounced xiàng.
11 The Khitan ruler passed through Yúnzhōu from Shàngdǎng,
and Dàtóng Jiédù Shǐ Shā Yànxún went out to welcome him.
The Khitan ruler detained him,
not allowing him to return to his post.
The Jiédù Pànguān Wú Luán, who was in the city,
said to his people:
"We are people of a civilized and righteous society,
how can we submit to barbarians!"
The people pushed Luán to lead the prefecture's affairs,
closed the city gates, and refused to accept the Khitan's orders.
The Khitan attacked,
but could not capture it.
Guō Chóngwēi, the cavalry commander of Yìngzhōu and a native of Jīnchéng, also felt ashamed to submit to the Khitan,
and fled south.
The Jīnchéng of the Hàn dynasty
is the Wǔquán County of Lánzhōu in the Táng dynasty.
The Jīnchéng of the Táng dynasty
was originally the territory of Zhīyáng County in the Hàn dynasty.
During the Liáng dynasty, Guǎngwǔ Jùn was established there,
and in the Suí dynasty, the commandery was abolished and renamed Guǎngwǔ County.
In the second year of the Qiányuán era of the Táng dynasty, it was renamed Jīnchéng,
belonging to Lánzhōu.
However, this is not the Jīnchéng of Lánzhōu,
but the Jīnchéng County of Yìngzhōu.
Táng Míngzōng was born in Jīnfèngchéng in northern Dàiběi,
and after ascending the throne,
he established Jīnchéng County there,
and also established Yìngzhōu,
making it the administrative seat.
Guō Chóngwēi was likely a local appointed as the commander of this garrison.
Additionally, the Xīongnú Xūzhī states: Yìngzhōu is 850 lǐ east of Yōuzhōu;
Jīnchéng County is 800 lǐ northeast of Shuòzhōu.
According to the Xūzhī,
Yìngzhōu and Jīnchéng County seem to be two separate places,
completely unrelated to each other,
and it is unclear which is correct.
One must ask those who have been to the area for clarification.
Tǐng,
means to pull out.
The Khitan ruler passed through Xīnzhōu,
and ordered Wēisāi Jiédù Shǐ Zhái Zhāng to collect 100,000 strings of cash to reward the army.
Earlier,
when the Khitan ruler Ābǎojī grew powerful,
the Shìwéi, Xī, and Xí tribes all became his subjects.
The Xī chieftain Qùzhū suffered under the Khitan's greed and cruelty,
and led his people west to Guīzhōu,
relying on Liú Réngōng and his son,

the Western Xī moved to Guīzhōu,
settling near the northern mountains.
His son Sǎolá succeeded him.
When Táng Zhuāngzōng destroyed Liú Shǒuguāng,

fled to Shàowēi,
and Shàowēi took him in;
the Khitan grew angry,
attacked him,

After Shàowēi died,
his son Yèlá succeeded him.
When the Khitan ruler Déguāng returned north from Shàngdǎng,

At that time, Zhú Bùlǔ had also died,
and the Khitan ruler said:
"You are indeed innocent,
but Sǎolá and Zhú Bùlǔ betrayed me."

ground into powder, and scattered.
The various Xī tribes, fearing the Khitan's cruelty,
mostly fled or rebelled.
The Khitan ruler consoled Zhái Zhāng, saying:
"I will replace you,
and let you return south."
On the Jǐhài day,
Zhāng submitted a request to be summoned to the court.
However, the Khitan later sent Zhāng to lead troops to suppress the rebellious Xī and attack Yúnzhōu.
After achieving merit,
they detained him and did not allow him to leave.
Zhāng died in depression.
Zhāng Lì fled from the Khitan but was captured by pursuing cavalry.
The Khitan ruler reprimanded him, saying:
"Why did you abandon me?"
He replied:
"I am a Huá person,
and my food, clothing, and lifestyle are all different from here.
I would rather die than live like this,
so I wish to be executed soon."
The Khitan ruler turned to the interpreter Gāo Yànyīng and said:
"I have often warned you to treat this man well.
The Khitan appoint interpreters to manage Huá people,
selecting those familiar with Huá customs and language.
Sòng Bái said: The Khitan ruler's confidants who could speak Huá were called interpreters,
meaning they were well-versed in various affairs.
If I lose him,
how could I find another like him?"
He flogged Yànyīng and apologized to Lì.
Lì served the Khitan ruler with great loyalty and honesty,
speaking out on matters without hesitation,
and the Khitan ruler held him in high regard.
The historical record states that the Khitan ruler knew how to value Confucian scholars.
12 Earlier,
Yuán Guàn, the youngest son of Wúyuè King Liú,
had achieved several military merits,
and Liú rewarded him with weapons.
After Wúyuè King Yuán Guàn ascended the throne,
Yuán Guàn was appointed as Tǔkè Mǎbù Jūn Dū Zhǐhuī Shǐ
and concurrently Zhōngshū Lìng.
Relying on the emperor's favor, he became arrogant and domineering,
increasing his arsenal to several thousand weapons,
and many in the state sided with him.
Yuán Guàn grew suspicious of him
and sent someone to hint that Yuán Guàn should surrender his weapons
and be appointed as the administrator of Wēnzhōu.
Yuán Guàn refused.
An official of the Tóngguān Temple reported that Yuán Guàn had sent a trusted follower to pray to the gods,
asking to rule over Wúyuè's territory.
He also used wax-sealed messages passed through water channels
to conspire with his elder brother Yuán Guàn.
Wax-sealed messages refer to
wax-sealed letters,
where the letter is enclosed in a wax ball.
On the Wùwǔ day,
Yuán Guàn sent an envoy to summon Yuán Guàn to a banquet in the palace.
After he arrived,
attendants claimed that Yuán Guàn had a hidden blade in his sleeve,
and he was immediately killed.
Yuán Guàn was also executed.
Yuán Guàn had been imprisoned (see volume 278, in the fourth year of Táng Míngzōng's Chángxīng era).
His son Rénjùn advised:
"In the past, when Guāngwǔ defeated Wáng Láng,
and Cáo Gōng defeated Yuán Shào,
they both burned their correspondence to calm the restless.
Guāngwǔ's story is recorded in volume 39, in the second year of Hàn Gēngshǐ.
Cáo Gōng's story is recorded in volume 64, in the fifth year of Xiàndì's Jiàn'ān era."
Yuán Guàn followed his advice.
Someone obtained the pelvic and thigh bones of the Táng Lù Wáng and presented them.
On the day of Gēngshēn,
an imperial edict was issued to bury him with royal rites south of Huīlíng.
When the funeral of the Mǐn Emperor of Táng was at Huīlíng,
the grave was barely a few feet deep,
and those who saw it mourned.
When Lù Wáng was buried south of Huīlíng,
no one mourned him,
perhaps because of the fairness of public opinion!
The emperor sent an envoy to Shǔ to announce his ascension,
and to confirm marital ties;
the ruler of Shǔ, Mèng Zhīxiáng, was also the son-in-law of the Later Táng emperor,
the Shǔ ruler married a niece of Jìn Wáng Kèyòng,
the emperor married the daughter of Emperor Míngzōng,
thus establishing a brotherly bond with the successor of Shǔ,
thereby formalizing marital ties.
The use of "hǎo" is pronounced similar to "fān."
They exchanged diplomatic ceremonies of a rival state.
Fàn Yánguāng gathered soldiers and reinforced defenses,
summoning all the regional inspectors of Wèizhōu,
with five prefects from Bèi, Bó, Wèi, Chán, and Xiāng states.
The emperor planned to move the capital to Dàliáng,
Sāng Wéihàn stated:
"Dàliáng connects to Yàn and Zhào in the north,
links to the Jiāng and Huái rivers in the south,
being a hub for both land and water trade,
with abundant resources.
Now that Yánguāng's rebellion is evident,
Dàliáng is only ten relays away from Wèi,
according to Táng's system,
a relay is thirty lǐ,
ten relays,
three hundred lǐ.
The army will soon arrive,
a situation like ‘a thunderclap leaving no time to cover one's ears.’”
On the day of Bǐngyín,
an edict was issued,
justifying the move to Luòyáng's supply disruptions,
to tour Biànzhōu.
Wú Xú Zhīgào established his son Jǐngtōng as heir apparent;
he firmly declined the position.
He honored his father Zhōngwǔ Wáng Wēn as Tàizǔ Wǔ Wáng,
and his mother Lady Lǐ of Míngdé as the Queen Mother.
On Rénshēn,
he changed his name from Zhào to something simpler.
On the day of Gēngchén,
the emperor departed Luòyáng,
leaving the former Shuòfāng Military Commissioner Zhāng Cóngbīn as the inspector of the Eastern Capital.
The Hàn ruler recovered from illness,
granting a general amnesty.
Jiāozhōu's general Jiǎo Gōngxiàn killed the military commissioner Yáng Tíngyì of Ānnán to replace him.
In the second year of Chángxìng, Yáng Tíngyì obtained Jiāozhōu,
see the records of Táng Míngzōng.
Jiǎo is a surname.
In the summer,
in April,
on the day of Bǐngxū,
the emperor arrived in Biànzhōu;
on Dīnghài,
a general amnesty was granted.
The King of Wúyuè Yuánguàn restored the state,
in accordance with Tóngguāng's precedent.
Initially, Yuánguàn suspended the establishment of the state,
this incident is recorded in the 278th volume of the records of Táng Míngzōng’s third year.
On Bǐngshēn,
a pardon was granted inside the borders,
and his son Hóngzūn was made heir apparent.
Cāo Zhòngdá, Shěn Sōng, and Pí Guāngyè were appointed as chancellors,
and the official Lín Dǐng was responsible for issuing decrees.
On the day of Dīngyǒu,
Xuānwǔ Military Commissioner Yáng Guāngyuǎn was also appointed as Shìzhōng.
The ruler of Mǐn built the Zǐwēi Palace,
adorned it with crystals,
doubling the grandeur of the Bǎo Huáng Palace.
In the second year of Chángxìng, the Mǐn ruler Lín built the Bǎo Huáng Palace.
He sought out people's hidden faults.
In May,
Wú Xú Zhīgào accepted Sòng Qíqiū's strategy,
intending to ally with the Khitans to seize China,
sending envoys with beauties and treasures across the sea to establish goodwill,
and the Khitan ruler also sent envoys in response.
On Bǐngchén,
a decree named the temporary headquarters at the defense city in Biànzhōu to Dàníng Palace.
At the time, the Censorate reported:
“Biànzhōu was once the capital of Liáng,
but during Zhuāngzōng's reign, it was downgraded to Xuānwǔ Military Command.
During Míngzōng’s inspection tour,
the then official restored the city’s defenses,
and hung plaques of the old Liáng palaces,
which some knowledgeable people quietly disputed.
Recently, when the imperial chariot temporarily resided at Liáng's estate,
the names of places inside the city were as in Míngzōng’s tour,
having no capital title but palace names,
this seems inappropriate according to precedent.
Since the Qín and Hàn dynasties,
where the imperial chariot reached,
they often established palace names.

In Suí, at Yángzhōu, they established Jiāngdū Palace, in Tàiyuán established Fényáng Palace, in Qízhōu established Rénshòu Palace, and during Táng, at Tàiyuán, they established Jìnyáng Palace, at Tóngzhōu established Chángchūn Palace, at Qízhōu established Jǐuchéng Palace.
Palaces inside were labeled with plaques to signify imperial residence.
I request to follow precedent,
to temporarily hang a palace name plaque at the city gate of Biànzhōu,
then other rooms may follow for convenience.”
The decree stated:
“The temporary palace shall be named Dàníng Palace.”
On Rénshēn,
Fàn Yánguāng was advanced in title as the King of Línqīng County,
to stabilize his mind.
The posthumous honor of four ancestral generations as emperors and empresses was announced.
According to the Wǔdài Huìyào,
Gāozǔ Jǐng received the posthumous title of Jìngzǔ Xiàoān Huángdì,
his consort Lady Qín posthumously as Yuán Empress;
the great-grandfather Chēn was posthumously Sùzǔ Xiàojiǎn Huángdì,
his consort Lady Ān as Gōng Empress;
the grandfather Yù was Ruìzǔ Xiàopíng Huángdì,
his consort Lady Mǐ as Xiàn Empress;
the father Shào Yǒng was Xuànzǔ Xiàoyuán Huángdì,
his consort Lady Hé as Yì Empress.
If earlier histories claimed the name of Emperor Kao was Nièlièjī Tui,
then it suggests that the names of these four generations were likely created by officials.
On Jǐmǎo,
an edict allowed the recovery and burial of the Táng dynasty criminals' heads stored in Tàishè.
Initially, former general Lord Lóu Jìyīng served Liáng Jūn Wáng,
as an internal officer,
now requesting the burial of his head.
Táng had stored the head of Liáng Jūn Wáng in Tàishè, as recorded in volume 272 of Zhuāngzōng Tóngguāng first year.
The history records Lord Lóu Jìyīng’s unfinished request for burial.
In June,
Wú’s vice-commander of multiple provinces Xú Jǐngqiān passed away.
Fàn Yánguāng had long entrusted military administration to Yuán Suí's left escort officer Sūn Ruì,
who, feeling confident in his favor, acted arbitrarily,
ripping orders displeasing him in front of Yánguāng.
At that time, Yánguāng was ill for several weeks,
Sūn Ruì secretly summoned the prefect of Chánzhōu, Féng Huī,
plotting together to force Yánguāng into rebellion;
Yánguāng also considered Zhang Sheng’s advice,
as recorded in the previous month.
On Jiǎwǔ,
the East Pavilion official Zhāng Yán returned from a mission to Wèizhōu,
reporting Yánguāng’s rebellious intent;
the Yìchéng Military Commissioner Fú Yànráo reported Yánguāng sending troops across the river,
burning down a straw market;
at that time, due to constant wars,
people outside city walls mostly lived in straw huts forming villages,
because of their low cost and ease of construction,
sudden military fires would not greatly damage their wealth and lives.
This straw market was outside the city of Huàzhōu,
Báimǎ Ferry is in Huàzhōu's Báimǎxiàn.
This person was from Yúnzhōu.
On Dīngyǒu,
Zhāng Cóngbīn, the inspector of the Eastern Capital, was appointed as the chief commander of Wèifǔ’s southwest front.
On Wùxū,
the imperial guards' commander Yáng Guāngyuǎn
was sent,
followed by the command to Dū Zhòngwēi to station troops in Wèizhōu.
According to the Wǔdài Huìyào, in the sixth year of Tiānfú, Chengde's two armies were renamed Husheng’s left and right armies.
By this time, the Husheng army must have existed.
The person originated from Shuòzhōu,
married the emperor's sister Princess Lèpíng.
Fàn Yánguāng made Féng Huī chief commander,
Sūn Ruì in charge of military affairs,
leading twenty thousand infantry and cavalry along the western river to Lìyáng Pass.
Lìyáng is southwest of Wèizhōu,
thus they first followed the western river up to reach it.
On Xīnchǒu,
Yáng Guāngyuǎn reported leading troops across Huliang Crossing.
This is the crossing used by Shǐ Sīmíng,
located on the north bank of Huàzhōu in Chánzhōu's territory.
According to another history: in the sixth year of Tiānfú,
an edict proclaimed the construction of the Great Tong Army at Yuecheng of Huliang Crossing,
with the floating bridge named the Great Tong Bridge.
30. Hé Níng, who held the positions of Hanlin Academician and Vice Minister of Rites, was appointed as Academician of the Duānmíng Hall.
Hé Níng posted a notice at his gate,
refusing to receive guests.
Former Tuánliàn Tuīguān of Yàozhōu, Zhāng Yì from Xiāngyì County
(Xiāngyì County was under the jurisdiction of Sòngzhōu.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì, it was located 170 lǐ southeast of Dàliáng.)
believed that
"a close official position serves as the eyes and ears of the Son of Heaven,
and one should be aware of the benefits and harms across the land.
How can one refuse guests!
Although it may be convenient for personal safety,
what about betraying the state!"
Hé Níng found him remarkable,
and recommended him to Sāng Wéihàn.
Not long after,
he was appointed as Left Reminder.
Zhāng Yì submitted a memorial stating:
"The Northern Di have the merit of supporting the establishment of the state.
We should outwardly maintain friendly relations with them,
while internally strengthening border defenses.
We must not indulge in leisure,
lest we provoke their ambitions."
The Emperor deeply agreed with him.
31. The Khitan attacked Yúnzhōu,
but after half a year, they were unable to capture it.
Wú Luán sent an envoy via a hidden route to submit a plea for rescue.
The Emperor wrote a letter to the Khitan ruler on his behalf, requesting his release.
The Khitan ruler then ordered Zhái Zhāng to lift the siege and withdraw.
The Emperor summoned Wú Luán to return,
appointing him as Deputy Military Commissioner of Wǔníng.
32. On Dīngwèi,
Yáng Guāngyuǎn, the Imperial Guard Commissioner, was appointed as Overall Commander of the Four Sides of Wèifǔ.
(The Imperial Guard Commissioner is the same as the Imperial Guard Army Commissioner;
the historical record uses an abbreviated title.)
Gāo Xíngzhōu, the Military Commissioner of Zhāoyì, led his own troops to station in Xiàngzhōu,
serving as the Western Commander of Wèifǔ.
(Xiàngzhōu is located west of Wèizhōu,
so Gāo Xíngzhōu was ordered to lead troops from Lùzhōu to station in Xiàngzhōu to confront Fàn Yánguāng.)
The soldier Guō Wēi was formerly under Liú Zhīyuǎn's command.
He was supposed to follow Yáng Guāngyuǎn on the northern campaign.
(The campaign from Dàliáng to Wèizhōu was considered a northern campaign.)
According to the Old History of the Five Dynasties, Zhou Annals,
Guō Wēi initially served under Lǐ Jìtāo;
after Jìtāo was executed,
he was assigned to the Cóngmǎzhí.
When the Jin founder served as Deputy Imperial Guard Commissioner,
he summoned Guō Wēi to his command,
and thus Guō Wēi came to serve under the Han founder.
When asked about the reason,
Guō Wēi said:
"Lord Yáng possesses cunning talent,
but lacks heroic spirit.
What use would he have for me?
The one who can truly use me is Lord Liú!"
(This sets the stage for Guō Wēi becoming Liú Zhīyuǎn's key supporter.)
33. An edict ordered Zhāng Cóngbīn to mobilize several thousand troops from Hénán to attack Fàn Yánguāng.
(Hénán troops refer to the troops of Hénán Prefecture.
Zhāng Cóngbīn was then the Patrol and Inspection Commissioner of Luòyáng,
so he was ordered to mobilize them.)
Zhāng Cóngbīn then rebelled together with them,
killing the imperial prince, Military Commissioner of Héyáng, Chóngxìn,
and appointing General-in-Chief Zhāng Jìzuò as Acting Military Commissioner of Héyáng.
(Jìzuò
was the son of Zhāng Quányì.
Zhāng Quányì served as Prefect of Hénán from the late Táng dynasty,
through the Táng and Liáng dynasties.)
He also killed the imperial prince, Acting Eastern Capital Guardian, Chóngyì,
appointing Deputy Guardian of the Eastern Capital and Patrol and Inspection Commissioner Zhāng Yánbō to administer the affairs of Hénán Prefecture,
and joining the army.
He took money and silk from the imperial treasury to reward his troops;
the Guardian Judge, Lǐ Xiá, refused to comply,
and the soldiers killed him.
Zhāng Cóngbīn led his troops to block the Sìshuǐ Pass.
(The Sìshuǐ Pass is named after the county,
also known as the Hǔláo Pass.
For details, see the discussion on corrections.)
An edict ordered the Commander of the Fèngguó Army, Hóu Yì, to lead 5,000 imperial guards to join Dù Chóngwēi in attacking Zhāng Cóngbīn;
another edict ordered the Palace Affairs Commissioner, Liú Chùràng, to lead troops from Líyáng to attack him.
At that time, urgent military dispatches were flying everywhere,
and all officials in Dàliáng were terrified.
(Urgent military dispatches flying everywhere means military documents were piling up.
The families of the officials were all left in the Eastern Capital,
while they themselves were accompanying the emperor in Biàn.
With their roots already severed,
they were terrified.
Zòng
is pronounced zǐ róng fān.
Cóng
is pronounced cái yòng fān.
Xiōng
is pronounced xǔ gǒng fān.)
Sāng Wéihàn remained calm and composed,
receiving and responding to guests
without changing his usual demeanor,
which somewhat reassured the people.
(The history records that Sāng Wéihàn was able to calm the situation with composure.)
34. A Taoist priest told the King of Mǐn
that a white dragon had appeared at night on Luó Peak;
the King of Mǐn then built the White Dragon Temple.
At that time, numerous corvée duties were imposed,
and state funds were insufficient.
The King of Mǐn said to the Vice Minister of Personnel and Acting Commissioner of the Three Departments, Cài Shǒuméng from Hòuguān:
(The Eastern Hòuguān County was established in the Later Hàn dynasty,
abolished and merged into Mǐn County during the Sui dynasty,
and reestablished as Hòuguān County during the Táng dynasty,
under the jurisdiction of Fúzhōu.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì, its administrative seat was in the prefectural capital.)
"I have heard that officials all accept bribes when appointing people to positions.
Is this true?"
Cài Shǒuméng replied:
"Such rumors are not worth believing."
The King of Mǐn said:
"I have known about this for a long time.
Now I entrust this matter to you.
Select the worthy and appoint them,
but do not refuse the unworthy or those who seek positions through deception.
(Deception refers to those who seek official positions through fraud and impersonation.
Deceiving superiors with things that do not exist in reason is called 'wǎng';
pretending to possess what belongs to others to cover up falsehood is called 'mào'.)
Record them and present them to me."
Cài Shǒuméng was originally honest and believed this was unacceptable;
the King of Mǐn grew angry,
and Cài Shǒuméng, out of fear, complied.
From then on, appointments were made solely based on the amount of bribes offered.
(This sets the stage for Cài Shǒuméng being executed for selling official positions.)
Official appointments were made through the Hall Edict,
which is what people today call a Provincial Directive.
Blank ones
did not have the appointed person's name written on them;
after selling them for money, the names were filled in.
(Kōng
is pronounced kǔ gòng fān.)
There was no end to the greed.
Another edict ordered that those who concealed their age be caned on the back,
those who concealed their household registration be executed,
and those who fled be exterminated along with their clans.
Fruits, vegetables, chickens, and pigs
were all heavily taxed.
35. In autumn,
the seventh month,
Zhāng Cóngbīn attacked Sìshuǐ,
killing the Patrol and Inspection Commissioner, Sòng Tínghào.
The Emperor donned military attire,
prepared light cavalry,
and was about to flee to Jìnyáng to avoid the attack.
Sāng Wéihàn kowtowed and earnestly advised:
"Although the rebels' momentum is strong,
it cannot last long.
Please wait a little longer;
do not act rashly."
The Emperor then stopped.
(The history records that Sāng Wéihàn had courage and strategy,
and the Jin court relied on him as a pillar of the state.
Shǎo
is pronounced shī zhǎo fān.)
36. Fàn Yánguāng sent envoys with wax-sealed letters to recruit those who had lost their positions.
Right Wuwei General-in-Chief Lóu Jìyīng and Right Guard General-in-Chief Yǐn Huī, who were in Dàliáng,
as well as Wēn Tāo's sons Yánjùn, Yánzhǎo, and Yángǔn, who lived in Xǔzhōu,
all responded to him.
(Yǐn Huī surrendered his army to the Prince of Lù to obtain a military commission;
now serving in the Imperial Guard,
he held a sinecure position.
Wēn Tāo was executed during the reign of Táng Emperor Míngzōng,
and his sons were dismissed from office.
Since Lóu Jìyīng's daughter-in-law was the daughter of Wēn Yánzhǎo,
and Jìyīng also held a sinecure position,
they all responded to Yánguāng.)
They gathered a following of nearly a thousand people.
When Jìyīng and Huī's plot was exposed,
they both fled.
On Rénzǐ,
an imperial decree stated that due to Yánguāng's treacherous schemes,
which slandered loyal officials,
from then on, anyone who captured Yánguāng's spies would be rewarded,
the spies would be killed,
and wax-sealed letters would be confiscated
without reporting them to the emperor.
(This was to avoid knowing the names of those recruited,
in order to pacify the wavering.)
Jìyīng fled to Xǔzhōu,
seeking refuge with the Wēn family.
The Military Commissioner of Zhōngwǔ, Cháng Cóngjiǎn, made extensive preparations,
so Yánjùn and the others were unable to act.
They wanted to kill Jìyīng to clear themselves,
but Yánzhǎo stopped them,
and they fled together to join Zhāng Cóngbīn.
Jìyīng learned of their plan,
and advised Cóngbīn to arrest the three Wēns,
all of whom were executed.
37 Bái Fèngjìn was in Huázhōu.
In the sixth month of this year, he was dispatched to station troops at Báimǎ.
Báimǎ
was the seat of Huázhōu's administration.
They arrested them,
capturing five men,
three of whom were under Bái Fèngjìn's command,
and two under Fú Yànráo's command.
Bái Fèngjìn had them all executed;
Fú Yànráo was greatly angered because he had not been informed beforehand.
He was very angry.
The next day,
Bái Fèngjìn went with several horsemen to apologize to Fú Yànráo.
Fú Yànráo said:
"The armies each have their own jurisdictions.
How could you take soldiers from Huázhōu and execute them all together,
showing absolutely no regard for the propriety between guest and host!"
Fú Yànráo considered himself the host as the defender of Huázhōu,
and Bái Fèngjìn, stationed in Huázhōu, as the guest.
"When soldiers break the law,
what distinction is there between yours and mine!
I have already admitted my fault and apologized to you,
yet your anger does not subside.
Is it not that you wish to rebel together with Yánguāng?"
He flicked his sleeves and rose to leave.
Fú Yànráo did not detain him;
the armored soldiers under the tent clamored loudly,
seized Bái Fèngjìn,
and killed him.
His accompanying horsemen ran out,
shouting loudly outside.
The various armies vied to don armor and take up weapons,
the uproar and clamor impossible to suppress.
Mǎ Wàn, the Left Wing Capital Commander of the Fèngguó Army, was bewildered and did not know what to do.
He led his infantry intending to join the rebellion,
when he encountered Lú Shùnmì, the Right Wing Capital Commander, leading his troops out of camp.
Lú sternly said to Mǎ Wàn:
"Commander Fú has recklessly killed Commander Bái,
he must be in conspiracy with the city of Wèi.
It is only two hundred *li* from here to the imperial traveling palace.
The city of Wèi,
refers to the city of Wèizhōu.
At that time, Fàn Yánguāng held Wèizhōu in rebellion.
*Jiǔyù Zhì*: Huázhōu is two hundred *li* south to Dàliáng.
At that time, the Emperor was in Dàliáng.
Why do you not think of repaying the state,
but instead wish to aid the rebellion,
seeking the extermination of your own clan?
Today we should together capture Commander Fú,
send him to the Son of Heaven,
and achieve great merit.
Soldiers who obey orders will be rewarded,
those who disobey will be executed.
Do not hesitate any further!"
Among Mǎ Wàn's troops, there were still some who shouted and leaped about.
Lú Shùnmì killed several men,
and the multitude dared not act.
Mǎ Wàn had no choice but to comply.
Together with Fāng Tài, the Capital Inspector of the Fèngguó Army, and others, they attacked the headquarters compound,
captured Fú Yànráo,
and ordered Fāng Tài to escort him under guard to Dàliáng.
On the day Jiǎyǐn,
an imperial decree ordered Fú Yànráo executed at the Bānjīng Lodge.
*Zuǒzhuàn* records
that Chǔ's Wǔ Jǔ and Shēngzǐ were close friends.
Wǔ Jǔ fled into exile,
and Shēngzǐ met him in the outskirts of Zhèng.
They spread rushes and sat together to eat and talk.
Dù Yù's commentary states: Bān means
to spread;
they spread rushes on the ground and sat together to discuss.
Using
"Bānjīng"
to name the lodge
derives from this.
This lodge must have been in the outskirts of Biànzhōu.
Note: Fú Cúnshěn's sons all had talent and spirit,
and Fú Yànqīng was also a renowned general of the time.
Fú Yànráo could not control his subordinates,
and a sudden disturbance erupted.
The brothers were not initially in conspiracy,
and guilt should not extend to them—
this is the ancient law.
Yáng Guāngyuǎn led troops from Báigāo towards Huázhōu.
The soldiers, hearing of the disorder in Huázhōu,
wanted to support Yáng Guāngyuǎn as their leader.
Yáng Guāngyuǎn said:
"The Son of Heaven is not a plaything for you lot to trade and manipulate!
My surrender at Jìnyáng was due to dire straits.
This refers to killing Zhāng Jìngdá at the Jìn'ān Stockade and surrendering,
the event is recorded in the previous volume, last year.
Surrender,
pronunciation: *xiáng*, *hù jiāng fān*.
I am a true rebel."
His subordinates then dared not speak.
At that time, the three military districts of Wèi, Mèng, and Huá rebelled in succession.
Wèi,
refers to Fàn Yánguāng.
Mèng,
refers to Zhāng Cóngbīn.
Huá,
refers to Fú Yànráo.
The Emperor asked Liú Zhīyuǎn for advice.
He replied:
"The rise of an emperor
is naturally ordained by Heaven's Mandate.
When Your Majesty was formerly in Jìnyáng,
provisions did not last five days,
yet soon you achieved the great enterprise.
Now the realm is already settled.
Within, you have powerful troops;
to the north, you have allied with a strong foreign power.
The strong foreign power,
refers to the Qìdān.
I hope Your Majesty will soothe the generals and ministers with kindness,
and I request to restrain the soldiers with authority.
When kindness and authority are both manifest,
the capital will naturally be pacified.
If the root is deep and firm,
then the branches and leaves will not be harmed."
Liú Zhīyuǎn then strictly established regulations and prohibitions.
*Kē* means
articles or clauses.
There was a soldier who stole a bundle of paper money.
The owner caught him.
The owner,

Examination of Discrepancies: The Veritable Records state:
"In the eleventh month of the second year of the Tiānfú era,
Yuánguàn was appointed Deputy Commander-in-Chief and King,
with Chéng Xùn and others as envoys to confer the additional honors.
In the tenth month, on the bǐngwǔ day of the fourth year,
because Chéng Xùn perished at sea,
court was suspended,
and he was posthumously awarded office."
The Biography of Chéng Xùn states:
"In autumn of the third year of Tiānfú, he was sent as envoy to Wúyuè,
and on his return journey, he drowned."
The Biography of Yuánguàn states:
"In the third year of Tiānfú, he was enfeoffed as King of Wúyuè."
Probably the decree was issued in winter of the second year,
and Chéng Xùn and others arrived in Hángzhōu in the third year.
It is unknown in which year he drowned,
but the Jìn court only learned of it in the tenth month of the fourth year.
The Supplementary History of Wúyuè states:
"In the fourth month of the second year of Tiānfú, an imperial order was sent with Chéng Xùn and others to confer upon the King the titles of Deputy Commander-in-Chief and King.
On the jiǎwǔ day,
the King ascended the throne,
using the rituals for founding a state,
following the precedent of the Tóngguāng era.
That year, Chéng Xùn returned to the capital,
and drowned at sea."
According to this, when Yuánguàn first succeeded,
citing Liú's final instructions,
he only used the rituals for a regional military governor.
The next year, Míngzōng enfeoffed him as Prince of Wú,
and at the beginning of the Mǐndì era, Emperor Mǐn enfeoffed him as Prince of Wúyuè.
Therefore, he assumed the kingship in the third year of Tiānfú.
The Supplementary History's claim that he received the titles of Commander-in-Chief and King before ascending the throne
is mistaken.
