the deputy magistrate of the Eastern Capital.
"Your Majesty has responded to Heaven and complied with the people;
your affairs are not seized by force.
'Seized by force'
originates from the words of Hàn Lù Jiǎ about 'seizing by force but governing by righteousness.'
These are not urgent matters,
and should not be followed."
The Southern Tang ruler agreed with him.
12 The military governor of Hénán, Gāo Xíngzhōu, proposed repairing the Luòyáng Palace.
On the day Bǐngxū,
the Left Grand Master of Remonstrance Xuē Róng admonished:
"Although the palace buildings have been burned down,
they are still more extravagant than Emperor Yáo's thatched huts;
(Emperor Yáo of Táng had earthen steps three feet high,
with thatch untrimmed.)
and still more numerous than Emperor Wén of Hàn's open terrace.
(The matter of the open terrace is recorded in the Annals of Emperor Wén of Hàn.)
He mentioned that Fàn Yánguāng still held Wèi Prefecture,
and Yáng Guāngyuǎn's attack had not yet succeeded.
This is truly not the time for Your Majesty to repair palaces and halls;
wait until the land is peaceful and tranquil,
then it will not be too late to construct them."
The Emperor accepted his advice,
and further bestowed an edict praising him.
13 On the day Jǐchǒu,
the Director of the Bureau of Revenues, Zhāng Zhù, memorialized:
"I have observed the floating households in the villages,
(floating households
refer to those without fixed registered residence;
meaning they drift like duckweed,
not settling in one place,
as if floating on water.)
not because they do not wish to live in peace,
but because if the trees they plant have not yet reached ten years,
or the land they cultivate has not reached three qǐng,
and it seems they are beginning to establish their livelihood,
the county authorities already impose corvée labor on them,
demand heavy taxes,
and intimidate them with severe punishments.
Therefore, they cannot avoid abandoning their work and property,
and consider moving elsewhere.
I beg that from now on, when people cultivate land up to five qǐng or more,
only after three years should the county authorities impose corvée labor."
This was approved.
14 In autumn,
the seventh month,
the Secretariat memorialized:
"Although dynasties differ,
regulations and systems are not different.
We request that officials be appointed to take the edicts from the Mingzong and Qīngtài periods,
review and determine those that can be long-lasting, and compile them."
On the day Jǐyǒu,
an edict ordered the Left Grand Master of Remonstrance Xuē Róng and others to review and determine.
15 On the day Xīnyǒu,
an edict was issued to create the Seal of Mandate,
with
"Having received Heaven's bright mandate,
only virtue ensures prosperity"
as the inscription.
This was because the Seal of Mandate had been burned by the Prince of Lù.
At that time, the Secretariat-Chancellery memorialized:
"According to the edict to make the emperor's Seal of Mandate,
we note that in the sixteenth year of the Zhēnguàn era, Emperor Tàizōng Wén of Táng carved the Xuán Seal,
with white jade as the dragon-head knob,
and the inscription read: 'The emperor receives the mandate,
the virtuous prosper.'"
The edict used
"Having received Heaven's bright mandate,
only virtue ensures prosperity"
as the inscription.
According to the Táng Liù Diǎn: the Seal of Mandate
was used by the Son of Heaven when performing the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices,
and when worshiping the gods and spirits.
The 16th day. The Emperor presented honorary titles to the Khitan ruler and the Empress Dowager.
On the Wùyín day,
Féng Dào was appointed as the envoy to present the ceremonial documents to the Empress Dowager.
The Textual Analysis states: The Veritable Records of Emperor Shìzōng of the Later Zhōu, in the biography of Féng Dào, says:
"The barbarians sent an envoy to confer an honorary title upon the Jìn ancestor,
and Jìn also presented an honorary title to the barbarians.
Initially, they ordered Wáng Quán, the Minister of War, to carry out the mission,
but Wáng Quán declined due to old age and illness.
The Jìn ancestor said to Féng Dào: 'For this mission, no one but you will do.'
Féng Dào showed no sign of difficulty."
According to the Veritable Records of Emperor Gāozǔ of the Later Jìn:
"On the Wùyín day of the eighth month in the third year of Tiānfú,
Féng Dào served as the envoy to present the ceremonial documents to the Khitan Empress Dowager.
On the Wùyín day of the tenth month,
the Northern Dynasty ordered an envoy to present an honorary title to the Emperor.
On the Wùzǐ day,
Wáng Quán was dismissed from his post for refusing to serve as envoy to the North."
The Veritable Records of Emperor Shìzōng of the Later Zhōu is mistaken.
The character 'Xù' was originally written as 'Xù'.
He went to the Khitan to perform the ceremonies;
the Khitan ruler was greatly pleased.
The Emperor served the Khitan with extreme deference,
submitting memorials and calling himself a subject,
addressing the Khitan ruler as
"Father Emperor";
whenever Khitan envoys arrived,
the Emperor would receive the imperial edicts and decrees with bows in a separate hall.
In addition to the annual tribute of 300,000 units of gold and silk,
(The 300,000 was the originally agreed annual tribute amount from the peace treaty.)
seasonal gifts,
curiosities, treasures, and rarities
were sent continuously along the roads.
Even Empress Dowager Yìngtiān, the Marshal Crown Prince, Prince Wěi, the Southern and Northern Princes, Hán Yánhuī, Zhào Yánshòu, and other high officials all received bribes;
if they were even slightly displeased,
they would come to reproach and blame,
and the Emperor would always apologize with humble words.
Empress Dowager Yìngtiān was the Khitan ruler's mother, the Lady Shùlǜ;
the title Yìngtiān was likely conferred by the Emperor.
The Khitan were arrogant and haughty,
often using disrespectful language.
When the envoys returned and reported this,
both the court and the common people considered it a disgrace,
yet the Emperor served them tirelessly,
and thus, throughout his reign, there was no rift with the Khitan.
However, the gold and silk paid did not exceed the tax revenue of a few counties,
often using the pretext of the people's hardship
to not fulfill the full amount.
Later, the Khitan ruler repeatedly stopped the Emperor from submitting memorials calling himself a subject,
only ordering him to write letters addressing himself as
"the son emperor",
following the etiquette among family members.
Initially, after the Khitan obtained Yōuzhōu,
they named it Nánjīng. (The Khitan first obtained Yōuzhōu in the first year of Tiānfú.)
Sīwēn's son Yánzhào was in Jìn,

and the Emperor appointed him as Prefect of Qízhōu. (In the third year of Jǐngfú under Emperor Zhāozōng of the Táng, Wáng Chùcún, the military commissioner of Yìwǔ, petitioned to establish Qízhōu from the two counties of Wújí and Shēnzé in Dìngzhōu.)
He requested to bring Yōuzhōu to submit to the interior;
the Emperor did not permit it.
Zhào Yánzhào later entered Khitan territory
and was employed by the Khitan.
The 17th day. The Khitan sent an envoy to the Southern Táng.
Sòng Qíqiū advised the Southern Táng ruler to bribe him generously,
and when he reached north of the Huái River,
to secretly send someone to kill him,
intending to create a rift with Jìn.
The 18th day. On the Rénwǔ day,
Yáng Guāngyuǎn reported that Féng Huī, the former Prefect of Chánzhōu, had come out of Guǎngjìn city to fight
and had thus come to surrender. (Féng Huī entered Guǎngjìn from Chánzhōu to join Fàn Yánguāng in rebellion; see the sixth month of last year.)
On the Jǐchǒu day,
Féng Huī was appointed as military commissioner of Yìchéng.
By generously rewarding Féng Huī,
they intended to split Fàn Yánguāng's faction.
Yáng Guāngyuǎn attacked Guǎngjìn

for over a year without capturing it. (Yáng Guāngyuǎn attacked Fàn Yánguāng since the sixth month of last year; he defeated Féng Huī and others in the seventh month and then advanced to attack Guǎngjìn. It has now been over a year, and it still has not fallen.)
When Emperor Zhuāngzōng of the Later Táng ascended the throne, he changed Wèizhōu to Xìngtáng Prefecture;
when the Emperor founded the new dynasty, he changed it to Guǎngjìn.
He sent the palace attendant Zhū Xiàn into the city to persuade Fàn Yánguāng,
(Palace attendants were likely eunuchs.)
saying:
"If you surrender and I kill you,
may the bright sun above bear witness,
I shall not enjoy the state."
Fàn Yánguāng said to his deputy military commissioner Lǐ Shì:
"The sovereign values trustworthiness;
if he says I will not die, then I will not die."
He then removed the defensive preparations,
but still delayed without making a decision.
Liú Chùràng, the Commissioner of the Southern Bureau of the Palace Administration, entered again to persuade him,
and Fàn Yánguāng then made up his mind.
In the ninth month,
on the first day, Yǐsì,
Yáng Guāngyuǎn sent Fàn Yánguāng's two sons, Shǒutú and Shǒuyīng, to Dàliáng.
On the Jǐyǒu day,
Fàn Yánguāng sent his officer to submit a memorial awaiting punishment.
On the Rénzǐ day,
the imperial decree arrived at Guǎngjìn.
Fàn Yánguāng led his followers in plain clothes at the yámén,
and the envoy proclaimed the decree pardoning him.
Zhū Xiàn was from Biànzhōu.
The 19th day. The Khitan sent an envoy to Luòyáng

to fetch Zhào Yánshòu's wife, the Táng Princess of Yān, and bring her back. (Zhào Yánshòu's wife was a daughter of Emperor Míngzōng of the Later Táng. Yánshòu entered Khitan territory, but his wife remained in Luò. Now that Yánshòu held a position of power in the north, they came to fetch her.)
Cháng is pronounced zhǎng.
The 20th day. On the Rénxū day,
Zhào Kěfēng, the Minister of the Court of the Imperial Treasury of the Southern Táng, requested that the Southern Táng ruler restore the surname Lǐ
and establish ancestral temples for the Táng dynasty.
The 21st day. On the Gēngwǔ day,
Yáng Guāngyuǎn submitted a memorial requesting to come to court;

Liú Chùràng was ordered to temporarily administer the affairs of the Tiānxióng military prefecture. (When Yáng Guāngyuǎn was suppressing Fàn Yánguāng, an edict ordered him to concurrently administer the affairs of the Tiānxióng military headquarters. After Yánguāng surrendered, Guāngyuǎn requested to come to court. At that time, Liú Chùràng had been sent into Wèi with an imperial decree to persuade Yánguāng to surrender, so he was thus made to temporarily administer the military prefecture.)
On the Jǐsì day,
an edict appointed Fàn Yánguāng as military commissioner of Tiānpíng,
and furthermore bestowed upon him an iron pledge. (Bestowing an iron pledge meant pardoning his death and making it clear with a pledge of faith.)
Today refers to the day the edict reached Wèizhōu.
He was also pardoned.
Fàn Yánguāng's trusted generals and aides, Lǐ Shì, Sūn Hànwēi, and Xuē Bà, were all appointed as defense commissioners, training commissioners, and prefects.
The yá troops were all promoted to the Imperial Guard.
Initially, Lǐ Yànxún, the行军司马 of Héyáng,
was from Xíngzhōu.
His parents were in his hometown,
and he had never provided for them.
Later, he rebelled together with Zhāng Cóngbīn.
After Zhāng Cóngbīn's defeat, (Zhāng Cóngbīn rebelled in the sixth month of last year and was defeated after over a month.)
he fled to Guǎngjìn
and was made to climb the city walls to defend.
Yáng Guāngyuǎn captured his mother
and placed her beneath the city walls to summon him,
but Yànxún drew his bow and shot his mother dead.
After Yánguāng surrendered,
the Emperor appointed Yànxún as Prefect of Fāngzhōu.
Close ministers said that Yànxún had killed his mother,
and the heinous crime of matricide was unforgivable; (The law has the Ten Abominations; killing one's parents is a heinous crime not covered by amnesty.)
but it was said,
"The pardon decree has already been issued;
it cannot be changed."
He was then sent to take up his post.
Your subject Guāng remarks: Those who govern a state certainly cannot be without trustworthiness.
However, the evil of Yànxún was intolerable to the Three Spirits. (The Three Spirits refer to the heavenly gods, earthly deities, and human ghosts.)
Punishing his crime of matricide—how would that damage trustworthiness!
The 22nd day. On the Xīnwèi day,
Yáng Guāngyuǎn was appointed as military commissioner of Tiānxióng.
The 23rd day. In winter, the tenth month,
on the Wùyín day,
the Khitan sent an envoy to present a precious document,
conferring upon the Emperor the honorary title of "Valiant, Martial, Enlightened, and Righteous Emperor."
The Emperor, considering Dàliáng as a convergence point for boats and carts,
convenient for water transport,
on Bǐngchén day,
established the Eastern Capital at Biànzhōu.
From then on, through the Hàn and Zhōu dynasties until the Sòng,
all made their capital at Biàn.
The Liáng dynasty established the Eastern Capital at Biànzhōu,
making Biànzhōu into Kāifēng Prefecture.
In the third year of Kāipíng,
it annexed Suānzǎo and Chángyuán from Huázhōu,
Zhōngmóu and Yángwǔ from Zhèngzhōu,
Xiāngyì from Sòngzhōu,
Dàiyì from Cáozhōu,
Fúgōu and Yānlíng from Xǔzhōu,
and Tàikāng from Chénzhōu—nine counties in total—
and placed them all under the jurisdiction of Kāifēng Prefecture.
In the second year of Tóngguāng of the Táng, an edict assigned Yángwǔ, Kuāngchéng, Fúgōu, and Kǎochéng counties to Biànzhōu,
while the rest were returned to their original jurisdictions.
Kuāngchéng was Chángyuán.
In the first year of Tiānchéng, Fúgōu was again placed under Xǔzhōu.
At this point,
an edict decreed that Biànzhōu should be elevated to the Eastern Capital,
and further elevated Kāifēng and Jùnyí counties to imperial counties,
with the rest becoming metropolitan counties.
All counties originally under the jurisdiction of the established Kāifēng Prefecture were to be, as before, annexed and administered,
and also elevated to metropolitan counties.
The Eastern Capital was made the Western Capital,
and the Western Capital was made the Jìnchāng Army military governorship.
The Táng had made Cháng'ān the Western Capital,
and Luòyáng the Eastern Capital.
The Liáng dynasty first made its capital at Biàn,
making Biànzhōu the Eastern Capital,
Luòyáng the Western Capital,
and making Cháng'ān a military governorship.
The Later Táng destroyed Liáng,
restored the old Táng system of two capitals,
and made Biànzhōu a military governorship.
The Jìn now again established the Eastern Capital and Kāifēng Prefecture at Biànzhōu,
making the former Eastern Capital at Luòyáng the Western Capital,
and making the former Western Capital at Cháng'ān the Jìnchāng Army.
The Emperor sent Minister of War Wáng Quán as envoy to the Qìdān to thank them for the honorific title.
Quán, considering himself a descendant of generations of generals and ministers,
felt it a disgrace,
Wáng Quán,
was the great-grandson of Qǐ, the Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs of the Táng,
his father Ráo held office up to Vice Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs.
Qǐ's ancestor Bō
served as Chancellor under Emperor Wénzōng of Táng.
The Old History of the Five Dynasties: Wáng Qǐ held office up to Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs and Military Commissioner of Shānnán Xīdào,
and was posthumously granted the title of Grand Commandant.
"I am old,
how can I kneel before a felt tent!"
He thus declined on grounds of old age and illness.
The Emperor was angry,
on Wùzǐ day,
Quán was punished by dismissal from office.
Initially,
after Guō Chóngtǎo died,
(Guō Chóngtǎo's death is recorded in the 274th scroll, first year of Tiānchéng of Emperor Míngzōng of Táng.)
when the Emperor ascended the throne,
Sāng Wéihàn and Lǐ Sōng held both positions,
the Palace Affairs Commissioner Liú Chùràng and the eunuchs were all displeased.
When Yáng Guāngyuǎn besieged Guǎngjìn,
Chùràng several times carried military orders back and forth,
Guāngyuǎn's memorials and requests often exceeded proper bounds,
the Emperor often vacillated,
but Wéihàn alone used the law to check and refute him.
"Vacillated" means
seeming to comply yet seeming to oppose,
without a definite yes or no.
Refute,
is pronounced as in "to break".
Chùràng said:
"These are all the intentions of the chief ministers."
Guāngyuǎn thus harbored resentment against the chief ministers.
When Fàn Yánguāng surrendered,
Guāngyuǎn secretly submitted a memorial discussing the faults of the chief ministers;
after Guāngyuǎn had pacified Fàn Yánguāng,
he leveraged his achievement to make demands of the Emperor,
in order to denounce the chief ministers.
Wéihàn was promoted to Minister of War,
Sōng to Minister of Works,
and both were relieved of their posts as Privy Councilors;
Textual Analysis says: Dòu Zhèngù's Veritable Records of the Jìn Shàodì and the Old History of the Five Dynasties biography of Liú Chùràng states:
"Yáng Guāngyuǎn came to court,
and then spoke before Gāozǔ about the faults of the chief ministers;
then Wéihàn and others were relieved of their posts as Privy Councilors,
and Chùràng was appointed to the position."
The biography of Yáng Guāngyuǎn states:
"After Fàn Yánguāng surrendered,
Guāngyuǎn personally memorialized that Wéihàn monopolized power;
Gāozǔ, considering Guāngyuǎn had just rendered meritorious service to the state,
then sent Wéihàn out to govern Ānyáng,
and made Guāngyuǎn the Military Commissioner of the Western Capital."
Now, according to the Veritable Records of Jìn Gāozǔ,
on Rénchén day of the tenth month of the third year of Tiānfú,
Wéihàn and Sōng were relieved of their posts as Privy Councilors.
On Gēngzǐ day,
Guāngyuǎn first came to court,
and had an audience in the informal hall;
on Wùshēn day of the eleventh month,
Guāngyuǎn was made Military Commissioner of the Western Capital.
On Rénshēn day of the intercalary seventh month of the fourth year of Tiānfú,
Wéihàn was sent out as Military Commissioner of Xiàngzhōu.
This is probably an error in the biographies of Chùràng and Guāngyuǎn.

The Veritable Records of Jìn Shàodì and the Old History of the Five Dynasties biography of Sāng Wéihàn narrate that after Guāngyuǎn was stationed in Luòyáng, he submitted a memorial leading to Wéihàn being sent out to Xiàngzhōu,
which is correct.
The Minister of Ceremonies memorialized:
"Now the Eastern Capital is established,
yet the ancestral temples and altars of soil and grain are all in the Western Capital,
we request they be moved to Dàliáng."
An imperial decree stated:
"Let them remain as before for now."
On Wùxū day,
a general amnesty was declared.
Wú Quán, a former general of Yáng Yányì, raised troops from Àizhōu to attack Jiǎo Gōngxiàn in Jiāozhōu,
"Yányì"
should be
"Tíngyì".
Jiǎo Gōngxiàn's killing of Yáng Tíngyì is recorded in the previous year of this scroll.
Liú Xù said: Àizhōu is 460 lǐ east to the mouth of the Xiǎohuáng River, entering the territory of Jiāozhōu.
Based on the following text,
"Xiàn"
should have
"Gōng"
above it.
[Zhang: In the eleventh line of the B edition, it correctly has
"Gōng"
character.]
He appointed his son, the Prince of Wàn, Hóngcāo, as Military Commissioner of Jìnghǎi,
and transferred his title to Prince of Jiāo,
meaning he intended to make Jiāozhōu Hóngcāo's fief.
The King of Hàn personally led troops and stationed them at Hǎimén,
to provide support.
The King of Hàn asked for strategy from the Director of the Chongwen Institute, Xiāo Yì,
Yì said:
"Now it has been raining heavily for ten days,
the sea route is dangerous and distant,
Wú Quán is fierce and cunning,
we cannot take him lightly.
The main army should act with caution,
use many local guides,
and only then advance."
He did not listen.
He ordered Hóngcāo to lead warships from the Báiténg River towards Jiāozhōu.
The Báiténg River should be within the boundaries of Fēngzhōu,
from here advancing to Huābù,
reaching Fēngzhōu.
Lead,
read as "command".
Towards,
is pronounced qī yù.
Wú Quán, occupying Jiāozhōu,
led his troops to meet the battle,
first planting many large stakes at the harbor entrance,
sharpening their tips,
and covering them with iron.
He sent light boats to take advantage of the tide to challenge battle and feign retreat.
In a short while, the tide fell,
the Hàn warships were all impeded by the iron stakes and could not return,
the Hàn troops were badly defeated,
more than half the soldiers drowned;
Hóngcāo died,
the King of Hàn wailed in grief,
gathered his remaining troops, and returned.
Previously,
the Assistant Editorial Director Hóu Róng had advised the King of Hàn to cease warfare and give the people rest.
Now, because the military was not successful,
he blamed Róng posthumously,
split open his coffin and exposed his corpse.
Yì
was the grandson of Fǎng.
The Shùnxián Lady Péng of Chǔ died.
Lady Péng was plain in appearance but managed the household with discipline,
the King of Chǔ, Xīfàn, was in awe of her;
after her death,
Xīfàn began to indulge in music and women,
drinking through the long nights,
with no distinction between inner and outer quarters.
There was a merchant whose wife was beautiful,
Xīfàn killed her husband and seized her.
The wife vowed not to suffer disgrace,
and hanged herself.
The historian, because the woman was able to preserve her chastity,
recorded the event but lost her surname,
yet Mǎ Xīfàn's lewdness and cruelty could not be concealed.
The Yellow River breached at Yùnzhōu.
In the eleventh month,
Fàn Yánguāng came to court from Yùnzhōu.
(Fàn Yánguāng surrendered,
was moved from Wèi to Yùn,
now he comes to court from Yùnzhōu.)
On the 33rd day, Bingwu,
the ruler of Mǐn, Wáng Chǎng, was appointed as the King of the Mǐn Kingdom.
Referring to him as the "ruler of Mǐn"
indicates that he had already usurped the imperial title;
referring to him as being appointed as the "king of the kingdom"
signifies the command of the Jìn court.
Chǎng was granted a crimson robe.
The crimson robe
was worn by the Son of Heaven;
bestowing it upon him was an acknowledgment of his usurped title.
On the 48th day, Wùshēn,
Wáng Jìgōng, the military commissioner of Wēiwǔ, was appointed as the Prince of Línhǎi Commandery.
When the ruler of Mǐn heard of this,
he dispatched his memorial-presenting official Lín Ēn to inform the chief ministers,
stating that since he had already assumed the imperial title,
he declined the imperial patent and the envoys.
Huáng Fěng, the remonstrance official of Mǐn, due to the ruler's debauchery and tyranny,
bade farewell to his wife and children and went to remonstrate.
The ruler of Mǐn intended to have him caned,
but Fěng said:
"If I were deluded about the state and disloyal,
I would have no resentment even in death;
but to be caned for straightforward remonstrance,
I will not accept."
The ruler of Mǐn was enraged
and dismissed him to commoner status.
34 The Emperor was troubled by the overbearing and difficult-to-control nature of Yáng Guāngyuǎn, the military commissioner of Tiānxióng.
Sāng Wéihàn proposed dividing the forces of Tiānxióng
and promoting Guāngyuǎn to Grand Preceptor, Western Capital Resident, and concurrent military commissioner of Héyáng.
From then on, Guāngyuǎn harbored resentment,
secretly sending bribes to plead his case to the Qìdān,
maintaining a personal army of over a thousand men,
and constantly nurturing rebellious intentions.
Although Yáng Guāngyuǎn harbored rebellious intentions,
as long as the Emperor and the Qìdān remained on good terms,
he had no opportunity to act.
It was only when Emperor Chū and the Qìdān became estranged
that he enlisted the Qìdān's aid and hastened the disaster.
On the 51st day, Xīnhài,
the secondary capital Yèdū was established at Guǎngjìn Prefecture.
When Emperor Zhuāngzōng of the Later Táng first ascended the throne,
he established the Eastern Capital at Wèi Prefecture,
making Wèi Prefecture the Xīngtáng Prefecture.
It was later changed to Yèdū,
but was abolished in the fourth year of Emperor Míngzōng's Tiānchéng era.
After the Jìn received the Mandate,
Wèi Prefecture was made Guǎngjìn Prefecture,
and now Yèdū was reestablished.
Chán and Wèi were placed under its jurisdiction;
the Zhāodé Army,
which had been established during the Zhēnmíng era of the Later Liáng,
was abolished shortly after Zhāng Yàn's rebellion,
and was now reestablished.
Bó and Jì were placed under its jurisdiction.
Bèi and Bó from Tiānxióng,
and Jì Prefecture from Chéngdé, were formed into the Yǒngqīng Army.
The Emperor, concerned about the Qìdān being a future threat,
dispatched the former prefect of Zī Prefecture, Jí native Liú Jìxūn, to relocate Chán Prefecture across Déshèng Ford,
moving Dùnqiū there as well.
Chán Prefecture was originally administered from Dùnqiū County,
but now both the prefecture and county were moved to Déshèng.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì, Chán Prefecture was 130 lǐ from Wèi Prefecture;
the Chán Prefecture at Déshèng,
according to Jìn officials, was 150 lǐ from Wèi Prefecture,
a difference of 20 lǐ.
This is because from the north wall of Chán Prefecture to Wèi Prefecture was only 130 lǐ,
but if one went from the south wall, crossed the river including the pontoon bridge,
the calculated distance would be 150 lǐ.
Wáng Tíngyìn, the defense commissioner of Bèi Prefecture, was appointed military commissioner of Zhāodé,
and Wáng Zhōu, Right Divine Martial Commander, was appointed military commissioner of Yǒngqīng.
This marked the elevation of Bèi Prefecture to the Yǒngqīng Army.
He was the grandson of Wáng Chùcún;
at the end of the Táng, Wáng Chùcún governed Yìdìng.
He was a native of Yèdū.
35 Fàn Yánguāng repeatedly requested to retire.
On the 54th day, Jiǎyín,
an edict was issued granting him retirement as Grand Preceptor of the Heir Apparent,
and he resided in Dàliáng.
Whenever he attended banquets,
he was treated no differently from the current officials.
When Yánguāng rebelled,
Wáng Jǐng, the prefect of Xiàng Prefecture and a native of Yè, resisted and did not follow him.
Fàn Yánguāng commanded Tiānxióng,
and Xiàng Prefecture was under his jurisdiction.
Yè
was a Hàn dynasty county,
attached to Lái Prefecture in the Táng.
Xiàng,
pronunciation Xīliàng.
On the 58th day, Wùwǔ,
Jǐng was appointed as training commissioner of Yào Prefecture.
36 On the 63rd day, Guǐhài,
an edict was issued allowing both government and private casting of copper coins,
prohibiting adulteration with lead or iron,
stipulating that ten coins should weigh one liǎng,
with
"Tiānfú Yuánbǎo"
as the inscription,
and ordering the Salt and Iron Commission to issue the molds.
"Salt and Iron"
refers to the Salt and Iron Commission.
"Issue,"
pronunciation Hùjià.
37 Shí Guì, Left Imperial Guard General-in-Chief, was established as Prince of Zhèng,
and appointed as Prefect of Kāifēng.
The Zīzhì Tōngjiàn often records the enfeoffment of sons and nephews as princes with the term "enfeoff,"
but sometimes uses "establish,"
likely following the wording of contemporary historians,
without a fixed rule.
38 On the 63rd day, Guǐhài,
an edict was issued: previously, both government and private coin casting were permitted,
but due to concerns about the difficulty of obtaining copper,
it was allowed to cast coins of varying weights as convenient,
provided they were not defective or leaky.
Allowing private casting by the people
was already not a sustainable policy,
and moreover, allowing them to vary the weight as convenient
meant the people would certainly cast lighter coins.
Who would cast heavier ones?
The only worry was that the coins would not be light and thin enough.
If they became excessively light and thin,
they would inevitably become defective and leaky.
How could such coins remain in circulation for long?
39 On the 21st day, Xīnchǒu,
the Abdicated Emperor of Wú passed away.
He was thirty-eight years old.
Examination of discrepancies: The Old History of the Five Dynasties and the Supplementary Records of the Táng both state that Pǔ died in confinement over a year after abdicating.
The New History of the Five Dynasties simply states he died.
The History of the Ten Kingdoms states:
"Pǔ was able to entrust his fate and accept his end,
not suffering the calamity of usurpation and murder,
which shows he was deeply strategic."
The Annals of the Ten Kingdoms states:
"On Xīnchǒu,
the men of Táng murdered the Abdicated Emperor."
The matter cannot be clarified,
so here it is simply stated he passed away.
The ruler of Táng, regarding the death of the former ruler,
based the number of days for suspending court on the Hàn dynasty system where ministers observed mourning for their ruler by substituting days for months.
Since ancient times,
among rulers who changed dynasties, only the ruler of Táng treated the former ruler with such apparent generosity.
Judging by his true intentions,
this was like twisting one's elder brother's arm to take his food,
and after taking the food,
pulling his arm to massage it,
saying:
"I love my elder brother!"
Court,
pronunciation Zhíyáo.
That year,
the ruler of Táng transferred the Prince of Wú, Lǐ Jǐng, to be Prince of Qí.
40 Lǐ Cóngyǎn, the military commissioner of Fèngxiáng,
favored literary men but slighted military men,
loved the farmers but was strict with the soldiers,
causing the officers and men to resent him.
When troops were dispatched to garrison the western frontier,
after leaving the suburbs,
they mutinied,
stormed the city gates,
and plundered the markets.
They stormed the city gates and entered to plunder.
Plunder,
pronunciation Pǐmiào.
The mutinous soldiers were defeated,
fled eastward,
intending to appeal to the imperial court.
When they reached Huá Prefecture,
Zhāng Yànzé, the military commissioner of Zhènguó,
intercepted and attacked them,
and executed them all.
