Later Student from Tiāntāi
Fourth year of Tiānfú (Jǐhài, 939)
1 Spring,
first month,
on the 51st day, Xīnhài,
Zhāng Cóng'ēn, defense commissioner of Chán Prefecture and a native of Tàiyuán, was appointed Vice Commissioner of the Bureau of Military Affairs.
2 Zhāng Xīchóng, the military commissioner of Shuòfāng, passed away,
and the Qiāng and Hú tribes raided and plundered,
no longer showing any fear.
On the 54th day, Jiǎyín,
Féng Huī, the military commissioner of Yìchéng, was appointed military commissioner of Shuòfāng.
The Dǎngxiàng chieftain Tuòbá Yànchāo was the most powerful.
When Huī arrived,
Yànchāo came to offer congratulations,
entering Líng Prefecture city from his tribe to do so.
Huī then had a residence built for him in the city,
richly furnished with clothing and curios,
and detained him, not allowing him to leave.
The territory then became peaceful.
By holding Yànchāo hostage in the city,
the various Dǎngxiàng tribes did not dare to raid and plunder outside,
hence the peace.
3 The ministers of Táng, including Jiāngwáng Zhīzhèng and others, repeatedly submitted memorials requesting that the ruler of Táng restore the surname Lǐ,
establish the ancestral temple of the Táng dynasty,
on the Yǐchǒu day,
the ruler of Táng agreed.
The ministers further requested that he be honored with a reverential title,
but the ruler of Táng said:
"Reverential titles are empty praise,
and moreover, they are not ancient practices."
He therefore did not accept it.
Thereafter, his descendants all followed this precedent,
not accepting reverential titles,
nor employing maternal relatives to assist in governance,
not allowing eunuchs to participate in affairs,
all of which were unmatched by other states.
In the second month,
on the Yǐhài day,
the temple name of Tàizǔ was changed to Yìzǔ.
When the ruler of Táng first accepted the abdication,
he honored Xú Wēn as Tàizǔ;
now that he had restored the surname Lǐ,
he regarded Wēn as his righteous father,
hence he changed the temple name to Yìzǔ.
On the Jǐmǎo day,
the ruler of Táng held mourning ceremonies for his Lǐ lineage parents,
together with the empress, he wore the coarse mourning garments and resided in a mourning hut,
observing the rituals of initial mourning,
conducting morning and evening lamentations for a total of fifty-four days.
Jiāngwáng Zhīzhèng and Ráowáng Zhī'è requested to also wear the coarse mourning garments;
this was not permitted.
Zhīzhèng and Zhī'è were both sons of Xú Wēn.
It was as if mourning for one's own parents.
The wife of Lǐ Jiànxūn
was a daughter of Xú Wēn;
where power and profit lie,
kinship is formed not by blood but by closeness.
Zhǎng,
read as liǎng.
On the Xīnsì day,
an edict was issued entrusting state affairs to Qíwáng Jǐng for detailed decision-making,
with only military matters to be reported.
On the Gēngyín day,
the ruler of Táng changed his name to Biàn.
An edict was issued for the百官 to deliberate on the ritual for the joint offering to the two ancestral lines.
The two ancestral lines,
refer to the ancestors of the Xú and Lǐ surnames.
On the Xīnmǎo day,
Sòng Qíqiū and others proposed that Yìzǔ be placed in the eastern chamber of the seven rooms.
The ruler of Táng ordered Gāozǔ to be placed in the western chamber,
with Tàizōng next,
and Yìzǔ after that,
all as unremovable lords.
The ministers said:
"Yìzǔ was a feudal lord,
and should not enjoy offerings together with Gāozǔ and Tàizōng.
We request that a separate temple be built behind the main hall of the Grand Temple to offer sacrifices to him."
The Emperor said:
The Zizhi Tongjian refers to him as Emperor since the Jìn dynasty,
this character for Emperor is confused with the Emperor of Jìn,
this also follows the old histories of Jiāngnán,
and fails to make corrections.
"Since childhood, I entrusted myself to Yìzǔ,
the event is recorded in the 260th volume, in the second year of Qiánníng under Táng Zhāozōng.
How could I have initiated this restoration of the dynasty?"
The ministers then dared not speak further.
The ruler of Táng wished to claim descent from Wúwáng Kè,
but someone said:
"Kè was executed,
Wúwáng Kè died during the reign of Táng Gāozōng,
falsely implicated by Fáng Yí'ài,
and was not guilty of any crime.
The ruler of Táng ordered officials to investigate the descendants of the two kings,
and because Wúwáng's grandson Huī had achievements,
and Huī's son Xiàn served as prime minister,
during Xuánzōng's reign, Xìn'ānwáng Huī had achievements on the borders,
and Xiàn served as prime minister under Sùzōng.
Xiàn,
read as hù diǎn fān.
It was said that from Xiàn, it was five generations to his father Róng.
These names were all fabricated by the officials.
The Textual Analysis states: The Shízǔ of Zhōu Shìzōng and the Old History of the Five Dynasties claim that Biàn was a descendant of Táng Xuánzōng's sixth son, Yǒngwáng Lín,
while the Jiāngnán Lù states he was a great-great-grandson of Xiànzōng's eighth son, Jiànwáng Kè.
Lǐ Hào's Shízǔ of Shǔ Hòuzhǔ states:
"Táng's successor Xuēwáng Zhīróu served as the military governor of Lǐngnán,
and died in office.
His son Zhīgào wandered to Jiāng-Huái,
and thus became the adopted son of Xú Wēn."
The Wúyuè Bèishǐ states:
"Biàn was originally surnamed Pān,
from Ānjí, Húzhōu.
His father was a fort commander in Ānjí.
The Wú general Lǐ Shénfú attacked the Yìjǐn Army,
passed through Húzhōu,
captured Biàn and took him back,
making him a servant.
Xú Wēn once visited Shénfú,
admired Biàn's diligence and honesty,
and requested to adopt him as a son.
Because of the prophecy 'the carp of the Eastern Sea flies to the heavens,'
Biàn first served Shénfú,
later returned to Wēn,
thus falsely claiming the surname Lǐ to match the prophecy."
Liú Shù believed that Biàn's restoration of the surname and attachment to ancestors
was certainly not of the Lǐ lineage,
and as Wúyuè and Táng were enemy states,
this was also not a true record.
Biàn was orphaned young and suffered through turmoil,
and no one knew his ancestral lineage;
Biàn's great-grandfather Chāo,
grandfather Zhì,
had the same names as the great-grandfather and grandfather of Yìzǔ,
showing that these were all fabrications.
It is doubtful that ten generations is too few.
The officials said:
"Thirty years constitute a generation,
Your Majesty was born during the Wéndé era,
and it has already been fifty years."
Wéndé
was the reign title of the last years of Táng Xīzōng.
This means that from the birth of the ruler of Táng to this year was fifty years.
4 Lǔ Sǔn arrived in Fúzhōu,
Lǔ Sǔn was sent as an envoy with credentials to Mǐn last November,
and only now reached Fúzhōu.
He ordered his younger brother Jìgōng to host him.
He dispatched his Vice Minister of Rites, Zhèng Yuánbì, to present Jìgōng's memorial and accompany Sǔn to present tribute.
The ruler of Mǐn did not treat Sǔn with courtesy,
and a scholar named Lín Shěngzōu privately said to Sǔn:
"My lord does not serve his sovereign,
does not love his relatives,
does not care for his people,
does not revere the spirits,
is not friendly with his neighbors,
and does not treat his guests with courtesy."
The guest refers to Lǔ Sǔn.
"I will don monastic robes and flee north,
and we shall meet again in the superior state."
At that time, those who falsely claimed authority in remote regions referred to the Central Plains as the superior state.
In my view,
Lín Shěngzōu was also not a virtuous scholar,
having the ambition of Fán Ruòshuǐ but unable to fulfill it.
5 In the third month,
on the Gēngxū day,
the ruler of Táng posthumously honored Wúwáng Kè as Dìngzōng Xiàojìng Huángdì,
and posthumously honored all ancestors from his great-grandfather downward with temple names and posthumous titles.
6 On the Jǐwèi day,
an edict was issued adding the titles of Tóng Píngzhāng Shì to both Guīdé military governor Liú Zhīyuǎn and Zhōngwǔ military governor Dù Chóngwēi.
Zhīyuǎn believed that he had contributed to the founding of the dynasty,
while Chóngwēi rose through maternal relatives,
without great achievements,
and felt ashamed to receive the same appointment.
Appointment,
refers to the hemp edict of appointment.
Huáng Zhōng had achievements,
yet Guān Yǔ still felt ashamed to be ranked alongside him;
what kind of person is Dù Chóngwēi,
how could Liú Zhīyuǎn be willing to receive the same appointment as him!
The stubborn and unyielding spirit of a hero,
is generally like this.
He shut his doors and submitted four memorials declining the appointment.
The Emperor was angered,
and said to Zhào Yíng:
"Chóngwēi is my brother-in-law,
although Zhīyuǎn has achievements,
how can he firmly refuse the imperial appointment!
He may be stripped of his military authority."
Liú Zhīyuǎn at that time commanded the various imperial guard armies.
Yíng bowed and pleaded:
"When Your Majesty was in Jìnyáng,
with no more than five thousand troops,
attacked by over a hundred thousand Táng soldiers,
the event is recorded in the previous volume of the previous year.
If not for Zhīyuǎn's heart being like iron and stone,
how could the great enterprise have been achieved!
How can he be abandoned for a minor fault!
I fear that if these words are heard outside,
it would not demonstrate the magnanimity of a ruler."
The Emperor's anger then subsided,
and he ordered Duānmíngdiàn academician Hé Níng to go to Zhīyuǎn's residence to convey the imperial will.
Zhīyuǎn was alarmed,
rose and accepted the appointment.
When a ruler humbles himself to安抚 his ministers,
then the ministers also naturally repent.
To tame the fierce and unyielding spirit of meritorious veterans,
this approach is indispensable.
7 The garrison commander of Língzhōu, Wáng Yànzhōng, rebelled and occupied Huáiyuǎn City.
Huáiyuǎn County belonged to Língzhōu.
Zhào Xún's *Jù Mǐ Tú Jīng* states: The Táng dynasty Huáiyuǎn Garrison was located about one hundred and several tens of *lǐ* north of Língzhōu.
During the Sòng period, the Western Xià grew powerful,
and established Xīngzhōu in that area.
About ninety *lǐ* to its west was the Hèlán Mountains.
Yànzhōng surrendered,
but Yán Zuò killed him.
The Emperor was furious and said:
"Since I ascended the throne,
I have never broken faith with anyone.
Yànzhōng had already laid down his arms and come out to welcome us;
how could Yán Zuò dare to kill him!"
Yán Zuò was stripped of his official status,
severely caned, and exiled.
Commentators still believed Yán Zuò should not have escaped the death penalty.
Because he killed those who surrendered and broke faith,
from now on there would be no way to win over people from distant regions.
8 On Xīnyǒu day,
the Uighur Khagan Rénměi was enfeoffed as the Fènghuà Khagan.
At that time, the Uighurs had been sending envoys to present tribute for several consecutive years,
hence the enfeoffment.
According to the *Wǔdài Huìyào*: The Uighurs were defeated by the Kirghiz during the Huìchāng era of the Táng dynasty,
fled west, and settled in Gānzhōu.
In the first year of Qiánhuà of the Liáng dynasty, they sent envoys to present tribute.
In the second year of Tóngguāng of the Táng dynasty, in the fourth month,
the acting Khagan of their state, Rénměi, sent envoys to present tribute.
Zhèng Jì and Hé Yánsì were ordered to hold the credentials and enfeoff Rénměi as the Yīngyì Khagan.
In the eleventh month of that year,
Rénměi died.
His younger brother Díyín succeeded him,
and sent the Commander Ān Qiān and others to court with tribute.
Díyín died,
Āduōyù was established,
and also sent envoys with tribute.
In the third year of Tiānchéng,
their acting Khagan Rényù sent envoys to present tribute.
In the third month of that year,
an envoy was ordered to enfeoff Rényù as the Shùnhuà Khagan.
In the third year of Tiānfú of the Jìn dynasty,
they sent envoys to court with tribute;
in the fourth year, in the third month,
they again sent envoys to court,
along with local products as tribute.
That month,
the Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud, Xíng Dézhāo, was ordered to hold the credentials and proceed to enfeoff him as the Fènghuà Khagan.
If based on the *Huìyào*,
then
"Rénměi"
should be
"Rényù".
9 In summer,
the fourth month,
the Táng dynasty's Prince of Jiāng, Xú Zhīzhèng, and others requested to also adopt the surname Lǐ;
they wished to change their original surname to the imperial surname to show closeness.
10 On Xīnsì day,
the Táng sovereign performed the suburban sacrifice to Heaven;
on Guǐwèi day,
a general amnesty was declared.
11 Since Emperor Tàizǔ of Liáng,
for major military and state affairs,
the Son of Heaven often consulted with the Chóngzhèng and Shūmì envoys.
The Liáng consulted with the Chóngzhèng envoys,
the Táng consulted with the Shūmì envoys.
The Chóngzhèng envoy was the same office as the Shūmì envoy.
They handled the issuance of edicts,
discussed precedents and regulations,
and managed literary affairs, nothing more.
The Emperor, wary of the autocratic and domineering ways of Ān Zhònghuì during the reign of Emperor Míngzōng of Táng,
(the matter of Ān Zhònghuì's autocracy is recorded in the Annals of Emperor Míngzōng of Táng.)
(The pronunciation of "橫" is hèng,
with the *fǎnqiè* spelling "hù mèng fān".)
only appointed Sāng Wéihàn to concurrently serve as Shūmì envoy.
When Liú Chùràng became Shūmì envoy,
his memorials and responses often did not meet the Emperor's wishes.
(The matter of Liú Chùràng usurping Sāng Wéihàn's position as Shūmì envoy is recorded in the previous year's scroll above.)
(The pronunciation of "稱" is chèng,
with the *fǎnqiè* spelling "chǐ zhèng fān".)
On Jiǎshēn day,
the Shūmìyuàn was abolished.
Its seal was handed over to the Zhōngshūshěng,
and all its affairs were entrusted to the chancellors to handle separately.
Vice Envoy Zhāng Cóng'ēn was appointed Xuānyuánshǐ.

Academicians-in-Waiting, Director of the Bureau of Revenues Sītú Xǔ and Director of the Bureau of Works Yán Kàn were both dismissed from their concurrent posts and returned to their substantive offices.
(Zhèng Qiáo's *Shìzú Lüè* states: According to *Dìwáng Shìjì*,
Shùn served as Yáo's Minister of Education (Sītú),
and his descendants took that as their surname.)
(Academician-in-Waiting refers to Shūmìzhí Xuéshì.)
(The substantive offices of these two men were
in the Bureau of Revenues and the Bureau of Works.)
(The pronunciation of "衎" is kàn,
with the *fǎnqiè* spelling "kǔ hàn fān".)
Accustomed to the old system,
he often wished to restore it.
The historian states that when an emperor appoints a chancellor,
he should fully entrust him with governmental affairs,
and should not establish a Shūmì envoy to divide his power.
12 The Emperor, considering that the Táng dynasty's high officials who had been stripped of their ranks and were living in the two capitals were all impoverished and haggard,
(The dismissal of Lǐ Zhuānměi and others is recorded in the first year of the previous scroll above.)
(The pronunciation of "悴" is cuì,
with the *fǎnqiè* spelling "qín zuì fān".)
on Bǐngxū day,
appointed Hán Zhāoyìn as Minister of War,
Mǎ Yǐnsūn as Tutor to the Heir Apparent,
and Fáng Gǎo as General of the Right Flank Guards of the Rapid as Cavalry,
and all were granted retirement.
13 The Mǐn sovereign was jealous of the talent and reputation of his paternal uncles, the former Prefect of Jiànzhōu Yánwǔ and the Minister of Revenue Yánwàng.
The shaman Lín Xīng bore a grudge against Yánwǔ.
He pretended to convey words from ghosts and spirits, saying:
"Yánwǔ and Yánwàng are about to rebel."
The Mǐn sovereign did not further interrogate,
but sent Xīng with strong men to their residences to kill them,
along with their five sons.
The Mǐn sovereign, following the advice of Chén Shǒuyuán,
built a Sānqīng Hall within the palace grounds.
(In Daoism, Shàngqīng, Yùqīng, and Tàiqīng are the Three Purities.)
Day and night, music was played,
incense was burned, and prayers and sacrifices were offered,
seeking the divine elixir.
Regardless of the importance of governmental affairs,
they were all decided by Lín Xīng transmitting the commands of the Bǎohuáng.
14 On Wùshēn day,
the Prince of Chǔ, Xī Fàn, was promoted to Tiāncè Shàngjiāngjūn,
granted a seal,
and permitted to establish a personal administration and appoint officials.
(In the fourth year of Kāipíng of the Liáng dynasty, the Prince of Chǔ, Mǎ Yīn, had already been promoted to Tiāncè Shàngjiāngjūn;
now the Jìn again bestowed this title upon his son Xī Fàn.)
15 On Xīnhài day,
the Táng transferred Prince Jí Jǐngsuì to become Prince of Shòu,
and established the Duke of Shòuyáng, Jǐngdá, as Prince of Xuānchéng.
16 On Yǐmǎo day,
the Táng dynasty's Military Commissioner of Zhènhǎi and concurrently Zhōngshūlìng, Prince of Liánghuái, Xú Zhī'è, died.
17 The Táng people moved the clan of the Abdicated Emperor to Tàizhōu,
naming it the Yǒngníng Palace,
with very strict security.
(Tàizhōu was originally Hǎilíng County of Yángzhōu.
During the Wú dynasty, in the Qiánzhēn era, a Control Commission was established.
In the first year of Shēngyuán of the Southern Táng, it was elevated to Tàizhōu.)
*Kǎoyì* states: According to *Shíguó Jìnián*:
"The Táng people moved the clan of the Abdicated Emperor to Tàizhōu,
naming it the Yǒngníng Palace.
The guard was extremely strict;
they did not dare to intermarry with the people of the state.
After a long time, the men and women matched themselves as couples."
*Jiāngbiǎo Zhì* states:
"When the son of the Abdicated Emperor reached five years of age,
a palace envoy was sent to confer an official title
and bestow court robes.
He died that very day."
According to this, when Emperor Lièzǔ of Táng received the abdication,
he had the Abdicated Emperor reside in his former palace,
present himself as a subject, and submit memorials,
admiring his reputation for benevolence and magnanimity.
If he hated the Yáng clan, he would have simply exterminated them.
Why would he go to such迂 lengths!
Other books do not mention this.
It is unknown what source *Jìnián* relied upon.
I do not adopt it here.
He was dismissed and returned to the Yǒngníng Palace.
(The Kānghuà Army was also a military district established by the Wú within its territory,
or perhaps established by the Southern Táng.
Its location is now impossible to verify.)
On Yǐchǒu day,
the Military Commissioner of Pínglú and concurrently Zhōngshūlìng, Yáng Liǎn, was appointed Military Commissioner of Kānghuà.
Liǎn firmly declined,
requesting to complete the mourning period.
(To complete the mourning for the Abdicated Emperor.)
18 The Táng sovereign intended to establish Prince of Qí, Jǐng, as Crown Prince.
Jǐng firmly declined.

He was then appointed Grand Marshal of the Armies of All Circuits, Supervisor of the Six Armies and Various Guards, Grand Commandant, Director of the Department of State Affairs, and Governor of Shēng and Yáng Prefectures.
(The Southern Táng made Shēngzhōu the Western Capital,
and Yángzhōu the Eastern Capital,
hence these two prefectures had governors.)
19 The Mǐn dynasty's Supervisor of the Six Armies and Various Guards, Prince Jiàn Jìyán, had won the hearts of the soldiers.
The Mǐn sovereign was jealous of him.
In the sixth month,
he was stripped of his military authority,
and his name was changed to Jìyù.
His younger brother Jìróng
was made Supervisor of the Six Armies,
removing the words "and Various Guards".
Lín Xīng's deception was discovered,
and he was exiled to Quánzhōu.
An observer of celestial phenomena said there would be a disaster in the palace.
On Yǐwèi day,
the Mǐn sovereign moved to reside in the Chángchūn Palace.
20 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on Gēngzǐ, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
The military commissioner of Chéngdé, Ān Chóngróng, rose from the ranks of common soldiers.
His nature was coarse and rash.
"Coarse"
is the same as "rough."
He often said to people:
"In this age, the one who becomes Son of Heaven
is simply the one with strong soldiers and sturdy horses."
Ān Chóngróng was merely a violent brute;
even if he had acted with force, what could he have achieved?
However, the reason he dared to act forcefully
was also because he was accustomed to seeing the affairs of that time,
and thus developed presumptuous ambitions.
Once, holding a bow and arrows, he said to his attendants:
"If I can hit the dragon
on the pole,
I must possess the Mandate of Heaven."
With one shot he hit it,
and from then on became even more self-assured.
When the Emperor dispatched Chóngróng to replace Mì Qióng,
see the second year in the previous scroll.
"If Qióng does not accept the replacement,
We shall assign you another military command.
Do not seize it by force,
lest the trouble grow deeper."
Chóngróng therefore considered the Emperor timid,
and said to people:
"Mì Qióng is just an ordinary fellow,
yet the Son of Heaven still fears him.
How much more so for someone of my importance as a general and minister,
with numerous troops and horses!"
His memorials and requests were often excessive,
and were approved or rejected by those in power.
If approved, he followed them;
if rejected, he did not comply.
He then gathered desperadoes,
purchased warhorses,
and harbored soaring ambitions.
The Emperor learned of this.
The military commissioner of Yìwǔ, Huángfǔ Yù, was related by marriage to Chóngróng.
On the jiǎchén day,
Yù was transferred to be the military commissioner of Zhāoyì.
Since Zhèn and Dìng shared a border,
the Emperor feared they might join forces and cause trouble,
so he transferred Yù farther away to separate them.
On the yǐsì day,
the northern palace of Mǐn caught fire,
and the palace buildings were almost completely burned down.
On the wùshēn day,
Xuē Róng and others presented the compiled statutes they had finalized,
and they were implemented.
In the third year,
Xuē Róng and others were ordered to carefully determine the compiled statutes;
now they were finally presented and implemented.
"Presented"
is pronounced shàng, shí zhǎng fān.
On the bǐngchén day,
an edict was issued:
"Previously, it was ordered that both public and private parties throughout the land may cast coins.
See the previous year in the previous scroll.
As they are small, weak, flawed, and thin,
they should all be prohibited,
and only the official authorities shall be allowed to cast them."

The留守 of the Western Capital, Yáng Guāngyuǎn, submitted a memorial accusing the Vice Director of the Secretariat and同平章事 Sāng Wéihàn of unfair promotions and demotions, and of operating shops and markets in both capitals,
competing with the people for profit.
The Emperor had no choice;
in the intercalary month,
on the rénshēn day,
he sent Wéihàn out to be the military commissioner of Zhāngdé兼侍中.
Initially,
Wáng Wēi, son of the military commissioner of Yìwǔ Wáng Chùzhí,
to avoid the troubles caused by Wáng Dū,
fled to the Khitan.
The troubles caused by Wáng Dū
refer to his imprisonment of Chùzhí;
see the first year of the Lóngdé era of Emperor Mò of Liáng in scroll 271.
"Troubles"
is pronounced nàn, nǎi dàn fān.
The military command of Yìwǔ lacked a commander.
Huángfǔ Yù was transferred to Lù,
hence Yìwǔ lacked a commander.
"Commander"
is pronounced shuài, suǒ lèi fān.
"We request that Wēi be allowed to inherit his father's territory,
according to the laws of our dynasty."
"Our dynasty"
refers to the Khitan themselves.
"Dynasty"
is pronounced cháo, zhí yáo fān.
"According to the laws of the Central Kingdom, one must progress in sequence from prefect, to团练, to防御, and finally to military commissioner.
We request that Wēi be sent here,
and gradually promoted and employed."
The Khitan ruler was angered,
and again sent an envoy to say:
"You yourself rose from military commissioner to become Son of Heaven.
Was there any such sequence of ranks?"
The Emperor, fearing the situation would escalate endlessly,
sent generous bribes to the Khitan,
and also requested that Wáng Tíngyìn, the grandson of Chùzhí's elder brother and the military commissioner of Zhāngdé, be appointed as the military commissioner of Yìwǔ to satisfy their wishes.
The Khitan's anger gradually subsided.
Initially,
the Mǐn Emperor Huìzōng formed the拱宸控鹤都 from the original followers of太祖.
The temple name of the King of Mǐn, Wáng Shěnzhī, was太祖.
"Followers"
is pronounced cóng, cái yòng fān;
the same below.
He further recruited two thousand strong men as his trusted confidants,
named them the宸卫都,
and their salaries and rewards were more generous than those of the two other units.
Some said the two other units resented this,
and were about to rebel.
The ruler of Mǐn intended to assign them separately to the two prefectures of Zhāng and Quán,
which made the two units even angrier.
The ruler of Mǐn was fond of holding all-night drinking parties,
forcing his ministers to drink.
When they were drunk, he would order his attendants to watch for their faults.
His younger cousin Jìlóng, drunk and having breached etiquette, was executed.
He repeatedly executed members of the imperial clan out of suspicion and anger.
His uncle, the Left Vice Director and同平章事 Yánxī, pretended to be mad and foolish to avoid disaster.
The ruler of Mǐn bestowed upon him Daoist robes,
and placed him in the Wǔyí Mountains.
The Wǔyí Mountains are located thirty lǐ south of Chóng'ān County in Jiàn Prefecture.
In the preface to the "Wǔyí Illustrations," Zhū Yuánhuì said: The name of Lord Wǔyí
was recorded since the Hàn dynasty.
He was offered sacrifices with dried fish,
but it is unknown what deity he actually was.
Nowadays, there is a mountain in Chóng'ān named Wǔyí,
traditionally said to be the dwelling place of immortals.
Its peaks, cliffs, and ravines
are elegant, lofty, strange, and grand.
The clear stream with nine bends
flows through them.
On the sheer cliffs of both banks,
in places inaccessible to humans,
there are often withered logs inserted into rock crevices,
used to support boats, coffins, and the like.
Inside the coffins are remains,
with pottery vessels arranged outside,
still not decayed.
It is rather suspected that in ancient times, when roads were blocked and impassable,
and rivers were obstructed and not yet cleared,
these were the dwellings of barbarian customs.
The one the Hàn people sacrificed to was their chieftain.
Probably also a recluse who withdrew from the world,
who was revered by the masses during his lifetime,
and after death was transmitted as an immortal.
There is a Daoist temple in the Wǔyí Mountains;
the ruler of Mǐn probably placed Yánxī in this temple.
He was confined in a private residence.
The ruler of Mǐn repeatedly insulted the commanders of the拱宸 and控鹤 armies, Zhū Wénjìn of Yǒngtài and Lián Chóngyù of Guāngshān,
and both men resented him.
When the northern palace caught fire,
the arsonist could not be found.
The ruler of Mǐn ordered Chóngyù to lead the inner and outer garrison troops to clean up the ashes,
employing ten thousand men daily,
which caused the soldiers great hardship.
He also suspected that Chóngyù knew about the arson plot,
and intended to execute him.
The inner academician Chén Tán privately informed Chóngyù.
On the xīnsì night,
Chóngyù was on duty in the palace.
He led the troops of the two units to set fire to the Chángchūn Palace
and attack the ruler of Mǐn.
They sent someone to fetch Yánxī from amidst the rubble,
and hailed him with "Long live!"
They also summoned the outer garrison troops to jointly attack the ruler of Mǐn.
Only the宸卫都 resisted and fought.
The ruler of Mǐn then went with Empress Lǐ to the宸卫都.
Empress Lǐ
was Lǐ Chūnyàn.
"Went"
means to go to.
The rebel troops set fire to the宸卫都.
The宸卫都 was defeated in battle,
and the remaining thousand or so men escorted the ruler of Mǐn and Empress Lǐ out of the north gate,
reaching Wútóng Ridge,
where the crowd gradually scattered and fled.
Yánxī sent his elder brother's son, the former prefect of Tīng Prefecture, Jìyè, to lead troops in pursuit.
They caught up at a village house.
The ruler of Mǐn was skilled at archery,
and drew his bow, killing several men.
Soon, the pursuing troops gathered like clouds.
Knowing escape was impossible,
the ruler of Mǐn threw down his bow and said to Jìyè:
"Where is your loyalty as a subject?"
Jìyè replied:
"If the ruler lacks the virtue of a ruler,
how can the subject have the loyalty of a subject?
The new ruler
is your uncle;
the old ruler
is your brother.
Which is closer, which is more distant?"
The ruler of Mǐn said no more.
Jìyè returned with him.
Upon reaching Tuózhuāng,
he gave him wine to drink,
and when he was drunk, strangled him.
Empress Lǐ and all the sons, including Wáng Jìgōng, were also killed.
The remaining troops of the宸卫都 fled to Wúyuè.
Yán Xī proclaimed himself Military Commissioner of Wǔwēi and King of the Mǐn Kingdom,
changed his name to Xī,
and adopted the era name Yǒnglóng.
Examination of Discrepancies states: According to the Shíguó Jìnián,
in the fourth year of Tōngwén,
Yán Xī proclaimed himself Military Commissioner of Wǔwēi,
changed the era name to Yǒnglóng,
which corresponds to the fourth year of Tiānfú of Jìn.

The Veritable Records of Emperor Shìzōng of Zhōu, the Old History of the Five Dynasties, the Táng Yúlù, the Veritable Records of Emperor Lièzǔ of Nán Táng, the Bèishǐ of Wúyuè, the Yùnlì Tú, and the Jìnián Tōngpǔ all concur.
Only the Qǐyùn Tú of Mǐn states:
"In the fourth year of Tōngwén, jǐhài,
intercalary seventh month,
Yán Xī was established,
the following year, gēngzǐ,
the era name was changed to Yǒnglóng,
in the fifth year, jiǎchén,
he was assassinated."
Lín Rénzhì was a native of the Mǐn Kingdom,
and his record of Yán Xī's change of era name should not be erroneous.
However, scholars of the Five Dynasties often compiled national histories not based on old texts,
but from memory and hearsay,
so even recent events of their own states sometimes contain contradictions.
Gāo Yuǎn's narrative is quite coherent,
and although Yú Gōngchuò lived after Rénzhì,
he was also a native of Mǐn,
therefore I dare not solely follow Rénzhì's record.
Moreover, after Wáng Xī was established,
if he only claimed to be a military commissioner,
then he should not have changed the era name and appointed his ministers as the Three Dukes and Chancellors.
According to the Veritable Records of Emperor Gāozǔ of Jìn,
on the jiǎshēn day of the eleventh month in the fifth year of Tiānfú,
Yán Xī, King of the Mǐn Kingdom, was appointed Military Commissioner of Wǔwēi and King of the Mǐn Kingdom.
This shows that Xī had already proclaimed himself King of the Mǐn Kingdom earlier,
and the Shíguó Jìnián omitted this.
He bestowed rewards throughout the court and the country.
He reported the assassination of the Mǐn ruler by the Imperial Guards to neighboring states;
posthumously honored the Mǐn ruler as Emperor Shèngshén Yīngruì Wénmíng Guǎngwǔ Yìngdào Dàhóng Xiào,
with the temple name Kāngzōng.
He sent merchants by secret routes to present memorials and pledge allegiance to Jìn;
however, within his own state,
he established all official positions according to the system of the Son of Heaven.
He appointed Lǐ Zhēn, who had retired as Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince, as Minister of Works concurrently serving as Vice Director of the Secretariat and Chancellor.
When Lián Chóngyù attacked Kāngzōng,
Chén Shǒuyuán was in the palace,
changed clothes intending to flee,
but soldiers killed him.
Chén Shǒuyuán had deluded the rulers of Mǐn for two generations,
his death came too late!
He was executed for the crime of selling official positions.
After Wáng Xī of Mǐn was established,
he sent an envoy to execute Lín Xīng in Quánzhōu.
Lín Xīng was exiled to Quánzhōu; see above, sixth month.
The Shǔ edition
writes "execute"
as
"pursue."
28 The Yellow River breached at Bózhōu.
"Bózhōu"
should be
"Bózhōu."
29 In the eighth month,
on the xīnchǒu day,
Féng Dào was appointed as Defender of the Minister of Education and concurrently Palace Attendant.
On the rěnyín day,
an edict was issued that the seal of the Secretariat should only be entrusted to the senior chancellor,
according to the old system: chancellors took turns daily holding the seal.
All were entrusted to Dào.
The Emperor once consulted him on military strategy,
to which he replied:
"Matters of war and conquest
are for Your Majesty's own decisive judgment.
I am but a scholar,
who only knows to carefully adhere to the established regulations of past dynasties."
The Emperor agreed.
Dào once pleaded illness and requested to retire,
the Emperor sent Prince Zhèng, Chóngguì, to visit him at his residence,
saying:
"If you do not come out tomorrow,
I will personally go to you."
Dào then came out to attend to affairs.
At that time, his favor and treatment
were unmatched by any other minister.
30 On the jǐyǒu day,
Yuán Guàn, King of Wúyuè, was appointed Grand Marshal of All Under Heaven's Military Affairs.
31 Péng Shìchóu, Prefect of Xīzhōu within the jurisdiction of Qiánnán, led over ten thousand barbarians from Jiǎng and Jǐnzhōu to invade Chén and Lǐzhōu.
During the prosperous era of Táng,
Xīzhōu was under the jurisdiction of the Qiánzhōng Surveillance Commissioner.
In the late Táng, the Qiánzhōng Surveillance Commission was elevated to the Qiánnán Military Commission,
later called the Wǔtài Army,
at that time within Shǔ territory.
"Within the jurisdiction"
means within the area under patrol.
"Jiǎng"
should be
"Jiǎng."
In the fourth year of Cháng'ān of Táng, Wǔzhōu was established from the two counties of Yèláng and Wèixī of Yuánzhōu.
In the thirteenth year of Kāiyuán, because
"Wǔ"
and
"Wǔ"
sounded similar,
it was renamed Hèzhōu,
in the twentieth year it was renamed Yèzhōu,
and in the fifth year of Dàlì it was renamed Jiǎngzhōu.
Chén and Lǐzhōu were then under Chǔ.
Qián,
pronounced qú jīn fān,
also qí lián fān.
They sent envoys to Shǔ to request troops;
the ruler of Shǔ, considering the distance,
did not grant it.
In the ninth month,
on the xīnwèi day,
King Xīfàn of Chǔ ordered Liú Qíng, Commander of the Left Jìngjiāng, and Liào Kuāngqí, Commander of Juéshèng, to lead five thousand troops from Héngshān to suppress them.
32 On the guǐwèi day,
Cóngyì, Prince Xǔ of Táng, was enfeoffed as Duke of Xún,
to continue the sacrifices of Táng.
Cóngyì was still young,
Empress Lǐ raised Cóngyì in the palace,
serving Wáng Shū as if she were her mother.
Empress Lǐ
was the daughter of Empress Cáo, wife of Emperor Míngzōng of Táng.
Wáng Shū,
was the secondary consort of Míngzōng,
therefore the Empress served her as a mother.
33 In winter,
tenth month,
on the gēngxū day,
the envoy Zhèng Yuánbì sent by Kāngzōng of Mǐn arrived at Dàliáng.
In the twelfth month of this year,
Mǐn sent Zhèng Yuánbì to accompany Lú Sǔn to present tribute,
arriving at Dàliáng by now,
but Kāngzōng had already been assassinated by the people of Mǐn in the intercalary seventh month.
"The Mǐn Kingdom, once rising to fortune,
has passed many years,
seeing the imperial throne of the North Star frequently shift,"
meaning China had repeatedly changed rulers.
Therefore, they did not perform their tribute duties.
The Emperor was angered by their disrespect,
on the rénzǐ day,
he issued an edict rejecting their tribute goods and the shipments from Fú and Jiànzhōu,
and ordered Yuánbì and the tribute officer Lín Ēn to escort them back quickly.
Lǐ Zhīsǔn, Vice Director of the Ministry of War, submitted a memorial stating:
"Wáng Chǎng has been arrogant and disrespectful,
we should detain his envoys,
and confiscate their goods."
Thus, Yuánbì and Ēn were imprisoned.
34 The Lady Mǎ, Gōngmù of Wúyuè, passed away.
The Lady
was the daughter of Mǎ Chuò, Military Commissioner of Xióngwǔ.
Lù Zhèn's Jiǔguó Zhì states: Mǎ Chuò,
a native of Yúháng,
in his youth served Dǒng Chāng together with Qián Liú,
married his younger sister to Liú,
and Liú in turn married Yuán Guàn to Chuò's daughter.
According to the Old History of the Five Dynasties,
in the fourth year of Zhēnmíng of Liáng,
Mǎ Chuò, Military Commissioner of Qínzhōu, Acting Grand Tutor, and Chancellor, was promoted to Acting Grand Preceptor.
Qínzhōu
was the Xióngwǔ Army.
The biography of Liú also states: Liú relied on his exalted status,
divided Liǎngzhè into several military commands,
appointing military commissioners and then reporting it.
Thus, all military commissioners within his state received court appointments.
King Wǔsù, Liú, prohibited the keeping of singing girls and entertainers both inside and outside the court,
King Wénmù, Yuán Guàn, was over thirty without a son,
the Lady pleaded with Liú on his behalf,
Liú joyfully said:
"The sacrifices of our family,
you indeed preside over them."
According to ritual: the principal wife presides over the sacrifices of the ancestors.
Now, Lady Mǎ, not jealous, broadened the succession,
therefore Liú was pleased that the responsibility was entrusted.
She gave birth to Hóng Zǔn, Hóng Cóng;
Lady Xǔ
gave birth to Hóng Zuǒ;
Lady Wú
gave birth to Hóng Chù;
various concubines gave birth to Hóng Zhǎn, Hóng Yì,
Hóng Wò, Hóng Yǎng, Hóng Xìn;
the Lady cared for and looked after them all with equal kindness and love.
She often placed a silver deer in front of the bed curtain,
seating the children on it to play.
35 In the eleventh month,
on the wùzǐ day,
the Khitan sent their subject Yáozhé as an envoy,
who then proceeded to Wúyuè.
Proceed,
means to go.
Envoy,
pronounced shū lì fān.
36. King Xīfàn of Chǔ first established the Tiāncè Mansion.
In the summer of that year, he was appointed as Grand General of Tiāncè,
and it was at this time that he began to establish the mansion.
Positions such as Commandant
and Army Marshal were established,
with his younger brothers and military officers appointed to these roles.
He also appointed eighteen of his staff, including Tuòbá Héng, Lǐ Hónggāo, Liào Kuāngtú, and Xú Zhòngyǎ, as Academicians.
This followed the example of Emperor Tàizōng of Táng's Tiāncè Mansion Literary Academy in establishing the Academician positions.

Lù Zhèn's *Jiǔ Guó Zhì* records Lǐ Duó, Pān Qǐ, Cáo Tuō, Lǐ Zhuāng, Xú Mù, Péng Jìyīng, Péi Háng, Hé Zhòngjǔ, Mèng Xuánhuī, Liú Zhāoyǔ, Dèng Yìwén, Lǐ Hóngjié, Xiāo Zhū, Péng Jìxūn, along with Tuòbá Héng and three others, making a total of eighteen people.
Héng,
the pronunciation of his surname is Hùdēng.
Liú Qíng and others advanced to attack Xīzhōu.
Péng Shìchóu's troops were defeated,
and he abandoned the prefecture and fled to defend a mountain stronghold;
the stone cliffs were sheer on all four sides.
Qíng built ladders and plank paths to surround it from above.
Liào Kuāngqí died in battle.
King Xīfàn of Chǔ sent condolences to his mother.
His mother did not weep,
and said to the envoy:
"Our Liào family of three hundred members has received the king's bounty of warmth and sustenance.
For the entire clan to give their lives in service
would still be insufficient to repay it,
let alone the loss of one son!
I hope the king will not dwell on this matter."
The king considered his mother virtuous,
and generously provided for his family.
37. In the twelfth month,
on the day Bǐngxū,
an edict was issued prohibiting the construction of Buddhist temples.
38. The King of Mǐn built a new palace
and moved to reside there.
The northern palace of Mǐn had been destroyed by fire,
so Xī renovated it into a new palace and moved in.
39. That year,
the Vice Director of the Chancellery and Tongpingzhangshi of Hàn, Zhào Guāngyì, said to the ruler of Hàn:
"Since Empress Mǎ passed away,
(the ruler of Hàn married a woman from Chǔ;
Empress Mǎ died in the first year of the Táng Qīngtài era).
Kinship, neighborly relations, and old friendships
should not be forgotten."
(The Liú and Mǎ families intermarried,
hence 'kinship';
Tán and Guǎng shared a border,
hence 'neighborly relations'.
Friendship,
pronounced Hàodào.)
The ruler of Hàn agreed;
Chǔ also sent an envoy in return.
Guāngyì served as chancellor of Hàn for over twenty years,
during which the treasury was full,
and the borders were free from worry.
After his death,

the ruler of Hàn again appointed his son, the Hanlin Academician Recipient of Edicts and Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, Zhào Sǔn, as Vice Director of the Chancellery and Tongpingzhangshi.
1. In spring,
the first month,
the Emperor received the Mǐn envoy Zhèng Yuánbì and others in audience.
Yuánbì said:
"King Chǎng is a ruler of barbarian tribes,
who does not understand ritual and righteousness.
If Your Majesty hears good words from him, it is not cause for joy;
if you hear harsh words, it is not cause for anger.
I, your envoy, have failed in my mission.
I am willing to submit to the executioner's axe to atone for Chǎng's crime."
The Emperor pitied him,
and on the day Xīnwèi,
issued an edict releasing Yuánbì and the others.
*Kǎoyì* says: *Luòzhōng Jìyì* states:
"After Chǎng was censured by the court's order,
he sent an envoy across the sea to pay tribute to the Qìdān,
offering the confiscated goods as tribute.
The Jìn ancestor was then using humble language to serve the northern ruler,
and the northern ruler issued a false edict saying:
'The gifts from the Mǐn state are all to be given to Qiáo Róng,
and its envoys are to be released to return to their own country.'
The Jìn ancestor did not dare to refuse.
Later, Chǎng again sent an envoy to the Qìdān to request horses,
traveling south via the Cāng, Qí, and Huáidiàn routes.
From then on, such exchanges occurred repeatedly,
and people of the time were all filled with indignation and regret."
According to this, Chǎng was assassinated in the intercalary seventh month of the fourth year of Tiānfú.
In the tenth month, Yuánbì and others arrived in the capital and were imprisoned.
How could Chǎng have known about this and informed the Qìdān!
This account is not adopted here.
2. The Chǔ general Liú Qíng and others, taking advantage of a strong wind,
used fire arrows to burn Péng Shìchóu's stronghold and attacked it.
Shìchóu led his followers and fled into the deep mountains of Jiǎng and Jǐn.
On the day Yǐwèi,
he sent his son Shígǎo to lead the various chieftains in presenting the seals of Xī, Jǐn, and Jiǎng prefectures,
and requested to surrender to Chǔ.
(This sets the stage for Péng Shígǎo's loyal service to the Mǎ family.)
Shì,
is read as Shuài.
3. In the second month,
on the day Gēngxū,
the Northern Capital Garrison Commander and Tongpingzhangshi Ān Yánwēi came to court.
(The Northern Capital has been located in Tàiyuán since the Later Táng.) The Emperor said to Yánwēi:
"What I value are trust and righteousness.
In the past, the Qìdān saved us out of righteousness,
and now I repay them with trust.
I have heard their demands are incessant.
If you can humble yourself to serve them,
it would greatly accord with my wishes."
He replied:
"For the sake of the common people, Your Majesty
still uses humble words and generous gifts to serve them.
How could there be any humiliation in my doing so!"
The Emperor was pleased.
4. Liú Qíng led his troops back to Chángshā.
King Xīfàn of Chǔ relocated Xīzhōu to a more convenient location.
(A convenient location means
moving it closer to the Chǔ border,
to facilitate the enforcement of orders.) He appointed Liú Qíng as Prefect of Jǐnzhōu.
From then on, the Mán people of Jǐ submitted to Chǔ.
Xīfàn considered himself a descendant of the Fubo General.
(The Hàn general Mǎ Yuán was the Fubo General.)
He had a bronze pillar cast,
twelve feet high,
with six feet buried in the ground.
An inscription of the oath was engraved on it,
and it was erected in Xīzhōu.
(Today, one li southwest of Huìxīchéng in Chénzhōu there is a bronze pillar,
which is the one erected by Mǎ Xīfàn.
The Tiāncè Mansion Academician Lǐ Gāo composed the inscription for it.)
5. The Táng Kanghuà Military Commissioner and concurrently Zhongshu Ling Yáng Liǎn, after paying respects at the Pínglíng tomb,
(Pínglíng is likely the tomb of Yáng Liǎn's father, the Abdicated Emperor.)
was returning,
(the pronunciation of 'return' is Cóngxuān,
or also Rúzì.)
when he became heavily intoxicated
and died on the boat.
(This was orchestrated by the Táng ruler.)
Lù Zhèn's *Jiǔ Guó Zhì* says: Yáng Liǎn paid respects at the imperial tomb,
and upon reaching Zhúxiǎokǒu,
moored the boat and became heavily intoxicated,
dying overnight.
He was posthumously enfeoffed and given the title Hóngnóng Jìng Wáng.
(Based on the commandery from which the Yáng clan ancestors received their enfeoffment, he was posthumously enfeoffed as Prince of Hóngnóng,
with the posthumous title Jìng.)
6. After King Xī of Mǐn ascended the throne,
he became arrogant, licentious, harsh, and cruel,
suspicious and jealous of his clan members,
often dredging up old grievances.
His younger brother, the Prefect of Jiànzhōu, Yánzhèng, repeatedly admonished him by letter.
Xī became angry
and wrote back insulting him.
He sent his close official Yè Qiāo to supervise the army in Jiànzhōu.
(Shǐ Zhào says:
"Yè"
should be
"Yè".
According to the *Fēngsú Tōng*,
during the Hàn dynasty there was a Magistrate of Liáng named Yè Fèng.)
Supervisor,
pronounced Gǔxián.
(Note: Fúzhōu borders Jiànzhōu to the northwest.
The ruler of Mǐn probably stationed the Nánzhèn Army on the border between Fú and Jiàn prefectures,
to control the strategic passage between them.
Hence, later, when Wáng Yánzhèng attacked Nánzhèn, the garrison troops on the western border of Fúzhōu all collapsed.)
From this, the brothers' mutual suspicion and hatred deepened.
One day,
when Qiāo and Yánzhèng disagreed during a discussion,
Qiāo rebuked him, saying:
"Are you rebelling?!"
Yánzhèng became furious
and wanted to behead Qiāo.
Qiāo fled to Nánzhèn.
Yánzhèng dispatched troops to attack him there,
defeating the garrison troops.
Qiāo and Hàn Chóng fled to Fúzhōu,
and the garrison troops on the western border all collapsed.
In the second month,
Xī sent the Commander-in-Chief Pān Shīkuí and Wú Xíngzhēn to lead forty thousand troops to attack Yánzhèng.
Shīkuí encamped west of Jiànzhōu city,
and Xíngzhēn encamped south of the city.
Both camps were positioned behind water barriers,
and they burned the houses outside the city walls.
Yánzhèng sought help from Wúyuè.
On the day Rénxū,
King Yuán Guàn of Wúyuè sent the Ningguó Military Commissioner and Tongpingzhangshi Yǎng Rénquán
(The Xuānzhōu Ningguó Army at that time belonged to Southern Táng.
Wúyuè had Yǎng Rénquán hold the title nominally;
at that time, the various states often made such appointments among themselves.)
Yǎng
is a surname;
the *Héshì Xìngyuàn* includes this surname.
Chancellor Lín Dǐng advised against it,
but he did not listen.
In the third month,
on the day Wùchén,
Shīkuí divided off three thousand troops,
and sent the Army Commander Cài Hóngyì to lead them into battle.
Yánzhèng sent his general Lín Hànchè and others to defeat them at Cháshān,
beheading over a thousand.
(Cháshān is located twenty-five li east of Jiànzhōu,
and is also called Fènghuángshān today;
the Běiyuàn tea processing area is located there.)
7 Ān Yànwēi and Wáng Jiànlì both requested to retire;
this was not permitted.
On the Xīnwèi day,
Guīdé Jiedushi, Imperial Guard Cavalry and Infantry Commander-in-Chief, and Tongzhongshu Menxia Pingzhangshi Liú Zhīyuǎn was appointed as Yèdū Liúshǒu.
Yànwēi was transferred to be Guīdé Jiedushi,
and additionally granted the concurrent title of Shìzhōng.
On the Guǐyǒu day,
Jiànlì was transferred to be Zhāoyì Jiedushi,
and his noble rank was advanced to Prince of Hán;
because Jiànlì was from Liáozhōu,
Liáo and Qìn prefectures were carved out and placed under Zhāoyì.
Liáo and Qìn prefectures had originally belonged to Hédōng Jiedushi since the Táng dynasty.
Qìn,
read as wǔ zhèn fān.
8 Shānnán Dōngdào Jiedushi and Tongzhongshu Menxia Pingzhangshi Ān Cóngjìn relied on his strategic and strong position,
the territory of Xiāngyáng precisely possessed the strategic advantage described by Qū Wán as
"using Fāngchéng as its walls,
and the Hànshuǐ as its moat."
This strategic advantage,
is why Ān Cóngjìn relied on it to show arrogance towards the imperial court.
He intercepted and seized the tribute goods from Húnán,
the Húnán tribute goods,
were those presented by Mǎ Xīfàn.
He increased and expanded his armored troops;
his personal Chief Yá Officer Wáng Lìngqiān and Yá Officer Pān Zhīlín remonstrated,
and he killed them both.
When Wáng Jiànlì was transferred to Lùzhōu,
the Emperor sent someone to ask him:
"We have left Qīngzhōu vacant awaiting your arrival,"
Qīngzhōu was the Pínglú Army.
Cóngjìn replied:
"If you move Qīngzhōu and place it south of the Hàn River,"
Xiāngyáng is south of the Hàn River.
The Emperor did not reprimand him.
The Emperor was not a ruler who indulged in appeasement,
but he was inwardly anxious, considering the means by which he had taken the Central Plains,
and pondering how to defend the Central Plains,
fearful and hesitant,
thus all the arrogant and unruly military governors lowered their brows and he pacified and tamed them.
9 On the Dīngchǒu day,
Wáng Yánzhèng recruited over a thousand daring warriors,
who crossed the river at night,
secretly entered Pān Shīkuí's camp,
took advantage of the wind to set fires,
and those on the city walls beat drums and shouted in response,
the Dūtóu of the Zhànzhào troops, Jiàn'ān's Chén Huī, killed Shīkuí.
Jiàn'ān,
was the territory of the Hàn dynasty's Yě County,
the Wú state established Jiàn'ān County,
and the Táng dynasty attached it to Jiànzhōu.
On the Wùyín day,
he led troops intending to attack Wú Xíngzhēn's camp.
Before the Jiàn troops had crossed the river,
Xíngzhēn and his officers and soldiers abandoned their camp and fled,
with tens of thousands dead.
Yánzhèng took advantage of the victory to capture Yǒngpíng and Shùnchāng, two cities.
The Wú state established Nánpíng County from part of Jiàn'ān,
and Emperor Wǔ of Jìn changed it to Yánpíng County.
Wáng Shěnzhī established Yánpíng Garrison,
and his son Yánhàn changed it to Yǒngpíng Garrison.
The present seat of Nánjiànzhōu's administration is that very location.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì,
Nánjiànzhōu's jurisdiction included Shùnchāng County,
located 180 lǐ west of the prefecture.
Sòng Bái said: Shùnchāng County was originally the territory of the Xiào Township of Jiàn'ān County.
In the third year of the Yǒng'ān era of Wú, Jiànglè County was established.
The Suí dynasty merged it into Shàowǔ,
and the Táng dynasty re-established it.
In the second year of the Jǐngfú era, Jiàngshuǐ Garrison was also established,
changed to Yǒngshùn Field,
and soon established as Shùnchāng County.
10 In summer,
the fourth month,

Shǔ's Grand Guardian concurrently Menxia Shìláng and Tongzhongshu Menxia Pingzhangshi Zhào Jìliáng requested to divide and judge the Three Departments together with Menxia Shìláng and Tongzhongshu Menxia Pingzhangshi Wú Zhāoyì and Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tongzhongshu Menxia Pingzhangshi Zhāng Yè.
On the Guǐmǎo day,
the Shǔ ruler ordered Jìliáng to judge the Ministry of Revenue,
Zhāoyì to judge the Salt and Iron Monopoly,
and Yè to judge the Ministry of Finance.
11 On the Gēngxū day,
the former Héng Hǎi Jiedushi Mǎ Quánjié was appointed as Ānyuǎn Jiedushi.
This was to replace Lǐ Jīnquán.
12 On the Jiǎzǐ day,
Wúyuè's Filial and Devoted Heir Apparent Hóng Zǔn passed away.
13 Wúyuè's Yǎng Rénquán and others arrived with troops at Jiànzhōu.
Wáng Yánzhèng, considering that the Fúzhōu troops had already been defeated and withdrawn,
presented cattle and wine to reward them,
and requested they withdraw their army.
Rénquán and others did not comply,
and encamped northwest of the city.
Yánzhèng became fearful,
seeing Yǎng Rénquán stationed close to the city,
harboring intentions to seize Jiànzhōu,
this is why he was afraid.
The Mǐn king appointed Quánzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Jìyè as the Field Army Commander-in-Chief,
leading twenty thousand troops to rescue him;
and furthermore sent a letter reproaching Wúyuè,
this is what is called blaming the straight for the crooked.
It happened that there was prolonged rain,
and Wúyuè's
provisions were exhausted.
In the fifth month,
Yánzhèng sent troops out to attack,
and inflicted a major defeat on them,
capturing and beheading them by the tens of thousands.
On the Guǐwèi day,
Rénquán and others fled at night.
14 Hú Hànjūn, having already disobeyed the imperial decree by not proceeding to the capital,
also heard that Jiǎ Rénzhǎo's two sons intended to bring a lawsuit to the court;
Jiǎ Rénzhǎo's death is recorded in the second year of the previous scroll.
Cháo,
read as zhí yáo fān.
Hànjūn deceived Jīnquán, saying:
"The memorial-presenting official dispatched someone who came by double-time march to report,
the memorial-presenting official,
refers to the chief clerk of the Ānyuǎn Army's memorial-presenting office in Dàliáng.
that they are investigating the circumstances of Jiǎ Rénzhǎo's death,
believing there must be treacherous plots."
Jīnquán was greatly alarmed.
Hànjūn then persuaded Jīnquán to defy the command,
and submit himself to Táng;
Jīnquán followed his advice.
On the Bǐngxū day,
the Emperor heard of Jīnquán's rebellion,
and ordered Mǎ Quánjié to lead troops from Biàn, Luò, Rǔ, Zhèng, Shàn, Sòng, Chén, Cài, Cáo, Pú, Shēn, and Táng to campaign against him.
In this manner, the troops from all the military governors south of the Yellow River and west of the Jì River were fully mobilized.
Shàn,
read as shàn.
Pú,
read as bǔ.
Shěn Huī,
was the elder brother of Shěn Qí.
Lǐ Jīnquán sent his Tuīguān Zhāng Wěi to present a memorial requesting to surrender to Táng,
and the Táng ruler sent Èzhōu Garrison Commander Lǐ Chéngyù and Duàn Chùgōng to lead three thousand troops to receive him.
15 The Táng ruler sent Kèshěng Shǐ Shàng Quángōng to Mǐn,
to reconcile Mǐn King Xī and Wáng Yánzhèng.
In the sixth month,
Yánzhèng sent a Yájiàng and a female slave holding the oath document and an incense burner to Fúzhōu,
to swear an alliance with Xī at the Xuānlíng.
In ancient times, when making oaths and alliances,
a pit was dug and sacrificial animals were used,
the covenant document was placed on top,
and blood was smeared on the lips to pledge before the spirits of heaven and earth and the ghosts and gods.
For ancestral temple sacrifices,
only mugwort was burned to blend the fragrant aroma.
As for libations, fragrant wine was still used,
and pepper was used in food offerings.
Xún Qīng spoke of fragrances like pepper and orchid,
the Hàn empress's Pepper Room,
took its name from its rich fragrance.
Court officials held cloves in their mouths when reporting affairs,
the Xījīng Zá Jì records the Cháng'ān skilled artisan Dīng Huǎn making an under-blanket incense burner,
Liú Xiàng inscribed the Bóshān incense burner,
the Hàn Guān Diǎn Zhí records,
that Shàngshū Láng were provided with two female scribes holding incense burners for burning incense,
none of these were used for serving ghosts and gods.
the Hàn Wǔ Nèi Zhuàn records the descent of the Queen Mother of the West,
burning various kinds of infant incense,
likely all later fabrications and elaborations.
Sòng's Fàn Yè wrote a preface on incense,
exhaustively discussing various incenses to criticize people of his time;
yet when he wrote the Hòu Hàn Shū,
he also did not record any Hàn people burning incense.
It is suspected that the custom of using incense in rituals for gods,
originated from the Wèi and Jìn dynasties onward.
Chéng Dàchāng's Yǎn Fán Lù says: Emperor Wǔ of Liáng first used aloeswood in sacrifices to heaven,
it was not used in antiquity;
for sacrifices to earth, héxiāng was used.
The note states: Because the earth is close to humans,
it is appropriate to add mixed fragrances,
meaning it was made by blending various incenses,
indicating it was not limited to a single incense.
When the Mǐn ruler Lín assumed the great title,
he honored his father Shěnzhī's tomb as the Xuānlíng.
On the 16th day, the guǐmǎo day,
Táng’s Lǐ Chéngyù and others arrived at
Ānzhōu.
That evening,
Lǐ Jīnquán led several hundred of his subordinates to the Táng army camp.
His singing girls, concubines, and wealth were all seized by Chéngyù,
who then entered and occupied Ānzhōu.
On the jiǎchén day,
Mǎ Quánjié advanced from Yìngshān to Dàhuàzhèn.
Yìngshān
was the ancient state of Yìng,
which during the Hàn dynasty belonged within the boundaries of Suí County.
The Liáng dynasty partitioned Suí County to establish Yǒngyáng County,
which the Suí dynasty renamed Yìngshān.
During the Táng dynasty, it belonged to Ānzhōu.
According to the Jiǔyùzhì: It is located 180 lǐ north of the prefecture.
Dàhuàzhèn belonged to Yìngshān County.
He inflicted a major defeat upon them.
Chéngyù plundered Ānzhōu and fled southward,
and Quánjié entered Ānzhōu.
On the bǐngwǔ day,
Ān Shěnhuī pursued and defeated the Táng troops at Huánghuāgǔ,
and Duàn Chùgōng died in battle.
On the dīngwèi day,
Shěnhuī again defeated the Táng troops within Yúnmèngzé.
Jiǔyùzhì: Ānlù County in Ānzhōu had a Yúnmèngzhèn.
Present-day Ānlù County has Yúnmèngzé 50 lǐ to its south.
Sòng Bái said: Yúnmèng County in Ānzhōu originally comprised territory of Hàn dynasty Ānlù County.
In the 16th year of the Dàtǒng era of the Later Wèi, Yúnmèng County was established at the old city of Yúnchéng.
Defeated,
bǔ mài fān.
The Táng general Zhāng Jiànchóng occupied Yúnmèng Bridge to resist,
so Shěnhuī withdrew.
Mǎ Quánjié beheaded Chéngyù and his 1,500 men beneath the city walls,
and sent the supervising army commander Dù Guāngyè and 506 others to Dàliáng.
The Emperor said:
"What crime have these men committed?"
He bestowed horses, utensils, and garments upon them all and sent them back.
Previously,
when Lú Wénjìn fled to Wú,
as recorded in the 280th scroll, first year.
he was admonished not to enter the city of Ānzhōu,
but to array his forces outside the city walls,
await Wénjìn's exit,
then escort him back,
and not to plunder.
From Lú Wénjìn to this point,
all refer to events when the Táng sovereign was serving Wú.
Escort,
dīng liàn fān.
Plunder,
pǐ miào fān.
He was admonished as if to fully preserve grace;
but Chéngyù greedily plundered,
fought with the Jìn troops and was defeated,
losing 4,000 men.
The Táng sovereign lamented and regretted this for several days,
blaming himself for not having admonished and instructed thoroughly enough.
When Dù Guāngyè and others reached Táng,
the Táng sovereign, because they had disobeyed orders and were defeated,
did not accept them,
but sent them back north of the Huái River,
sending a letter to the Emperor stating:
"Border commanders greedy for merit,
took advantage of the situation to occupy fortifications."
It also said:
"Military law and court regulations,
neither side can tolerate this."
Meaning, if judged by military law,
then those who lose armies must be executed here,
and those who encroach upon borders cannot be pardoned there;
if measured by court regulations,
then neither state can tolerate such men standing at court.
Court,
zhí yáo fān.
The envoy was about to cross the Huái River from Tóngxū,
Jiǔyùzhì: Qí County in Sùzhōu had a Tónglúzhèn.
From Tónglú southward,
reaching Wōkǒu, one then crosses the Huái River.
The Jīnrén Jiāngyùtú: Tóngxū is in Línhuàn County, Sùzhōu.
So he returned.
The Emperor appointed all the Táng generals to official posts,
forming their soldiers into the Xiǎnyì Corps,
and ordered the veteran general Liú Kāng to command them.
Veteran general,
likely one who rose with him from Jìnyáng.
Your subject Guāng remarks: Those who disobey orders are the generals,
the soldiers follow the orders of their generals,
so what crime have they committed?
Accept them, execute their generals to apologize to the enemy,
mourn the soldiers and comfort them,
that would be acceptable.
Why must the people be abandoned to benefit an enemy state?
On the 17th, the Táng sovereign sent a eunuch to sacrifice at Lúshān,
Lúshān is in Xúnyáng County, Jiāngzhōu.
South of the mountain is Táng's Dūchāng County,
north of the mountain is Táng's Xúnyáng County.
Dūchāng is now Nánkāngjūn,
15 lǐ north of the military city is Lúshān.
He praised him, saying:
"Your journey this time was very pure and clean."
The eunuch said:
"Your subject, since receiving the edict,
has eaten only vegetarian food until now."
The Táng sovereign said:
"You bought fish at such-and-such place to make soup,
and bought meat on such-and-such day to make minced meat dishes,
how can that be called vegetarian food?"
The eunuch was ashamed and submitted.
The granary officials at year's end presented over 10,000 dàn of surplus grain.
The Táng sovereign said:
"Income and expenditure have fixed amounts.
If not by extorting from the people or deducting from the army,
how could there be surplus?"
In autumn,
the seventh month,
the Mǐn sovereign Xī fortified the western outer wall of Fúzhōu to guard against the Jiàn people.
He also ordained commoners as monks.
Commoners, to avoid heavy taxes, mostly became monks.
In total, 11,000 people were ordained.
Alas!
If ordaining monks truly brought blessed rewards and benefits,
then the Mǐn state might have survived until today.
On the yǐchǒu day,
the Emperor bestowed silk upon Zhèng Yuánbì and others,
and sent them back.
Sent back to Mǐn.
They were imprisoned last October,
now released and sent back.
When Lǐ Jīnquán rebelled,
the deputy commander of the Ānzhōu infantry and cavalry Sāng Qiān, the commander of the Wēihé troops Wáng Wànjīn, and Chéng Yànwēn did not comply and died.
The commander of the infantry and cavalry Páng Shǒuróng ridiculed their foolishness,
to comply with Jīnquán's wishes.
On the jǐsì day,
an edict posthumously awarded official titles to Jiǎ Rénzhǎo and Sāng Qiān and others,
and sent an envoy to execute Shǒuróng at Ānzhōu.
Lǐ Jīnquán reached Jīnlíng,
and the Táng sovereign treated him very coldly.
Lǐ Jīnquán, deluded by treacherous generals,
betrayed his parents' state,
and entrusted himself to another domain.
It is fitting that he was treated coldly.
On the dīngsì day,
the Táng sovereign established the Prince of Qí, Jǐng, as Crown Prince,
concurrently Grand Marshal,
and in charge of the affairs of the Imperial Secretariat.
The retired Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince Fàn Yánguāng requested to return to his private residence in Héyáng.
Fàn Yánguāng served Táng,
and previously had a private residence in Héyáng.
Yánguāng traveled heavily laden.
The Western Capital留守 Yáng Guāngyuǎn concurrently administered Héyáng.
Coveting his wealth,
and also fearing he would be a trouble for his descendants—
when Fàn Yánguāng surrendered from Guǎngjìn,
Yáng Guāngyuǎn was the marshal,
and must have bullied and oppressed him,
hence he feared he would be a trouble for his descendants.
"Yánguāng is a rebel minister.
Instead of residing in Biàn or Luò, he goes to an outer province.
I fear he might escape to an enemy state.
He should be eliminated early!"
The Emperor did not permit it.
Guāngyuǎn requested an edict ordering Yánguāng to reside in the Western Capital,
and this was granted.
Guāngyuǎn sent his son Chéngguì to surround his residence with armored soldiers,
forcing him to commit suicide.
Alas!
Wealth burdens men so.
Mì Qióng thus killed Dǒng Wēnqí's family,
Fàn Yánguāng in turn thus killed Mì Qióng,
Yáng Guāngyuǎn again thus killed Fàn Yánguāng,
and Guāngyuǎn also ultimately did not escape.
Wealth burdens men so!
"The Son of Heaven is above,
he bestowed upon me an iron pledge,
promising I would not be put to death."
The bestowal of the iron pledge
is recorded in the third year of the previous scroll.
On the jǐwèi day,
Chéngguì drove Yánguāng onto a horse at sword-point,
and when they reached the floating bridge,
pushed him into the river.
Guāngyuǎn reported that he had thrown himself into the water and died.
The Emperor knew the truth,
but feared Guāngyuǎn's strength,
and dared not interrogate;
he suspended court for Yánguāng,
and posthumously awarded him the title of Grand Tutor.
Táng's Prince of Qí, Jǐng, firmly declined the position of Crown Prince.
Being the eldest legitimate son, he ought to be Crown Prince.
Declining it is not the way to secure the hopes of the officials and people.
On the yǐchǒu day,
the Táng sovereign granted his request,
and issued an edict that memorials from inside and outside the court should follow the etiquette for the Crown Prince.
On the dīngmǎo day,
he appointed the Hanlin Academician Recipient of Edicts and Vice Minister of Revenue Hé Níng as Vice Director of the Secretariat and Tongpingzhangshi.
On the jǐsì day,
the Yèdū留守 Liú Zhīyuǎn came to court.
In February of this year,
Liú Zhīyuǎn replaced Ān Yánwēi to guard Wèizhōu.
On the 26th day, Xīnwèi,
Lǐ Sōng memorialized:
"The grain stored in the granaries of the various prefectures
far exceeds the amounts recorded in the annual accounts."
The annual accounts
refer to the ledgers created each year based on the calculated figures and submitted to the Three Departments.
The granary clerks, when receiving grain, take extra by overfilling the hu measures,
and when issuing grain, they privately profit from it;
these are all corrupt practices colluded between officials and clerks,
and it remains so to this day.
Only by measuring and moving the grain can the surplus be known,
yet during the measuring and moving, even more corruption occurs.
I suspect Lǐ Sōng also memorialized this based on what people of the time were already saying.
"Taxing the people outside the law
is a crime equal to bending the law.
The granary clerks are merely spared the death penalty,
but each should be severely punished."
It is unknown what constituted severe punishment at that time,
but ultimately, it was spoken of yet could not be implemented.
On the 27th day, Hanlin Academician Lǐ Huàn,
being frivolous and irresponsible,
often committed offenses while drunk,
which the Emperor disliked.
On Bǐngzǐ day,
he was dismissed from the Hanlin Academy,
and his duties were merged with those of the Secretariat Drafter.
Huàn
was the younger brother of Lǐ Tāo.
On the 28th day, Yáng Guāngyuǎn came to court.
The Emperor intended to transfer him to another military command.
He said to Guāngyuǎn:
"During the campaign to besiege Wèi,
those around you all performed meritorious service,
yet they have not been rewarded."
The siege of Wèi
is mentioned in the second and third years of the previous scroll.
Consequently, several of his officers were appointed as prefects.
This was to divide Yáng Guāngyuǎn's faction and weaken his power.
On Jiǎshēn day,
Guāngyuǎn was transferred to be Military Commissioner of Pínglú,
and was advanced to the title of Prince of Dōngpíng.
At the beginning of the Kāiyùn era,
Yáng Guāngyuǎn eventually rebelled from Pínglú.
In the winter,
tenth month,
on Dīngyǒu day,
Wúyuè King Qián Yuánguàn was additionally appointed as Grand Marshal of All Under Heaven's Armed Forces and President of the Department of State Affairs.
On Rényín day,
the Táng state issued a general amnesty.
An edict was issued that memorials from inside and outside the court must not contain the words
"Ruì"
or
"Shèng",
and violators would be charged with disrespect.
The diviner Sūn Zhìyǒng, because four stars had gathered in the Dipper constellation,
and the corresponding terrestrial division would have disaster,
urged the Táng ruler to tour the Eastern Capital.
He urged him to travel east to Jiāngdū.
On Yǐsì day,
the Táng ruler ordered Prince Qí, Lǐ Jǐng, to supervise the state.

Vice Commissioner of the Guangzheng Institute and Junior Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud, Chén Jué, due to a personal grudge, memorialized that Prefect of Tàizhōu, Chǔ Rénguī, was corrupt and cruel.
Tàizhōu
was the location of the Hǎilíng granary of the Wú state during the Hàn;
the Eastern Jìn divided Guǎnglíng to establish Hǎilíng Commandery;
in the early Táng, Wúzhōu was established,
and Hǎilíng County was renamed Wúlíng County;
in the seventh year of the Wǔdé era, Wúzhōu was abolished,
and it reverted to Hǎilíng County;
the Southern Táng elevated it to Tàizhōu.
On Bǐngwǔ day,
Rénguī was dismissed and made Commander of the Imperial Escort Guard,
and Jué began to wield power.
This sets the stage for Chén Jué's disruption of Táng governance.
On Gēngxū day,
the Táng ruler departed from Jīnlíng;
on Jiǎyín day,
he arrived at Jiāngdū.
The Mǐn ruler, Wáng Xī, through merchants, submitted a memorial to explain himself;
stating that he had never assumed the imperial title.
The one who assumed the imperial title
was Wáng Chǎng.
On Jiǎshēn day,
Xī was appointed as Military Commissioner of Wēiwǔ,
concurrently Secretariat Director,
and enfeoffed as King of Mǐn.
The Táng ruler wished to reside permanently in Jiāngdū,
but because the water froze,
and water transport could not supply it,
he returned instead.
In the twelfth month,
on Bǐngshēn day,
he arrived at Jīnlíng.
The Táng Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, concurrently Vice Director of the Chancellery and Tongpingzhangshi, Zhāng Yánhàn, died.
This year,
the Hàn Vice Director of the Chancellery and Tongpingzhangshi, Zhào Sǔn, died.
Níngyuǎn Military Commissioner Wáng Dìngbǎo of Nánchāng was appointed as Vice Director of the Secretariat and Tongpingzhangshi,
but he also died within a year.
Previously,
