was trusted and favored by Yuánguàn,
who entrusted all military affairs to him.
The wet nurse of Yuánguàn's adopted son, Hóngyòu,
was a relative of Dài Yùn's wife.
Someone reported that Dài Yùn was plotting to install Hóngyòu.
Dé'ān kept the death secret and did not announce the mourning,
and plotted with the various generals.
They concealed armed soldiers behind the curtains.
On Rénzǐ,
when Dài Yùn entered the administrative office,
they seized and killed him.
They deposed Hóngyòu to commoner status,
restored his original surname Sūn,
and imprisoned him in Míngzhōu.
That day,
the officers and officials, in accordance with Yuánguàn's final decree,
by imperial authority appointed the Deputy Commissioner of Zhènhǎi and Zhèndōng, Hóngzuǒ, as Military Commissioner.
He was fourteen years old at the time.
The Old History of the Five Dynasties says
he was thirteen.
On Gēngshēn,
Hóngzuǒ ascended the royal throne,
and ordered Chancellor Cáo Zhòngdá to act as regent.
In the army, there were complaints that rewards and gifts were distributed unevenly.
Soldiers raised their weapons and refused to accept them,
and the generals could not control them.
Zhòngdá personally explained the situation to them,
and they all laid down their weapons and bowed.
Hóngzuǒ was gentle and respectful,
fond of books,
courteous to scholars,
and personally diligent in governmental affairs.
He exposed hidden treachery,
and people could not deceive him.
When a commoner presented auspicious grain,
Hóngzuǒ asked the granary official:
"How much is stored now?"
He replied:
"Enough for ten years."
The King said:
"Then military provisions are sufficient.
We can lighten the burden on our people."
He then ordered a three-year tax exemption within his domain.
23. On Xīnyǒu,
Huázhōu reported a breach in the Yellow River.

Examination of discrepancies: The Old History of the Five Dynasties' Basic Annals records that on Xīnyǒu in the ninth month, the Yellow River breached at Huázhōu, but does not record the breach at Púzhōu on Gēngwǔ;
the Veritable Records of Gāozǔ records that on Gēngwǔ, Púzhōu reported a breach, but does not record the breach at Huázhōu on Xīnyǒu.
The Institutional History of the Five Dynasties and the Treatises both state,
"In the sixth year of Tiānfú, in the ninth month, the Yellow River breached at Huázhōu,
and the boundaries of Yǎnzhōu and Púzhōu were all flooded and inundated."
The Biography of Shǐ Kuānghàn also states,
"In the sixth year of Tiānfú, the White Horse section of the Yellow River breached."
Considering that the Yellow River had already breached at Huázhōu on Xīnyǒu,
then the downstream areas would have dried up,
making it unreasonable for Púzhōu to breach again on Gēngwǔ.
It was likely that the breach at Huázhōu
caused flooding that reached Púzhōu.
24. Because Ān Chóngróng had killed Khitan envoys,
the Emperor feared they would invade the border.
On Yǐhài,
he sent Yáng Yànxún, the Military Commissioner of Ānguó, as an envoy to the Khitan.
When Yànxún reached their tents,
the Khitan
demanded an explanation for the death of their envoys.
Yànxún said:
"It is like a household having a wicked son
whom even the parents cannot control.
What can be done about it?"
The Khitan ruler's anger then subsided.
25. The Mǐn ruler Wáng Xī appointed his son, Prince of Lángyá, Yàchéng, as Military Commissioner of Wēiwǔ and concurrently Secretariat Director,
and changed his title to Prince of Chánglè.
26 Liú Zhīyuǎn sent his trusted general Guō Wēi with an imperial edict to persuade the Tǔyùhún chieftain Bái Chéngfú.
At the time, the court pretended to expel the Tǔyùhún while secretly placating and accepting them,
but they also feared that the Qìdān would find out and become angry.
Therefore, they dared not openly issue an edict.
So Liú Zhīyuǎn, following the emperor's secret directive,
had Guō Wēi claim to be acting under an imperial edict to persuade them.
(General,
pronounced as liàng.)
(Persuade,
pronounced as shuì.)
(Chieftain,
pronounced as qiú.)
(Chief,
pronounced as zhǎng.)
They promised him the authority of a military governor.
Guō Wēi returned
and said to Liú Zhīyuǎn:
"These barbarians are only interested in profit.
Ān Tiěhú merely bribed them with robes and trousers.
If we want them to come now,
there is no better way than offering substantial bribes to attract them."
Liú Zhīyuǎn agreed
and also sent a message to Bái Chéngfú, saying:
"The court has already ceded your people to the Qìdān.
You should keep your tribe at peace.
Yet now you have come south to aid Ān Zhòngróng in his rebellion.
Zhòngróng has already been abandoned by the world.
He will soon be defeated and perish.
It would be best for you to submit early.
Do not wait until troops are brought against you,
leaving you with no refuge north or south,
for then regret will be useless."
(This means that if the Tǔyùhún aid Ān Zhòngróng,
after Zhòngróng is defeated and perishes,
the Tǔyùhún will be unable to return to Jìn in the south
or to the Qìdān in the north.)
In winter,
during the tenth month,
Bái Chéngfú led his people to submit to Liú Zhīyuǎn.
Liú Zhīyuǎn settled them between the eastern mountains of Tàiyuán and the regions of Lán and Shí.
He petitioned for Bái Chéngfú to be appointed as the military governor of Dàtóng.
(The Dàtóng Army of Yúnzhōu
was then under Qìdān control.)
(This sets the stage for Liú Zhīyuǎn's later killing of Bái Chéngfú.)
Initially,
Ān Zhòngróng had circulated a manifesto to various circuits,
claiming he would rise in arms together with the Tǔyùhún, Dádá, and Qìbì.
However, Bái Chéngfú later surrendered to Liú Zhīyuǎn,
and the Dádá and Qìbì also did not join him.
Zhòngróng's momentum was greatly diminished.
27 The Mǐn ruler Xī ascended the imperial throne;
Wáng Yánzhèng proclaimed himself Marshal of the Armed Forces.
The Mǐn Tóngpíngzhāngshì Lǐ Mǐn passed away.
(Recording him as Mǐn Tóngpíngzhāngshì
distinguishes him from ministers of other states.)
28 When the emperor departed from Dàliáng,
Hé Níng requested:
"Your Majesty's carriage has already left.
If Ān Cóngjìn rebels,
how shall we prepare for it?"
The emperor said:
"What is your opinion?"
Hé Níng requested to secretly leave behind over a dozen blank imperial proclamations and edicts.
(Proclamations were issued by the Bureau of Military Affairs,
edicts by the Secretariat-Chancellery;
at that time, the Bureau of Military Affairs was merged with the Secretariat-Chancellery.)
(Blank,
pronounced as kòng.)
Upon hearing of a rebellion, the names of generals could be filled in
and they could be dispatched to attack;
the emperor agreed.
In the eleventh month,
Ān Cóngjìn raised troops and attacked Dèngzhōu.
The prefect of Tángzhōu, Wǔ Yánhàn, reported this.
(The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: From Xiāngyáng, it is 178 *li* north to Dèngzhōu,
and 150 *li* northeast to Tángzhōu.)
(In Hàn times, there was Yè County,
which was later abolished;
Suí re-established Yè County;
in Táng, it belonged to Rǔzhōu.)
(The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: It is 140 *li* southeast of the prefecture.)
(Yè,
pronounced as shè.)
(Originally from the Tūjué;
Sīràng
was from Yōuzhōu.)
On the *dīngchǒu* day,
the Western Capital留守 Gāo Xíngzhōu was appointed as the overall commander of the southern front army,
with former Tóngzhōu military governor Sòng Yànjūn as his deputy,
and Zhāng Cóng'ēn as supervisor;
Guō Jīnhǎi was also appointed as vanguard commander,
with Chén Sīràng as his supervisor.
(Yànjūn
was from Huázhōu.)
On the *gēngchén* day,
Yèdū留守 Lǐ Déchōng was appointed acting Eastern Capital留守,
and Zhèng Prince Zhòngguì was summoned to Yèdū.
Ān Cóngjìn attacked Dèngzhōu.
The military governor of Wēishèng, Ān Shěnhuī, defended the inner city against him.
(This refers to the inner city of Dèngzhōu.)
On the *guǐwèi* day,
Cóngjìn reached Huāshān.
(The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Húyáng County in Tángzhōu had the Huāshān silver mine.)
(Now note: Huāshān is north of Húyáng.)
Not expecting his arrival to be so swift,
they engaged in battle,
and were greatly defeated.
Cóng'ēn captured his son, the commander of the inner army, Hóngyì.
Cóngjìn fled back to Xiāngzhōu with several dozen cavalry,
and barricaded himself within the city walls for defense.
29 The Southern Táng ruler was frugal by nature.
He often wore straw sandals,
used an iron basin for washing his face,
slept under a green kudzu curtain in summer,
and kept only elderly and plain palace women around him for service,
with simple and rough clothing.
Those who died for the state
were all granted three years' salary.
He dispatched envoys to inspect the people's fields,
determining taxes based on fertility,
and the people praised it as fair.
From then on, when raising troops for campaigns or imposing other levies in Jiāngnán and Huáinán,
they were all based on the tax amounts,
and this practice continues to this day.
The Southern Táng ruler diligently attended to governance,
working day and night.
After returning from Jiāngdū,
he no longer held banquets or enjoyed music.
However, he was somewhat prone to impatience and haste.
The eunuch Wáng Shàoyán submitted a memorial,
stating that
"since this spring,
many officials have been punished,
causing suspicion and fear both inside and outside the court."
The Southern Táng ruler issued a handwritten edict explaining the reasons,
and ordered Shàoyán to inform everyone inside and outside the court.
30 In the twelfth month,
on the first day, *bǐngxū*,
Zhèng Prince Zhòngguì was transferred to become Prince of Qí,
and appointed as Yèdū留守;
Lǐ Déchōng was appointed as Eastern Capital留守.
31 On the *dīnghài* day,
Gāo Xíngzhōu was put in charge of the administrative office of Xiāngzhōu.
An edict ordered Jīngnán and Húnán to jointly attack Xiāngzhōu.
Gāo Cónghuì dispatched the commander-in-chief Lǐ Duān with several thousand naval troops to Nánjīn,
(the Nánjīn on the Hàn River)
and each also transported grain to supply them.
(Shàodí,
was the son of Jí.)
(Zhāng Jí
was one who rose to power together with King Mǎ Yīn of Chǔ.)
(Shào,
pronounced as shào.)
(Warship,
pronounced as jiàn.)
(Vessel,
pronounced as sōu.)
(Jí,
pronounced as jí.)
32 When Ān Zhòngróng heard that Ān Cóngjìn had raised troops in rebellion,
he decided to act.
He gathered a large number of famine-stricken people within his territory,
amassing a crowd of tens of thousands,
and headed south toward Yèdū,
claiming he was going to the court.
Initially,
Zhòngróng and the Shēnzhōu native Zhào Yànzhī had both served as scattered commandants,
and they got along very well.
(Scattered,
pronounced as sàn.)
(In the second year, Ān Zhòngróng began to command Zhènzhōu.)
Zhòngróng treated Yànzhī very generously,
having him recruit followers;
but in his heart, he actually distrusted him.
When he raised troops,
he only appointed him as a formation commander,
and Yànzhī resented this.
When the emperor heard of Zhòngróng's rebellion,
on the *rénchén* day,
he dispatched thirty-nine commands of imperial guard cavalry and infantry to attack him.
He appointed the military governor of Tiānpíng, Dù Zhòngwēi, as commander of the expedition,
with the military governor of Ānguó, Mǎ Quánjié, as his deputy,
and former military governor of Yǒngqīng, Wáng Qīng,
as cavalry and infantry commander.
33 Ān Cóngjìn sent his brother Cóngguì with troops to meet the prefect of Jūnzhōu, Cài Xíngyù.
(Xíngyù
was a prefect within Ān Cóngjìn's jurisdiction.)
(At that time, he was probably sending troops to aid Xiāngyáng,
so he sent his brother to meet him.)
Xíngyù defeated him,
captured Cóngguì,
cut off his feet, and sent him back.
On the Wùxū day (34th),
Dù Chóngwēi encountered Ān Chóngróng southwest of Zōngchéng.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Zōngchéng County is located 170 lǐ northwest of Wèi Prefecture.
The government troops attacked him again,
but he did not budge;
Chóngwēi grew fearful
and wanted to retreat.
The commander, Wǎnqiū's Wáng Chóngyìn, said:
"Military strategists consider retreat inauspicious.
If we retreat, the enemy will take advantage and press the attack;
furthermore, the soldiers might collapse into chaos because of the retreat,
hence it is considered inauspicious.
(Chén,
read as zhèn.)
I request that you, sir, divide your elite troops to attack his left and right flanks,
while I, Chóngyìn, for you, sir, charge straight into his center with the Khitan troops.
He will certainly be thrown into disarray."
Chóngwēi followed his advice.
The Zhèn troops' formation wavered slightly,
and Zhào Yànzhī furled his banners, spurred his horse, and came to surrender.
Yànzhī's armor, helmet, saddle, and bridle were adorned with silver,
and the government troops killed him and divided the spoils.
When Chóngróng heard of Yànzhī's defection,
he was greatly alarmed
and retreated to hide among the baggage train.
The government troops seized the opportunity and attacked,
and the Zhèn troops suffered a major collapse,
with fifteen thousand heads taken.
Chóngróng gathered his remaining troops
and fled to defend Zōngchéng.
The government troops advanced to attack,
and by midnight,
they captured it.
Chóngróng fled back to Zhèn Prefecture with a dozen or so cavalry,
barricading himself within the city walls for defense.
Coinciding with severe cold weather,
over twenty thousand people from Zhèn died in battle or from freezing.
When the Khitans heard that Chóngróng had rebelled,
they allowed Yáng Yànxún to return.
(In the ninth month of this year,
Yáng Yànxún was sent as an envoy to the Khitans.)
On the Gēngzǐ day,
Jì Prefecture Governor Zhāng Jiànwǔ and others captured Zhào Prefecture.
Both Jì and Zhào Prefectures were under Ān Chóngróng's jurisdiction.
(35) The Hàn ruler fell seriously ill.
A foreign monk told the Hàn ruler that his name, Gǒng, was inauspicious;
the Hàn ruler then created
the character "Yǎn"
to name himself,
its meaning derived from
"the flying dragon in the heavens."
(The Yì Jīng says: "The flying dragon is in the heavens;
it is beneficial to see the great man.")
(36) On the Gēngxū day,
an edict was issued appointing Qián Hóngzuǒ as Military Commissioner of Zhènhǎi and Zhèndōng Armies, concurrently Zhongshu Ling and King of Wúyuè.
(Diǎn biāo diǎn by Dèng Guǎngmíng, fù jiào by Niè Chóngqí)
(Compiled by Sīmǎ Guāng
by imperial order)
(Later
student from Tiāntāi)
The seventh year of Tiānfú (Rényín, 942)
1. Spring,
first month,
on the Dīngsì day,
a junior officer from Zhèn Prefecture led the government troops into the city through the Shuǐniǎn Gate in the western outer wall,
killing twenty thousand civilians defending the battlements,
capturing Ān Chóngróng,
and beheading him.
Dù Chóngwēi killed the guide,
claiming the credit for himself.
On the Gēngshēn day,
Chóngróng's head arrived at Yèdū.
The Emperor ordered it lacquered
and sent in a box to the Khitans.
2. On the Guǐhài day,
Zhèn Prefecture was renamed Héng Prefecture,
and the Chéngdé Army was renamed the Shùn'guó Army.
(Zhèn Prefecture was originally Héng Prefecture;
the Táng changed it to avoid the personal name of Emperor Mùzōng.
Now, because Ān Chóngróng rebelled,
the prefecture name was changed back to the old one,
and the army designation was also changed.
Héng,
pronunciation Hú Dēng fān.)
3. On the Bǐngyín day,
Menxià Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāng Shì Zhào Yíng was appointed Shìzhōng,
and Dù Chóngwēi was appointed Military Commissioner of Shùn'guó, concurrently Shìzhōng.
(Ān Chóngróng's private wealth and the treasury of Héng Prefecture
were all taken by Chóngwēi,
and the Emperor knew but did not inquire.
He also petitioned to appoint Wèiwèi Shǎoqīng, Fànyáng's Wáng Yú, as Deputy Commissioner.
Yú imposed heavy exactions on the people for him,
and the people of Héng could not bear the suffering.)
4. Zhāng Shì's father, Zhāng Duó, went to the capital to appeal the injustice.
(The matter of Zhāng Yànzé killing Zhāng Shì is recorded in the previous volume, last year.)
On the Rénwǔ day,
Héyáng Military Commissioner Wáng Zhōu was appointed Zhāngyì Military Commissioner,
replacing Zhāng Yànzé.
5. The Mǐn ruler, Xī, established Lady Lǐ as Empress,
the daughter of Tóng Píngzhāng Shì Lǐ Zhēn.
She was fond of drink and stubborn,
and Xī, though doting on her, also feared her.
6. Zhāngwǔ Military Commissioner Dīng Shěnqí
maintained a private army of a thousand men,
allowing them to commit violence within his jurisdiction.
Army officer Hè Xíngzhèng joined with various Hu tribes to stage a rebellion,
attacking Yán Prefecture.
The Emperor dispatched Cáo Prefecture Defense Commissioner Hé Chóngjiàn to lead troops to rescue them.
Reinforcements from Tóng and Fū arrived subsequently,
and thus they were saved.
In the second month,
on the Guǐsì day,
Chóngjiàn was appointed Acting Military Commissioner of Zhāngwǔ,
and Shěnqí was summoned back to court.
(Chóngjiàn
was a Hu man from between Yún and Shuò.)
7. The Táng Left Chancellor Sòng Qíqiū persistently requested to participate in government affairs.
The Táng ruler permitted him to enter the Zhōngshū Secretariat.
He further requested to head the Shàngshū Department.
Consequently, Shìzhōng, Prince Shòu Jǐngsuì, was relieved of his duty as head of the Shàngshū Department,
and instead put in charge of the Zhōngshū and Menxià Departments,
while Qíqiū was put in charge of the Shàngshū Department's affairs.
(This was to control Sòng Qíqiū.)
His close subordinate Xià Chāngtú embezzled three thousand strings of government money.
Qíqiū ruled to pardon him from death.
The Táng ruler was furious,
and had Chāngtú executed.
Qíqiū pleaded illness
and requested to be relieved of his departmental duties.
This was granted.
8. Jīng Prefecture reported that they had sent Yāyá Chén Yánhuī with an imperial edict to Liáng Prefecture,
and the officers and officials in the prefecture requested Yánhuī to be appointed Military Commissioner.
9. In the third month,
the Mǐn ruler Xī established Prince Chánglè, Yàchéng, as King of Mǐn.
10. While Zhāng Yànzé was in Jīng Prefecture,
he dispatched troops to attack various Hu tribes.
The troops were all defeated and lost,
and he requisitioned over a thousand civilian horses to replenish them.
Upon returning to Shǎn,
(i.e., returning to Shǎn after being replaced in Jīng Prefecture.)
(Huán,
pronunciation cóng Xuān fān.
Shǎn,
pronunciation shī Rǎn fān.)
while heavily drunk, he had their hands and feet cut off and then beheaded them.
Wáng Zhōu submitted a memorial listing twenty-six instances of Yànzé's corruption, cruelty, and lawlessness while in his post,
causing over five thousand households to flee and scatter.
(Wáng Zhōu replaced Yànzé,
hence he was able to report on his conduct while in his post.)
The Emperor, because Yànzé had military achievements
and was also connected by marriage to Yáng Guāngyuǎn,
released him without inquiry.
(According to Ōu Shǐ,
Zhāng Yànzé was connected by marriage to the Emperor,
and also had merit in suppressing Fàn Yánguāng.)
Summer,
fourth month,
on the Jǐwèi day,
Right Jiànyì Dàfū Zhèng Shòuyì submitted a memorial stating:
"The reason Yáng Hóng was massacred
was because last year Your Majesty handed Zhāng Shì over to Yànzé,
allowing him to indulge his will,
which led to Yànzé daring to act with extreme cruelty,
without any fear or restraint.
Those who saw or heard of this gnashed their teeth in anger,
yet Your Majesty showed not the slightest concern,
issuing not a single word of reprimand.
Good and evil are not distinguished,
rewards and punishments lack principle.
Both inside and outside the court, it is said that Your Majesty accepted a hundred horses offered by Yànzé,
and therefore allowed him to act thus.
I privately grieve for Your Majesty bearing such an ill reputation.
I beg that Yànzé be punished according to the law to cleanse the imperial virtue."
The memorial was submitted,
but kept within the palace without response.
(Shòuyì
was the nephew of Zhèng Cóngdǎng.
Zhèng Cóngdǎng appears in the annals of Táng Emperor Xīzōng.
Dǎng,
pronunciation dǎng.)
On the Gēngshēn day,
Lǐ Tāo, the Vice Director of the Ministry of Justice, and others prostrated themselves at the palace gate to vehemently denounce Zhāng Yànzé’s crimes,
their words extremely earnest and severe.
“Prostrating at the gate” means
kneeling at the palace gate to present a memorial,
with the gate officer reporting it to the emperor.
On the Xīnyǒu day,
an imperial decree was issued:
“Zhāng Yànzé is demoted by one rank
and reduced by one noble title.
‘Rank’ refers to
military honorary rank.
‘Noble title’ refers to
the grade of noble titles.
For the people of Jīngzhōu who have returned to their livelihoods,
their corvée and taxes are reduced.”
On the Guǐhài day,
Lǐ Tāo again, along with officials from the two departments and the Censorate, prostrated at the palace gate
to memorialize that Yànzé’s punishment was too light,
requesting that he be judged according to the law.
The emperor summoned Tāo to personally admonish him.
Tāo, holding his tablet upright, advanced to the foot of the palace steps,
his voice
and expression both severe.
The emperor grew angry,
repeatedly rebuking him,
but Tāo did not retreat.
The emperor said:
“We have already promised Yànzé that he would not die.”
Tāo said:
“Your Majesty promised Yànzé he would not die,
and you cannot break that promise;
but I wonder where Fàn Yánguāng’s iron pledge is!”
This refers to the promise that Fàn Yánguāng would not die,
but Yáng Guāngyuǎn killed him,
an event recorded in the fifth year of the previous volume.
He then entered the inner palace.
On the Bǐngyín day,
Yànzé was appointed as General of the Left Dragon Martial Army.
This sets the stage for Zhāng Yànzé being used by the Khitans to destroy the Jìn state and for Lǐ Tāo’s fearless confrontation with Yànzé.
11. The Hàn Emperor Gāozǔ fell ill,
and because his sons, Prince of Qín Hóngdù and Prince of Jìn Hóngxī, were both arrogant and unrestrained,
while his youngest son, Prince of Yuè Hóngchāng, was filial, prudent, and wise,
he plotted with the Right Vice Director and concurrent Western Imperial Court Commissioner Wáng Huī to send Hóngdù to govern Yōngzhōu,
Hóngxī to govern Róngzhōu,
and to establish Hóngchāng as heir.
This sets the stage for Hóngxī killing Hóngchāng and Huī.
Huī
is pronounced Qiúrén.
At that time, the Chongwen Commissioner Xiāo Yì came to inquire about his illness,
and he consulted him on the matter.
Yì said:
“The eldest son should be established as heir;
violating this will inevitably lead to chaos.”
Thus, he abandoned the plan.
Xiāo Yì cited classical principles to oppose the establishment of Hóngchāng.
“Eldest”
is pronounced zhǎng.
On the Dīngchǒu day,
Emperor Gāozǔ passed away.
He was fifty-four years old.
Emperor Gāozǔ was eloquent and perceptive,
skilled in strategy,
fond of boasting,
and often referred to the Chinese emperor as
“the Prefect of Luòzhōu.”
Since Lǐngnán was a gathering place for rare treasures,
he often indulged in extreme luxury and extravagance,
adorning his palaces entirely with gold, jade, pearls, and emeralds.
His punishments were cruel and brutal,
including methods such as pouring liquid into the nose, cutting out the tongue, dismemberment, disembowelment, roasting, boiling, and steaming;
sometimes he would gather poisonous snakes in water
and throw criminals into it,
calling it the “water prison.”
The Vice Director of the Secretariat Yáng Dòngqián remonstrated,
but he did not listen.
In his later years, he became particularly suspicious and jealous;
believing that scholars often acted for the sake of their descendants,
he exclusively employed eunuchs,
leading to a great proliferation of eunuchs in his state.
After Liú Yǎn,
eunuchs were exclusively employed,
and officials were referred to as “outsiders,”
a practice that continued until Chǎng, when the state perished.
Prince of Qín Hóngdù ascended the throne as emperor,
changing his name to Bīn;
he appointed Hóngxī to assist in governance,
changed the era name to Guāngtiān;
and honored his mother, Consort Zhào, as Empress Dowager.
12. The Khitans, because the Jìn had taken in the Tǔyùhún,
sent an envoy to reprimand them.
The emperor, worried and distressed, did not know what to do;
in the fifth month,
on the Jǐhài day,
he fell ill.
13. On the Yǐsì day,
Empress Dowager Liú was honored as Grand Empress Dowager.
The Empress Dowager
was the emperor’s stepmother.
Xú Wúdǎng said: She was the emperor’s birth mother.
14. The Táng Chancellor and Grand Guardian Sòng Qíqiū, after being dismissed from the Department of State Affairs,
no longer attended court audiences.
The Táng ruler sent Prince of Shòu Jǐngsuì to inquire after him,
promising him governance of Hóngzhōu,
and only then did he return to court.
The Táng ruler held a banquet for him,
and when the wine was flowing freely,
Qíqiū said:
“Your Majesty’s restoration of the dynasty
was due to my efforts;
how could you forget this!”
The Táng ruler angrily replied:
“You, as a wandering scholar, sought my favor,
an event recorded in the second year of Qiánhuà of Liáng Tàizǔ, volume 266.
That should be enough.
Yet you told others that I have a beak-like mouth like Gōujiàn,
difficult to share peace and happiness with;
did you say this?”
Fàn Lǐ of Yuè wrote to Wén Zhǒng, saying that the King of Yuè had a long neck and a beak-like mouth,
and could share hardships
but not peace and happiness.
“Gōu”
is pronounced like “gōu.”
“Lè”
is pronounced like “luò.”
“I did indeed say this.
When I was a wandering scholar,
Your Majesty was merely a minor officer.
Today, you may kill me.”
The next day,
the Táng ruler issued a handwritten edict apologizing:
“My narrow-minded nature
was well known to you, Zǐsōng, in the past.
To be close in youth
and resentful in old age—
is that acceptable!”
On the Bǐngwǔ day,
Qíqiū was appointed as Military Commissioner of Zhènnán.
This fulfilled the promise of Hóngzhōu.
Sòng Qíqiū was originally a Jìnshì from Hóngzhōu,
and this appointment honored him with a return to his hometown in glory.
15. The emperor fell ill,
and one day,
Féng Dào was alone in audience.
The emperor had his young son Chóngruì come out and bow to him,
and also ordered a eunuch to place Chóngruì in Dào’s arms,
his intention clearly being for Dào to assist in establishing him as heir.
In the sixth month,
on the Yǐchǒu day,
the emperor passed away.
He was fifty-one years old.
According to the Wǔdài Huìyào,
he died in the Bǎochāng Hall of the inner palace in Yèdū.
Dào consulted with the Military Commissioner of Tiānpíng and Deputy Commander of the Imperial Guard Cavalry and Infantry Jǐng Yánguǎng,
and they agreed that, given the many difficulties facing the state,
an older ruler should be established.
Thus, they supported Qí Wáng Chóngguì, the Governor of Guǎngjìn, as successor.
Jìn Gāozǔ entrusted his orphan to Féng Dào,
similar to how the Wú ruler Sūn Xiū entrusted his orphan to Púyáng Xīng and Zhāng Bù.
“Nàn”
is pronounced nàndàn.
Qí Wáng ascended the throne as emperor.
Yánguǎng considered this his own achievement
and began to wield power,
prohibiting the people of the capital from gathering to speak privately.
This was to prevent conspirators from plotting rebellion.
Earlier,
when Emperor Gāozǔ was critically ill,
he had issued an order summoning the Military Commissioner of Hédōng Liú Zhīyuǎn to assist in governance,
but Qí Wáng suppressed it;
because of this, Zhīyuǎn resented Qí Wáng.
This sets the stage for Liú Zhīyuǎn not sending reinforcements.
16. On the Dīngmǎo day,
the Empress Dowager was honored as Grand Empress Dowager,
the stepmother of Emperor Gāozǔ, Liú.
Emperor Gāozǔ’s empress was Lǐ.
17. In Mǐn, Prince of Fùshā Yánzhèng besieged Tīngzhōu,
and the Mǐn ruler Xī dispatched five thousand troops from Zhāngzhōu and Quánzhōu to relieve it.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì: From Quánzhōu west to Zhāngzhōu is 295 lǐ,
and from Zhāngzhōu west to Tīngzhōu is 540 lǐ.
Sòng Bái said: Liángshān has the Zhāngpǔ River,
also called the Zhāngxī River.
In the second year of Chuígǒng,
the southwestern part of Quánzhōu was separated to establish Zhāngzhōu.
The Quánzhōu of Chuígǒng
is present-day Fúzhōu.
The Commissioner of Dàmíng Palace Huáng Jìngzhōng stationed troops at Yóukǒu,
and according to the Jiǔyù Zhì: Yóuxī County is 155 lǐ south of Nánjiànzhōu,
likely established during the early Wáng clan period.
Yóukǒu
is the mouth of the Yóuxī River.
The Commissioner of State Finance Huáng Shàopō led eight thousand infantry as reinforcements for the two armies.
18. In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the Rénchén day,
Grand Empress Dowager Liú passed away.
The 19th: Wáng Yánzhèng, the Prince of Fùshā in Mǐn, attacked Tīngzhōu.
After forty-two battles,
he was unable to capture it and withdrew.
His generals Bāo Hóngshí and Chén Wàng
led the naval forces to resist the army from Fúzhōu.
On the dīngyǒu day,
they encountered them at Yóukǒu.
(Yóukǒu is the mouth of the Yóu River.)
The diviner said the time was not auspicious,
so they held their troops and did not advance.
Hóngshí and others led their troops ashore,
attacking from both land and water,
killed Jìngzhōng,
captured and beheaded two thousand men,
and Lín Shǒuliàng and Huáng Shàopō all fled back.
The 20th: On the gēngzǐ day,
a general amnesty was declared.
The 21st: On the guǐmǎo day,
Jǐng Yánguǎng was appointed Tóngpíngzhāngshì,
concurrently serving as Commander of the Imperial Guard Cavalry and Infantry.
This was to reward him for his merit in establishing the policy.
(This sets the stage for Jǐng Yánguǎng seizing power to control the emperor and creating conflict with the Qìdān.)
The 22nd: The meritorious veterans all wanted to reinstate the position of Shūmìshǐ.
(The abolition of the Shūmìshǐ is recorded in the previous volume, last year.)
They requested to yield the old duties of the Shūmì to him.
(The Shūmì was merged into the Zhōngshū,
hence the old duties of the Shūmìyuàn were referred to as old duties.)
The 23rd: A deity descended upon a commoner's home in Bóluó County.
(Bóluó is an ancient county from the Hàn Dynasty,
under Xúnzhōu in the Táng,
and at that time was territory of Hàn.
According to the Jùnguózhì: Xúnzhōu has Mount Bóluó,
which floated across the sea and came,
attaching to Mount Luó,
hence the name Bóluó.
In the Sòng Dynasty, Bóluó County belonged to Huìzhōu.
The Jiǔyùzhì states: It is forty-five lǐ north of the prefecture.
Sòng Bái said: Bóluó County borders Mount Luó,
hence the name Bóluó;
to the east it connects with Lóngzhōu,
to the south with Xīpíng,
to the west with the boundary of Zēngchéng.)
The common people went to divine good or bad fortune,
and it was often accurate,
so the county clerk Zhāng Yùxián served it with great reverence.
At that time, bandits rose up in Xúnzhōu,
with no unified leadership.
The bandit leaders together prayed to the deity,
and the deity loudly proclaimed:
"Zhāng Yùxián shall be your lord."
Thereupon,
they together supported Yùxián,
who proclaimed himself the King of the Eight Kingdoms of Zhōngtiān,
changed the era name to Yǒnglè,
established officials,
and attacked and plundered the coastal regions.
(Xúnzhōu is southeast, bordering the two prefectures of Cháo and Huì,
both coastal areas.)
He had no other strategy,
and his generals merely reported advances and retreats.
The Hàn ruler appointed Yuèwáng Liú Hóngchāng as commander-in-chief
and Xúnwáng Liú Hónggǎo as deputy to suppress them,
battling at Qiánbóguǎn.
The Hàn army was at a disadvantage,
and both princes were surrounded by the bandits.
The commander Chén Dàoxiáng and others fought strenuously to rescue them,
and they escaped.
Many eastern prefectures and counties were captured by Yùxián.
(Eastern prefectures and counties refer to those east of Pānyú,
namely the areas of Huì and Cháo.
The Jiǔyùzhì states: From Guǎngzhōu east to Huìzhōu is three hundred fifteen lǐ,
and from Huìzhōu east to Cháozhōu is eight hundred ten lǐ.)
(Chén Dàoxiáng was from Duānzhōu.)
The 24th: Gāo Xíngzhōu besieged Xiāngzhōu for over a year
without capturing it.
(Last November, Gāo Xíngzhōu besieged Xiāngzhōu; the matter begins in the previous volume.)
Wáng Qīng of Qūzhōu, the Dūyúhòu of the Fèngguó Army, said to Xíngzhōu:
(Qūzhōu County belonged to Míngzhōu.
In the third year of the Xīníng era of the Sòng,
Qūzhōu County was abolished and made a town,
incorporated into Jīzé County.)
"The enemy city is already in peril,
our troops are already weary,
the people's strength is already exhausted.
If we do not press the attack soon,
what are we waiting for!"
Together with Liú Cí of Yuánchéng, the Dūzhǐhuīshǐ of the Fèngguó Army, he led the troops in the first assault.
(Yuánchéng County was attached to Wèizhōu.
Shuài is read as shuài.)
They captured it.
Ān Cóngjìn burned himself and his entire family.
The 25th: On the jiǎzǐ day,
Zhào Yíng was appointed Zhōngshūlìng.
The 26th: The Mǐn ruler Xī sent an envoy with a handwritten edict, nine hundred gold vessels, ten thousand strings of cash, and six hundred forty official appointments for generals and officials
to seek peace with Prince Yánzhèng of Fùshā.
Yánzhèng did not accept.
On the bǐngyín day,
the Mǐn ruler Xī held a banquet for his ministers at the Jiǔlóng Hall.
His nephew Jìróu could not drink,
but he forced him.
Jìróu secretly reduced his wine,
and Xī became angry,
and had him and the guest general executed.
(Wáng Xī's drunken cruelty is of the same ilk as Sūn Hào.)
(Jiàng is read as liàng.)
The 27th: The people of Mǐn cast the Yǒnglōng Tōngbǎo large iron coins,
one equal to a hundred lead coins.
The 28th: Hàn buried the Heavenly August Emperor at Kānglíng,
with the temple name Gāozǔ.
The 29th: Since the Táng ruler became Chancellor of Wú,
he promoted benefits and eliminated harms,
changing many old laws.
(In the fourth year of the Zhēnmíng era of Liáng Jūnwáng,
the Táng ruler first obtained the governance of Wú,
which was the fifteenth year of Wúwáng Lóngyǎn.)
He ordered judicial officials and the Shàngshū to compile and establish the Shēngyuán Code in thirty scrolls.
(At that time, Táng used Shēngyuán as its era name.)
On the gēngyín day,
it was implemented.
The 30th: The Mǐn ruler Xī appointed Hóuguān Yú Tíngyīng, the Tóngpíngzhāngshì, as Prefect of Quánzhōu.
Tíngyīng was corrupt and vile,
seizing people's daughters,
falsely claiming he had received an edict to select them for the rear palace.
When the matter was discovered,
Xī sent a Censor to investigate him.
Tíngyīng became afraid,
went to Fúzhōu to surrender himself,
and Xī interrogated and reprimanded him,
intending to hand him over to the officials.
Tíngyīng withdrew,
and offered ten thousand strings of cash for a banquet.
Xī was pleased,
and the next day summoned him,
saying:
"The banquet has been bought,
but where are the tribute goods for the Empress?"
Tíngyīng again offered money to Empress Lǐ,
and was then sent back to Quánzhōu.
From then on, all the prefectures separately presented tribute to the Empress.
Not long after,
Tíngyīng was again summoned to be Chancellor.
The 31st: In winter,
the tenth month,
on the bǐngzǐ day,
Zhāng Yùxián captured Xúnzhōu,
killing the Hàn Prefect Liú Chuán.
The 32nd: The Chǔ ruler Xīfàn built the Tiāncè Mansion.
(Wáng Jǔ's Tiānxià Dàdìnglù states: Xīfàn built the Tiāncè Mansion northwest of the prefectural city,
constructing sixteen towers such as Tiāncè and Guāngzhèng,
and also building five halls such as Tiāncè and Qínzhèng.
The doors, windows, railings, and balustrades were all adorned with gold and jade,
and the walls were painted using several hundred thousand catties of cinnabar.
Cinnabar comes from Chén, Xī, Xù, Jǐn, and other prefectures and various stream valleys,
all within Chǔ's territory.
The Běncǎo Tújīng states: Cinnabar grows in deep mountain stone cliffs.
The locals dig pits several tens of feet deep
before seeing its sprout,
which is white stone,
called the cinnabar bed.
The cinnabar grows on the stone,
with large lumps like chicken eggs,
small ones like pomegranate seeds,
shaped like lotus heads or arrowheads connected on the bed.
It is dark purple like iron in color,
yet bright and translucent.
When broken,
it is jagged like a wall,
and also like mica sheets that can be split apart,
with no stone being best.
Beyond this, it is obtained by washing soil and stone.)
In spring and summer, they used horn mats.
(Horn mats are made by splitting bamboo into thin strips,
weaving them,
removing the nodes and outer skin,
making them smooth and lovely.
Some southern barbarians use white rattan to make them.)
Cotton,
is now abundant in the south.
In mid-spring, they make ridges and plant it.
By late summer and early autumn, it bears fruit.
By mid-autumn,
the outer skin of the fruit splits open in four places,
and inside it bursts forth,
white like silk floss.
The locals take it and spin it,
weaving it into cloth,
which is fine, dense, thick, and warm,
suitable for resisting winter.)
On the 33rd day of the eleventh month,
Gēngyín,
the Emperor Shèngwén Zhāngwǔ Míngdé Xiào was buried at the Xiǎnlíng tomb,
located in Shòu'ān County, Hénán Prefecture.
34 Previously, officials in various prefectures north and south of the Hé River had been selling sea salt themselves,
collecting 170,000 strings of cash annually;
they also distributed silkworm salt to collect money from the people.
Silkworm salt was used to treat cocoons.
In the second year of the Tiānchéng era of the Táng dynasty,
an imperial edict stipulated: each year in the second month, silkworm salt would be distributed once,
with payment due by the deadline for the summer tax.
Sòng Bái said: In the third year of the Zhōu Xiǎndé era,
an edict allocated silkworm salt in Qí Prefecture based on the autumn grain levy,
called chátóu,
with 3,000 cash levied per shí;
in Cāng, Dì, Bīn, Zī, and Qīng prefectures,
one bolt of silk was levied per shí.
Later, Qí Prefecture reduced its levy by half,
while the silk levy in the five prefectures was doubled.
Previously,
all recommendations were reviewed.
It was not as good as allowing private trade,
while annually collecting from the people the equivalent value of the salt sold by the government,
called the "salt consumption money";
Emperor Gāozǔ adopted this.
Soon, the price of salt suddenly dropped,
reaching as low as ten cash per catty.
By this time,
the Three Commissioners Director Dǒng Yù wanted to increase surplus profits,
but found it difficult to abruptly change the previous system,
so he heavily taxed salt merchants:
seven cash for those passing through,
ten cash for those staying to sell.
As a result, salt merchants nearly vanished,
and the government resumed selling salt itself.
The salt consumption money,
however, continued to be collected as before.
The Wǔdài Huìyào states: At that time, some petitioners suggested that the salt consumption money be allocated among the various circuits, prefectures, and commanderies,
with households divided into five grades, each paying from one string down to two hundred cash,
after which people would be free to engage in trade as they wished,
so that the government would not suffer losses,
and the people would benefit.
The court implemented this,
and the various salt offices initially continued as before.
Soon, the price of salt suddenly dropped,
and in prefectures and counties far from the salt-producing areas,
it did not exceed twenty cash per catty.
The officials in charge again found it difficult to abruptly change the system,
so they petitioned to reimpose heavy taxes.
Their aim was to stop private trade,
and return the profits to the government.
Although the salt offices sold much salt,
the household salt consumption money was not exempted,
causing great hardship for the people.
35 In Mǐn, the Salt and Iron Commissioner and Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, Lǐ Rényù,
son of Lǐ Mǐn,
(Lǐ Mǐn
was the father of the Yuán Liángguó Lady, consort of Mǐn ruler Chǎng).
was young
and handsome,
and won the favor of Xī.
He enjoyed the favor of a catamite.
Xī appointed Rényù as Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs and concurrently Vice Director of the Secretariat,
and Hànlín Academician and Vice Minister of Personnel Lǐ Guāngzhǔn as Vice Director of the Secretariat and concurrently Minister of Revenue,
both serving as Tongpingzhangshi.
Xī was excessively debauched and unrestrained.
Once, during a night banquet,
Guāngzhǔn, drunk, offended the emperor's wishes,
and Xī ordered him seized and sent to the market for execution;
the officials dared not kill him,
and imprisoned him instead.
The next day,
during court,
Xī summoned him and restored his position.
That evening,
another banquet was held,
and Hànlín Academician Zhōu Wéiyuè was arrested and imprisoned.
The jailers prepared a bed for him,
saying:
"The Grand Councilor stayed here last night,
Minister, do not worry."
When he sobered up, he was released.
On another day,
during another banquet,
all the attending officials left drunk,
only Wéiyuè remained.
Xī said:
"Wéiyuè's body is very small,
how can he drink so much?"
Someone nearby said:
"Wine has a separate gut,"
a common vulgar saying.
Xī was pleased,
and ordered Wéiyuè dragged down from the hall,
intending to cut open his belly to see his wine gut.
Someone said:
"If you kill Wéiyuè,
no one
will serve Your Majesty in heavy drinking."
So he spared him.
36 When the Emperor first ascended the throne,
the ministers discussed sending a memorial to the Qìdān declaring mourning and addressing them as subjects,
but Jǐng Yánguǎng requested sending a letter referring to themselves as "grandson" and not as subjects.
Jǐng Yánguǎng's proposal
was based on the Qìdān ruler ordering Emperor Gāozǔ to call himself "son emperor" three years prior,
using the etiquette of family correspondence.
"Bending one's body for the sake of the state—
what shame is there in that!
If Your Majesty acts like this,
in the future you will surely don armor yourself,
and fight the Qìdān,
and regret will be of no use then."
"Then" refers to
at that time.
Féng Dào vacillated between the two positions.
The Emperor ultimately followed Yánguǎng's advice.
The Qìdān were greatly angered,
and sent an envoy to reprimand them,
saying:
"How could you not first seek approval,
and hastily assume the imperial throne?"
Yánguǎng again replied with disrespectful language.
The Qìdān Lúlóng Military Commissioner Zhào Yánshòu wanted to replace the Jìn Emperor and rule China,
(Zhào Yánshòu and his father's desire to rule China
was already evident during the encampment at Tuánbǎi).
The Qìdān ruler largely agreed.
The first year of the Tiānfú era (Guǐmǎo, 943)
1 Spring,
first month,
Guǐmǎo,
the Shǔ ruler appointed the Commissioner of the Palace and Gardens and concurrently Xuānhuī Commissioner Tián Jìngquán to additionally hold the position of Military Commissioner of Yǒngpíng;
Jìngquán
was a eunuch,
and the ruler cited the precedent of the Former Shǔ's Wáng Chéngxiū in appointing him.
(The Former Shǔ ruler Wáng Yǎn appointed the eunuch Wáng Chéngxiū to command Qín Prefecture,
as recorded in the 273rd scroll of the Táng Zhuāngzōng Tóngguāng second year).
The Odes say: "The mirror of Yīn is not far,
it is in the time of the Xià sovereigns."
Mèng Chǎng failed to take the fall of Former Shǔ as a warning,
and instead cited Wáng Chéngxiū as a precedent to elevate eunuchs,
his state eventually fell to Sòng,
too late!
2 The Emperor heard that the Qìdān were about to invade,
and in the second month,
Jǐwèi,
departed from Yèdū;
Yǐchǒu,
arrived at the Eastern Capital.
The Emperor had ascended the throne before the coffin at the Bǎochāng Hall in Yèdū,
and only now reached Biàn.
There was not a single idle month.
3 The Táng Xuānchéng Prince Jǐngdá
was resolute, forthright, and open-minded,
and Lièzǔ loved him,
repeatedly wishing to make him heir;
(Lièzǔ
refers to the Táng ruler).
When the Táng ruler passed away,
his temple name was Lièzǔ,
and the Zīzhì Tōngjiàn follows the text of their state history in recording this.
The Táng ruler stopped because Prince Qí Jǐng was older.
Jǐng thus resented Qíqiū.
(He resented him both for supporting the plan to replace the heir
and for contending for power and harming the state;
Sòng Qíqiū thus could not escape).
The Táng ruler's youngest son, Jǐngtì,
his mother Zhǒngshi was favored,
while Prince Qí Jǐng's mother, Empress Sòng, rarely had audiences.
When the Táng ruler visited Jǐng's palace,
he encountered Jǐng personally tuning musical instruments,
became furious,
and reprimanded him for several days.
Zhǒngshi seized the opportunity to say
that although Jǐngtì was young, he was intelligent,
and could be made heir.
The Táng ruler angrily said:
"When a son has faults,
the father instructs him—
this is a common matter.
Matters of great state importance—
how can a woman interfere!"
He immediately ordered her married off.
The history records that the Táng ruler was clear and decisive,
not swayed by female favor.
The ruler of Táng once dreamed of swallowing a spiritual elixir.
The next morning, the alchemist Shǐ Shǒuchōng presented him with an elixir formula.
Believing it to be divine, he ingested it,
gradually becoming irritable and impatient.
Since Shūsūn Bào's time,
many have brought disaster upon themselves by acting upon ominous dreams.
He did not listen.
He once bestowed some of the medicine upon Lǐ Jiànxūn.
Jiànxūn said:
"Your servant has taken it for several days
and already feels agitated and feverish.
How much worse would it be to take more!"
The Táng ruler said:
"We have been taking it for a long time."
When ministers presented memorials,
he would often fly into a rage;
however, if someone argued with a stern expression and their reasoning was sound,
he would compose himself, express gratitude, and follow their advice.
The Táng ruler asked the Daoist priest Wáng Qīxiá:
"What way can bring about great peace?"
He replied:
"A king must first govern his heart and body,
then he can govern his family and state.
Now, Your Majesty has not yet been able to rid yourself of anger when hungry and joy when full.
How can we speak of great peace!"
Empress Sòng, from behind the curtain, praised this,
considering it the utmost truth.
All gifts bestowed by the Táng ruler,
Qīxiá refused to accept.
Qīxiá often submitted memorials on behalf of others.
The Táng ruler wanted to build an altar for him.
He declined, saying:
"The state's resources are currently lacking.
How is there leisure for this!
Only when the memorials I burn do not transform [i.e., fail to reach heaven]
should I then petition for it."
Daoist priests, when submitting memorials,
claim they ascend to heaven.
History states that Wáng Qīxiá was different from those who rely on techniques to seek favor and profit.
The Vice Director of the Bureau of Imperial Carriages, Féng Yánsì,
served as Chief Secretary in the Marshal's Office of Prince Qí.
His nature was cunning and obsequious.
He formed ties with Sòng Qíqiū and the Deputy Commissioner of the Palace Affairs, Chén Jué.
Those in the same office who were above him,
Yánsì gradually schemed to have them removed.
Yánsì once jokingly said to the Vice Director of the Secretariat, Sūn Shèng:
"What abilities do you possess,
to be Vice Director of the Secretariat?"
Shèng said:
"Shèng,
a rustic scholar from east of the mountains,
Sūn Shèng,
a native of Gāomì County, Mìzhōu,
fled south,
see the second year of Tiānchéng era of Táng Míngzōng, scroll 276.
is not as skilled in witty conversation as you,
nor as adept at flattery and deceit.
However, our sovereign appointed you to accompany and be with Prince Qí,
surely intending for you to guide and assist him with benevolence and righteousness.
How could it merely be to have a companion for music, women, dogs, and horses!
Shèng truly has no ability;
your abilities
are precisely sufficient to bring disaster upon the state."
Yánsì
was from Shèzhōu.
There was also another named Wèi Cén,
who was also in Prince Qí's residence.
The Supervising Secretary Cháng Mèngxī repeatedly stated that Chén Jué, Féng Yánsì, and Wèi Cén were all flattering and wicked petty men,
unfit to serve the heir apparent;
the Director of the Bureau of Gates and concurrent Judge of the Court of Judicial Review, Xiāo Yǎn, submitted a memorial accusing Chén Jué of being treacherous and disrupting governance.
The Táng ruler was somewhat moved to realization,
but before he could remove them,
a carbuncle broke out on his back.
He kept it secret, not letting others know,
secretly ordering physicians to treat it,
while continuing to hold court as usual.
On the day Gēngwǔ,
his illness became critical.
The imperial physician Wú Tíngyù
sent a trusted agent to summon Prince Qí Jǐng to attend to his illness.
The Táng ruler secretly ordered physicians to treat his illness;
one could still say he wished to calm and reassure people's hearts.
As for summoning the eldest legitimate son to attend in a critical situation,
it was done on the physician's suggestion.
Can this be taken as a model!
Treat,
zhí zhī fān.
"I ingested metal and stone [elixirs],
initially hoping to prolong life,
but instead harmed it further.
You should take warning from this!"
That evening,
he passed away.

this edict was issued in the twelfth month of last year;
now we follow Shí Guó Jìnián.
Jìnián says Sòng Qíqiū submitted the memorial;
now we follow Jiāngnán Lù.
It said:
"I served the late emperor for thirty years,
observing him receiving those distant (from power),
diligently and tirelessly,
yet there were still cases where the sentiments of those below did not reach him.
Your Majesty has newly ascended the throne,
whom have you appointed,
that you suddenly cut off and distance yourself from your ministers?
I am old,
and will likely not have the chance to serve you in person again."
Thereupon, he wept and sobbed.
The Book of Songs says: tears and snivel poured down.
The commentary states: from the eyes are called tears (tì),
from the nose is called snivel (sì).
(The ruler) hastily withdrew the previous edict.
The Táng ruler built a tall tower in the palace,
summoned his attending ministers to view it,
all marveled and praised it.
Xiāo Yǎn said:
"It is a pity there is no well below the tower."
The Táng ruler asked him why.
He replied:
"Because of this, it does not match the Jǐngyáng Tower."
The Chén later ruler built the Jǐngyáng Tower,
when the Suí troops arrived,
he threw himself into the well below the tower.
Xiāo Yǎn cited a case of a perished state to remonstrate.
(He) was demoted to Shūzhōu,
the observation commissioner Sūn Shèng sent troops to guard him,
Yǎn said:
"Yǎn was punished for remonstrating and admonishing,
I have no other intentions.
Back at the time of the late emperor's final decree,
you nearly endangered the state,
Jī,
pronounced jū yī fān.
Today you actually guard against me!"
Shèng felt ashamed and fearful,
and immediately stopped it.
6. The Emperor sent an envoy carrying a letter to the Khitan,
but the Khitan had already encamped at Yèdū,
at that time the Khitan were camped outside the city of Yèdū.
On Rénwǔ (a day),
(the Emperor) appointed Jǐng Yánguǎng, Commander of the Imperial Guard Cavalry and Infantry, as the Imperial Camp Commissioner,
and appointed Lǐ Zhōu, former military commissioner of Jìngnán, as the留守 (defense commissioner) of the Eastern Capital.
On that day,
Gāo Xíngzhōu set out first with the vanguard army.
At that time, the strategy, orders, and commands for military operations all came from Yánguǎng,
the Grand Councilors and below had no part in them;
Yánguǎng took advantage of his power and acted arrogantly,
insulting and bullying the various generals,
even the Son of Heaven could not control him.
This sets the stage for the later dismissal of Jǐng Yánguǎng.
On Yǐyǒu (a day),
the Emperor departed from the Eastern Capital.
On Dīnghài (a day),
Huázhōu reported that the Khitan had reached Líyáng.
Líyáng is on the west bank of Huázhōu,
separated only by the great river,
hence the report of the matter.
On Wùzǐ (a day)
the Emperor reached Chánzhōu.
Chánzhōu at that time was based at Déshèng Ford.
The Khitan ruler encamped at Yuánchéng,
Liú Xù said: Yuánchéng in Wèizhōu,
a Suí dynasty county,
administered the ancient Yīnchéng.
In the seventeenth year of the Táng Zhēnguàn era,
it was merged into Guìxiāng;
in the second year of the Shènglì era,
Guìxiāng and Shēnxiàn were divided,
and Yuánchéng County was established,
administering Wáng Mǎng's city;
in the thirteenth year of the Kāiyuán era,
the administration was moved below the city walls.
The ancient Yīnchéng,
is twelve lǐ northeast of Cháochéng.
At that time, the Khitan ruler probably encamped at the ancient Yīnchéng.
Nánlè,
was the Chānglè County of Wèizhōu in the Táng,
the Later Táng avoided the taboo of their ancestor Lǐ Guóchāng's name,
and changed it to Nánlè.
Jiǔyù Zhì: Nánlè County is forty-four lǐ south of Wèizhōu.
Lè,
pronounced luò.
He was enfeoffed as Prince of Wèi.
This was appointed by the Khitan ruler.
The Khitan invaded Tàiyuán,
Liú Zhīyuǎn joined forces with Bái Chéngfú, totaling twenty thousand troops, and attacked them.
On Jiǎwǔ (a day),
(the Emperor) appointed Zhīyuǎn as the campaign pacification commissioner of the Yōuzhōu circuit,
Dù Wēi as his deputy,
and Mǎ Quánjié as the Chief Inspector of the Army.
On Bǐngshēn (a day),
(the Emperor) sent Zhāng Yànzé, Senior General of the Right Martial Guard, and others to lead troops to resist the Khitan at Líyáng.
7. On Wùxū (a day),
the Shǔ ruler again had his generals and councilors hold military commissioner titles in absentia.
The Shǔ had stopped having generals and councilors hold military commissioner titles concurrently; see scroll 282, sixth year of Gāozǔ's Tiānfú era,
which was the fifth year of the Shǔ ruler's Guǎngzhèng era.
8 The Emperor again sent the translator Mèng Shǒuzhōng to deliver a letter to the Khitan,
seeking to restore the former friendship.
The Khitan ruler replied in a letter:
"The situation that has already formed
cannot be changed."
On the Xīnchǒu day,
Tàiyuán reported defeating the Khitan's Wěi King at Xiùróng.
Xiùróng
was the location of the Hàn dynasty's Fényáng County.
During the Suí dynasty, it was moved here from the old Xiùróng city,
and thus the county name was changed;
during the Táng dynasty, it was attached to Xīn Prefecture.
The Khitan fled from Yāmíng Valley.
From Yāmíng Valley, they exited through Lù Prefecture,
and to the east, they joined the main army of the Khitan ruler.
9 Yīn cast Tiāndé Tōngbǎo large iron coins,
each worth one hundred.
10 The Táng ruler sent an envoy to deliver letters to the Mǐn ruler Xī and the Yīn ruler Yánzhèng,
reproaching them for brothers taking up arms against each other.
Xī replied in a letter,
citing the Duke of Zhōu executing Guǎn and Cài,
and the Táng
executing Jiànchéng and Yuánjí as comparisons.
Yánzhèng replied in a letter,
denouncing the Táng ruler for seizing the state of the Yáng clan.
The Táng ruler was angered,
and thus broke off relations with Yīn.
This set the stage for Táng's later destruction of Yīn.
11 Deputy Military Commissioner of Tiānpíng and Administrator of Yùn Prefecture Yán Kǎn sent Observation Judge Dòu Yí to memorialize:
"Prefect of Bó Prefecture Zhōu Rú surrendered the city to the Khitan.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Yùn Prefecture is 170 lǐ northwest to Bó Prefecture.
Kǎn
is pronounced kǔ dàn,
also pronounced kǎn.
He led the Khitan to cross the river from Mǎjiākǒu,
capturing Left Martial Guard General Cài Xíngyù."
Last year in the twelfth month,
Cài Xíngyù was sent to garrison Yùn Prefecture.
"If the barbarians cross the river and join with Guāngyuǎn,
then the area south of the river will be in danger."
Yánguǎng agreed with this.
Yí
was from Jì Prefecture.
Zhāng Xīchēn punctuated, Niè Chóngqí proofread

Later student from Tiāntāi
First year of Kāiyùn (Jiǎchén, 944)
1 Second month,
on the Jiǎchén day, the first day of the month,
ordered former Bǎoyì Military Commissioner Shí Yūn to guard Májiākǒu,
former Wēishèng Military Commissioner Hé Chóngjiàn to guard Yángliú Fort,
Hùshèng Capital Command Officer Bái Zàiróng to guard Mǎjiākǒu,
and Western Capital Deputy Ān Yánwēi to guard Héyáng.
Not long after,
Zhōu Rú led the Khitan general Má Dá to cross the river from Mǎjiākǒu,
encamping on the eastern bank,
and attacking the northern ferry of Yùn Prefecture to coordinate with Yáng Guāngyuǎn.
Má Dá
was a cousin of the Khitan ruler.
On the Yǐsì day,
dispatched Capital

Commander of the Imperial Guard Cavalry and Yìchéng Military Commissioner Lǐ Shǒuzhēn, Divine Martial Commander Huángfǔ Yù, Chén Prefecture Defense Commissioner Liáng Hànzhāng, and Huái Prefecture Prefect Xuē Huáiràng to lead ten thousand troops,
advancing along the river by both land and water.
Shǒuzhēn
was from Héyáng;
Hànzhāng,
from Yìng Prefecture;
Huáiràng,
from Tàiyuán.
On the Bǐngwǔ day,
the Khitan besieged Gāo Xíngzhōu, Fú Yànqīng, and Vanguard Command Officer Shí Gōngbà at Qī City.
During the Spring and Autumn period,
Qī belonged to Wèi territory,
a city on the river.
The Dōngpō Zhǐzhǎng Tú considers it Wèi's Qī,
now within the boundaries of Bó Prefecture.
According to this, at that time, Jìn and the Khitan were confronting each other between Chán and Wèi.
This Qī City should have been north of Chán Prefecture,
south of Wèi Prefecture,
and likely not within the boundaries of Bó Prefecture.
They could not rescue each other.
Xíngzhōu and others reported an emergency,
Yánguǎng slowly informed the Emperor,
and the Emperor personally led troops to rescue them.
The Khitan lifted the siege and left,
and the three generals tearfully complained that the relief troops were too slow,
nearly causing their demise.
On the Wùshēn day,
Lǐ Shǒuzhēn and others arrived at Mǎjiākǒu.
The Khitan sent ten thousand infantry to build fortifications,
with scattered cavalry outside,
and tens of thousands of remaining troops stationed west of the river,
with thousands of boats ferrying troops.
Before they finished,
the Jìn troops pressed forward,
the Khitan cavalry retreated,
the Jìn troops attacked their fortifications,
and captured them.
The Khitan suffered a major defeat,
with thousands drowning after riding their horses into the river,
and thousands captured or killed.
The troops west of the river left wailing,
and from then on, they did not dare to advance east again.
Yáng Guāngyuǎn's reinforcements were cut off.
Fù
is pronounced fú yòu.
2 On the Xīnhài day,
Dìngnán Military Commissioner Lǐ Yíyīn memorialized that he led forty thousand troops from Lín Prefecture to cross the river,
invading Khitan territory.
The Dìngnán Army
was in Xià Prefecture.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Lín Prefecture is 120 lǐ northwest to Xià Prefecture.
From Lín Prefecture northeast to Fǔ Prefecture,
and then from Fǔ Prefecture northeast into Khitan territory.
Nán
is pronounced nǎi dàn.
On the Rénzǐ day,
Yíyīn was appointed as the Khitan Southwestern Front Recruitment Commissioner.
Initially,
when the Khitan ruler captured Bèi Prefecture and Bó Prefecture,
he pacified and consoled the people,
sometimes appointing them to official positions and bestowing robes and insignia.
After being defeated at Qī City and Mǎjiākǒu,
he became resentful and angry,
and all the captured civilians
were killed,
while captured soldiers
were burned and roasted.
Because of this, the Jìn people were furious,
and united their efforts to fight bravely.
Yáng Guāngyuǎn led the Qīng Prefecture troops intending to join the Khitan to the west;
on the Wùwǔ day,
an edict ordered Shí Yūn to divide his troops and station them in Yùn Prefecture to guard against this.
Shí Yūn was stationed at Májiākǒu at the time.
An edict ordered Liú Zhīyuǎn to lead his troops from Tǔmén to exit Héng Prefecture and attack the Khitan,
and another edict ordered him to join Dù Wēi and Mǎ Quánjié at Xíng Prefecture.
Zhīyuǎn led his troops and stationed them at Lèpíng, not advancing.
Lèpíng was only a little over 200 lǐ from Tàiyuán.
3 The Emperor observed a year of mourning,
yet within the palace, he had delicate-sounding female musicians perform.
Delicate-sounding female musicians
were meant not to be heard outside.
He often ordered attendants to play the three-stringed pipa,
accompanied by Qiāng flutes,
with drumming, singing, and dancing,
saying:
"This is not music."
On the Gēngshēn day,
the officials submitted a memorial requesting permission to listen to music,
but the edict did not permit it.
While in mourning, he took his uncle's wife;
how could listening to music be reproached!
4 On the Rénxū day,
Yáng Guāngyuǎn besieged Dì Prefecture,
but Prefect Lǐ Qióng led troops to attack and defeat him.
Yáng Guāngyuǎn passed through Zī Prefecture from Qīng Prefecture to besiege Dì Prefecture.
Bǎi
is pronounced bǔ mài.
On the Guǐhài day,
former Wēishèng Military Commissioner Hé Chóngjiàn was appointed as Eastern Front Horse and Foot Commander,
leading troops to station in Yùn Prefecture.
5 Jiē and Chéng Righteous Army Command Officer Wáng Jūnhuái led over a thousand of his troops to rebel and surrender to Shǔ,
requesting to serve as a guide to capture Jiē and Chéng.
On the Jiǎzǐ day,
the Shǔ people attacked Jiē Prefecture.
6 The Khitan feigned abandoning Yuánchéng and withdrew,
concealing elite cavalry in the ancient Dùnqiū city.
Dùnqiū,
an ancient county of the Hàn dynasty.
The Ěryǎ states: "A mound formed in a single layer is called Dùnqiū."
Later, the administrative seat was moved to Yīn'ān city.
In the Táng dynasty, Dùnqiū County
was again moved to the south of Yīn'ān city.
In the third year of Tiānfú,
Chánzhōu was relocated across Déshèng Ford,
and Dùnqiū County was moved there as well.
Dùnqiū was moved three times in total;
the ancient city is likely Yīn'ān city.
At that time, an edict ordered Dù Wēi and Mǎ Quánjié to bring troops to rendezvous,
and the Khitan intended to wait for their forces to combine and ambush them.
The main army wanted to advance and pursue them,
but halted due to continuous rain.
The Khitan laid in ambush for ten days,
and their men and horses grew hungry and weary.
Zhào Yánshòu said:
"The Jìn army is all at the river,
fearing our sharp edge,
they certainly dare not advance;
it would be better to go right up to their city walls,
'jí'
means 'to approach.'
seize their pontoon bridge,"
referring to the river bridge at Déshèng Ford in Chánzhōu.
The Khitan ruler followed this advice.
In the third month,
on the first day, guǐyǒu,
he personally led over a hundred thousand troops to array north of Chánzhōu city.
Sòng Bái said: The Khitan were then stationed at Tiěqiū in Chánzhōu.
"Chén,"
read as "zhèn";
same below.
Ascending the city wall to look out,
their forces seemed endless.
Gāo Xíngzhōu's vanguard was south of Qīchéng,
and engaged the Khitan in battle,
from noon until dusk,
with both sides having victories and defeats.
The Khitan ruler led elite troops attacking the center formation,
and the Emperor also deployed his formation to await them.
The Khitan ruler, seeing the formidable strength of the Jìn army,
said to his attendants:
"Yáng Guāngyuǎn said half the Jìn troops had already starved to death,"
Yáng Guāngyuǎn luring the Khitan to invade is recorded in the previous year's scroll.
Using elite cavalry to sweep left and right across the formation,
the Jìn army stood firm,
ten thousand crossbows fired simultaneously,
flying arrows covered the ground.
The Khitan retreated slightly;
they then attacked the eastern flank of the Jìn formation,
but could not overcome it.
Fierce fighting continued until evening,
with countless dead on both sides.
After nightfall,
the Khitan withdrew,
camping thirty lǐ away.
They dared not camp close to the city,
fearing an attack by the Jìn army.
On yǐhài,
a minor officer from the Khitan ruler's tent stole his horse and fled here,
reporting that the Khitan had already issued wooden tablets
to gather the army and return north.
Jǐng Yánguǎng suspected it was a trick,
and kept the gates closed, not daring to pursue.
7 The Hàn ruler ordered Zhōngshū Lìng
and Grand Marshal Yuèwáng Liú Hóngchāng to pay respects at Lièzōng's tomb at Hǎiqū,
Liú Gǒng assumed the imperial title,
posthumously honoring his elder brother Liú Yǐn as Lièzōng.
He had bandits kill him.
8 The Khitan ruler, after leaving Chánzhōu heading north, divided his army into two forces,
one passing through Cāngzhōu and Dézhōu,
the other through Shēnzhōu and Jìzhōu on their return.
Wherever they passed, they burned and looted,
across an area a thousand lǐ square,
leaving the people and goods nearly exhausted.
They left Zhào Yánzhào as Liúhòu of Bèizhōu.
Má Dá captured Dézhōu,
and seized Cìshǐ Yǐn Jūfán.
9 Mǐn's Gǒngchén Dū Commander Zhū Wénjìn,
and Gé Mén Shǐ Lián Chóngyù,
after assassinating Emperor Kāngzōng,
see scroll 282, fourth year of Tiānfú.
intermarried to solidify their alliance.
The Mǐn ruler Xī was ruthless in executions;
once while touring the West Garden,
he drunkenly killed Kònghè Commander Wěi Cónglǎng.
Cónglǎng
was a partisan of Zhū and Lián.
He also once, while heavily intoxicated, recited a poem by Bái Jūyì:
"Only between human hearts facing each other,
feelings across a short distance cannot be gauged,"
and then raised his cup to toast the two men.
The two men rose,
shedding tears and bowing twice,
saying:
"We, your servants and sons, serve our sovereign father,
how could we have any other intentions!"
Xī did not respond.
The two men were greatly frightened.
Empress Lǐ was jealous of the favor shown to Shàng Xián,
and wanted to assassinate Xī and install her son Yà Chéng.
Shàng Xián was favored,
see previous scroll, eighth year of Tiānfú,
which was the fourth year of Yǒnglóng of the King of Mǐn.
Yà Chéng was then enfeoffed as King of Mǐn.
"The sovereign is deeply displeased with you two gentlemen,
what is to be done?"
It happened that Empress Lǐ's father Lǐ Zhēn was ill.
On yǐyǒu,
Xī went to Zhēn's residence to inquire about his illness.
Wénjìn and Chóngyù had Gǒngchén Mǎbù Shǐ Qián Dá assassinate Xī on horseback.
They summoned all officials to the court hall,
and announced to them:
"Tàizǔ Zhāowǔ Huángdì
gloriously founded the Mǐn state,
but now his descendants are debauched and cruel,
recklessly abandoning his legacy.
Heaven has turned against the Wáng clan,
we should choose someone virtuous to establish instead."
None dared to speak.
Chóngyù then pushed Wénjìn to ascend the hall,
dressed him in imperial robes and crown,
and led the assembled ministers to bow northward twice and proclaim themselves his subjects.
Wénjìn proclaimed himself ruler of Mǐn,
rounded up over fifty members of the Wáng clan, young and old, from Yánxǐ downward,
and executed them all.
Yánxǐ
was the younger brother of the Mǐn ruler.
"Shào,"
read as in "zhào."
"Zhǎng,"
read as "zhī liǎng."
He was posthumously titled Ruìwén Guǎngwǔ Míngshèng Yuándé Lóngdào Dàxiào Huángdì,
with the temple name Jǐngzōng.
Chóngyù was put in command of the six armies.
Lǐbù Shàngshū and concurrent Sānsī official Zhèng Yuánbì protested and refused to submit,
so he was dismissed and sent back to his fields,
intending to flee to Jiànzhōu,
wanting to join Wáng Yánzhèng.
Wénjìn issued orders,
releasing palace women,
halting construction projects,
to reverse Xī's policies.
The Yīn ruler Yánzhèng sent Tǒngjūn Shǐ Wú Chéngyì to lead troops against Wénjìn,
but without success.
Wénjìn appointed Shūmì Shǐ Bào Sīrùn as Tóng Píngzhāng Shì,
made Yǔlín Tǒngjūn Shǐ Huáng Shàopō Cìshǐ of Quánzhōu,
and Zuǒjūn Shǐ Chéng Wénwěi Cìshǐ of Zhāngzhōu.
Tīngzhōu Cìshǐ Tóng'ān's Xǔ Wénzhěn,
surrendered his entire commandery.
Jiǔyù Zhì: Tóng'ān County in Quánzhōu is 135 lǐ west of the prefecture,
likely established by the Wáng clan.
Sòng Bái said: In the 19th year of Kāiyuán,
four townships from the border of Quánzhōu's Nán'ān County were separated to establish Dàtóng Chǎng,
and the Mǐn king elevated it to Tóng'ān County.
"Zhěn,"
read as "zhāng rěn."
10 On dīnghài,
an edict ordered the troops from Tàiyuán, Héngzhōu, and Ānzhōu
to return to their respective garrisons.
Because the Khitan had retreated.
11 On xīnmǎo,
Mǎ Quánjié attacked the Khitan's Tàizhōu,
and captured it.
Wǔdài Huìyào: In the third year of Tiānchéng of Later Táng,
Fènghuà Jūn was elevated to Tàizhōu,
with Qīngyuàn County as its administrative seat.
By the second year of Kāiyùn of Jìn, ninth month,
the seat was moved to Mǎnchéng County;
by the second year of Guǎngshùn of Zhōu, second month,
the prefecture was abolished,
and its Mǎnchéng County was transferred to Yìzhōu.
At that time, Mǎ Quánjié attacked Tàizhōu from Dìngzhōu.
12 An imperial order commanded the registration of local militia throughout the land,
with every seven households jointly providing weapons and supplies for one soldier.
13 Qínzhōu troops came to rescue Jiēzhōu,
emerging from Huángjiē Ridge,
and defeated Shǔ troops at Xīpíng.
14 Hàn appointed Hùbù Shìláng Chén Wò as Tóng Píngzhāng Shì.
In the summer of the 15th year,
in the fourth month,
on the day Dīngwèi,
the patrol commissioner of the Yellow River region, Liáng Jìn, recaptured Dézhōu using local militia forces.
These local militia forces
were civilian soldiers.
At that time, the Khitan were invading and plundering.
The people living along the Yellow River,
having prepared their own weapons and equipment,
each followed their own locality,
banded together to form associations,
in order to protect themselves.
The Khitan had captured Dézhōu and were returning north,
and Liáng Jìn took advantage of their departure to recapture it.
On the day Jǐyǒu,
the Emperor ordered the military commissioner of Guīdé, Gāo Xíngzhōu, and the military commissioner of Bǎoyì, Wáng Zhōu, to remain and guard Chánzhōu.
On the day Gēngxū,
the Emperor departed from Chánzhōu;
on the day Jiǎyín,
he arrived at Dàliáng.
The commander of the imperial guard cavalry and infantry, military commissioner of Tiānpíng, and concurrent grand councilor Jǐng Yánguǎng,
was already disliked by both superiors and subordinates.
"Superiors"
refers to the generals, ministers, and high officials;
"subordinates"
refers to the soldiers and common people.
"Disliked"
is pronounced wùlù fān.
Sāng Wéihàn brought up his crime of not rescuing Qìchéng.
"Brought up"
means to pull or drag out;
to drag out his crime
is like someone gathering clothes into their sleeves,
and then pulling them out from there.
On the day Xīnyǒu,
Yánguǎng was additionally appointed concurrent palace attendant,
and sent out to serve as the military governor of the Western Capital.
The Jìn dynasty moved its capital to Biàn,
making Hénán Prefecture the Western Capital.
Yánguǎng was depressed and discontented.
Petty men of low character,
when they gain power become arrogant and overbearing,
and when they lose power become depressed and discontented;
this is their constant nature.
He began to worry about the state being destroyed and himself being endangered,
and consequently indulged in drinking day and night.
Knowing he had no safe ground left,
he sought only momentary pleasure.
Because the Khitan had invaded,
the state's resources were increasingly depleted.
The court again dispatched thirty-six envoys along different routes to forcibly collect wealth from the people,
each given a sealed sword to authorize them.
The envoys were mostly accompanied by clerks and soldiers,
carrying chains, implements, knives, and staffs into people's homes.
Young and old were terrified,
with no place to seek death.
The prefectural and county officials further took advantage of the situation to commit fraud.
Hénán Prefecture was to contribute two hundred thousand strings of cash,
this being the total amount to be collected from the levy.
Jǐng Yánguǎng increased the levy by one hundred and seventy thousand strings,
intending to keep it for himself.
Lú Yì said to Yánguǎng:
"Your Excellency holds the positions of both general and minister,
your wealth and honor are at their peak.
Now the state is unfortunately
with empty treasuries,
and has no choice but to take from the people.
How can Your Excellency bear to further seek profit from this,
creating a burden for your descendants!"
Yánguǎng was ashamed and stopped.
The history states that Jǐng Yánguǎng was slightly better than Dù Chóngwēi.
Previously,
an edict had been issued because of Yáng Guǎngyuǎn's rebellion,
ordering Yǎnzhōu to repair its defenses.
Qīngzhōu and Yǎnzhōu were neighboring military districts,
hence the order to prepare.
"Previously"
is pronounced xī jiàn fān.
Under the pretext of repairing watchtowers and battlements,
he collected people's wealth to fill his private stores.
The chief minister of the Court of Judicial Review, Zhāng Rényuàn, was appointed as the levy commissioner,
and upon reaching Yǎnzhōu,
imposed a levy of one hundred thousand strings of cash.
It happened that Shěn Xìn was not present,
"not present" meaning
he happened to be away from the district.
Pointing to a storehouse of money,
it already met the required amount.
The history states that the Jìn dynasty's military governors
took advantage of the state's difficulties
to squeeze the people to enrich their own families.
