and Jiànzhōu is isolated and in peril.
If the Prince of Fùshā cannot protect Jiànzhōu,
how can he protect Fúzhōu!
In the past, Wáng Cháo and his brothers
were mere commoners from Guāngshān,
yet they seized Fújiàn as easily as turning over a hand.
This matter is recorded in the Táng annals.
If you plan for wealth and honor yourself,
why worry about not achieving as much as they did!"
Huáng Rénfèng agreed.
That evening,
Lǐ Réndá and others led armored soldiers to storm the government residence,
killing Jìchāng and Wú Chéngyì.
The Kǎoyì states: The Mǐnzhōng Shílù, Mǐn Wáng Lièzhuàn, and Jiǔguó Zhì
all record that Jìchāng was killed in the fourth month.
Here, we follow the Shíguó Jìnián.
Lǐ Réndá wanted to proclaim himself,
but feared that the people's hearts were not yet with him.
Knowing that the monk Zhuó Yánmíng of Xuěfēng Temple was highly respected by the masses,
Xuěfēng is located over a hundred lǐ west of Hòuguān County in Fúzhōu.
"This monk has double pupils in his eyes,
and his hands hang past his knees—
he is truly an emperor."
Together, they welcomed him.
On the Jǐhài day,
they established him as emperor.
The Kǎoyì states: The Mǐn Lù, Qǐyùn Tú, Qǐguó Shílù, and Jiāngnán Lù record
"Yánmíng."
The Mǐnzhōng Shílù, Mǐn Wáng Lièzhuàn, Jiǔguó Zhì, Xuē Shǐ, Táng Yúlù, Wáng Shěnzhī Zhuàn, and Wúyuè Bèishǐ record
"Yǎnmíng."
According to the Qǐyùn Tú,
Yánmíng's original name was Yǎn.
As a monk, his name was Tǐmíng.
Upon ascending the throne, he changed it to Yánmíng.
Here, we follow this.
The Jiāngnán Lù states:
"Jìchāng was killed by the deputy general Wáng Yánfèng.
Ten days later,
the former palace official Lǐ Yì killed Yánfèng
and established Yánmíng as ruler."
Here, we follow the Shíguó Jìnián.
They dressed him in imperial robes and crown,
and led the officers and officials to bow to him facing north.
However, they still used the tenth year of the Tiānfú era,
and sent envoys to submit memorials and pledge allegiance to Jìn.
When Yánzhèng heard of this,
he exterminated Huáng Rénfèng's family.
He ordered the Tǒngjūnshǐ Zhāng Hànzhēn to lead a navy of five thousand,
joining forces with the troops of Zhāng and Quán to attack Yánmíng.
11. On the Yǐsì day,
Dù Wēi and other armies assembled at Dìngzhōu,
appointing the Gòngfèng Guān Xiāo Chǔjūn as acting administrator of Qízhōu.
On the Gēngxū day,
the various armies attacked the Khitan.
Jìn Tíngqiān, the prefect of Tàizhōu, surrendered the entire prefecture.
Jìn
is a surname,
derived from the state name.
On the Jiǎyín day,
they captured Mǎnchéng.
According to the Wǔdài Huìyào,
in the ninth month of this year,
Tàizhōu's administration was moved to Mǎnchéng.
At this time, Tàizhōu was still administered from Qīngyuàn.
Sòng Bái said: Mǎnchéng was originally the Hàn dynasty's Běipíng County.
The Later Wèi established Yǒnglè County there.
In the first year of the Tiānbǎo era,
it was renamed Mǎnchéng County.
They also captured its two thousand soldiers.
On the Yǐmǎo day,
they captured Suìchéng.
Some of Zhào Yánshòu's subordinates who surrendered said:
"The Khitan ruler has returned to Hǔběikǒu.
North of the Fénshuǐ River in Tàiyuán,
there is also a place named Hǔběikǒu.
At that time, the Khitan army was retreating north from Qí and Yì,
so that was not their route.
This refers to the Gǔběikǒu north of Yōu and Tán.
The Sòng envoy's travel record to Liáo states: Traveling 80 lǐ north from Tánzhōu,
and another 80 lǐ to Hǔběikǒu Station.
Thus, the Gǔběikǒu in Tánzhōu is also called Hǔběikǒu.
He has gathered his forces again and is heading south,
with about over eighty thousand cavalry.
He is estimated to arrive tomorrow evening,
so we must quickly prepare."
Dù Wēi and others were afraid.
On the Bǐngchén day,
they retreated to defend Tàizhōu.
On the Wùwǔ day,
the Khitan arrived at Tàizhōu.
On the Jǐwèi day,
the Jìn army marched south,
with the Khitan following closely.
The Jìn army reached Yángchéng.
The Continued Hàn Treatise states: Púyīn County in Zhōngshān had a Yángchéng.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states: The Bóshuǐ River originates from Wàngdū County in Zhōngshān,
flows east past Yángchéng County,
and spreads into marshes and lakes,
which people call Yángchéng Diàn.
Yángchéng is located 30 lǐ southeast of Púyīn County.
On the Gēngshēn day,
the Khitan arrived in full force.
The Jìn army engaged them in battle,
pursued them over ten lǐ as they fled north,
and the Khitan crossed the Báigōu and left.
This refers to the southern Báigōu.
It is what the Shuǐjīng Zhù calls the Qíshuǐ River flowing north to become the Báigōu.
The northern Báigōu is located 60 lǐ south of Xīnchéng County in Zhuōzhōu.
The Sòng envoy's northward travel record states: North of Xióngzhōu,
south of the boundary river,
there is a Báigōu Station.
Also, Fàn Chéngdà's Běishǐ Lù states: Fifteen lǐ north from Ānsù Army's north gate,
one reaches the Báigōu River.
Another 105 lǐ leads to Zhuōzhōu.
This refers to the northern Báigōu.
On the Rénxū day,
the Jìn army formed ranks and marched south.
The barbarian cavalry surrounded them on all sides like mountains,
and the various armies fought desperately to resist them.
That day,
they advanced only a little over ten lǐ,
with men and horses hungry and exhausted.
On the Guǐhài day,
the Jìn army reached Báituánwèi Village.
(Textual note: The *Hàn Gāozǔ Shílù* records it as
"Báitán."
We now follow the *Jìn Shàodì Shílù*.)
The Khitan surrounded them in multiple layers,
and dispatched surprise troops behind the camp to cut off their supply route.
That evening,
a great wind arose from the northeast,
destroying houses and snapping trees.
Wells were dug within the camp,
but they collapsed just as they reached water.
The soldiers took the mud,
wrung it through cloth to drink,
with both men and horses suffering from thirst.
By dawn,
the wind was even stronger.
The Khitan ruler sat in a large Xī cart.
(Shěn Kuò said: The Xī people's occupations are felling mountains,
dryland farming,
and cart-making;
the Khitan's carts are all supplied by the Xī.
The construction of their baggage carts is similar to that of China,
wider at the back and narrower at the front, without a curved hull.
The materials are frugal and easily damaged,
unable to bear heavy loads but advantageous for traveling over mountains.
The axle is long and the wheel broad.
The rim of the wheel
is no more than four inches thick,
and the material for the carriage frame is no more than five inches.
Their carriages are drawn by camels,
with a canopy mounted on top.
Only the wealthy add decorations of felt curtains with embroidered patterns.)
In the Shǔ edition,
the characters "Xī cart"
are not preceded by
the character "large"
"The Jìn army is only this much;
we should capture them all,
and then march south to take Dàliáng!"
He ordered the Iron Falcons to dismount on all sides,
pull up the deer antler defenses, and advance,
wielding short weapons to attack the Jìn army.
(The Khitan called elite cavalry "Iron Falcons,"
meaning they wore iron armor,
and charged swiftly and lightly,
like a sparrowhawk seizing small birds.
Yào,
pronounced yì zhào fān.)
The soldiers were all furious,
shouting loudly
and saying:
"Why isn't the Chief Commander deploying troops,
letting the soldiers die in vain!"
The various generals requested to go out and fight.
Dù Wēi said:
"Wait until the wind subsides a bit,
then we can slowly assess the situation."
The Infantry and Cavalry Supervisor Lǐ Shǒuzhēn said:
"They are many, we are few.
Amidst the wind and sand,
it's impossible to gauge their numbers.
Only those who fight with all their strength will win.
This wind is actually helping us;
if we wait for the wind to stop,
we will be wiped out."
He immediately shouted:
"All troops, attack the enemy together!"
He also said to Dù Wēi:
"Your Excellency, please defend well."
(Dù Wēi held the title of Zhōngshū Lìng at the time,
hence he was addressed as such.)
The Left Wing Cavalry Formation Commander Zhāng Yànzé summoned the various generals to ask for plans.
They all said:
"The enemy has the advantage of the wind;
we should wait until the wind changes direction to fight."
Zhāng Yànzé also thought this was correct.
After the generals withdrew,
the Deputy Right Wing Cavalry Formation Commander, Tàiyuán's Yào Yuánfú, alone remained.
He said to Zhāng Yànzé:
"Now the army is extremely hungry and thirsty.
If we wait for the wind to change,
we will already be captives of the enemy.
The enemy believes we cannot fight against the wind.
We should take them by surprise and attack swiftly;
this is the deceptive way of warfare."
(Arrows do not go against the wind—this is an ancient rule.
But if using short weapons in close combat,
then there are many instances of winning while fighting against the wind.)
"Rather than being bound and captured,
why not sacrifice our lives for the state!"
He then, together with Zhāng Yànzé, Yào Yuánfú, and the Left Wing Formation Commander Huángfǔ Yù, led elite cavalry out of the west gate to attack them.
(This refers to the west gate of the marching camp.
The wind came from the northeast;
going out the west gate to engage in battle
was also following the wind's direction.)
The Khitan retreated several hundred paces.
Zhāng Yànzé and the others said to Lǐ Shǒuzhēn:
"Should we drag our forces back and forth?
Or charge straight ahead and fight fiercely,
aiming only for victory?"
Lǐ Shǒuzhēn said:
"Given the situation,
how can we turn back our reins!
We should drive straight through to achieve victory."
Zhāng Yànzé and the others galloped away.
The wind grew even stronger,
darkening the sky as if it were night.
Zhāng Yànzé and the others, with over ten thousand cavalry, struck the Khitan horizontally.
Their shouts shook heaven and earth.
The Khitan suffered a great defeat and fled,
their collapse like a mountain crumbling.
Lǐ Shǒuzhēn also ordered the infantry to pull up all the deer antler defenses and go out to fight.
Infantry and cavalry advanced together,
pursuing the fleeing enemy for over twenty *lǐ*.
The Iron Falcons, having dismounted,
were in such haste they could not remount,
and abandoned their horses, armor, and weapons, which covered the ground.
The scattered Khitan troops reached the water southeast of Yángchéng,
and gradually reformed their ranks.
Dù Wēi said:
"The enemy's courage is already broken;
we should not allow them to form ranks again!"
He dispatched elite cavalry to attack them,
and they all crossed the water and fled.
The Khitan ruler, riding a Xī cart, fled over ten *lǐ*.
With pursuing troops close behind,
he obtained a camel
and rode it to escape.
The various generals requested to pursue him urgently.
Dù Wēi declared loudly:
"We were fortunate not to die when we encountered the enemy;
are we to go seek clothing and supplies now?"
(Meaning: encountering the enemy and being robbed, yet fortunate to survive;
if we then go demand clothing and supplies from the enemy,
they will surely become angry and kill us.
Suǒ,
pronounced shān kè fān.)
"For two days, our men and horses have been extremely thirsty.
Now that we have water to drink, we are all heavily burdened,
making it difficult to pursue the enemy.
It is better to return with the army intact."
They then retreated and garrisoned Dìngzhōu.
The Khitan ruler reached Yōuzhōu,
and the scattered troops gradually gathered.
Because the army had been defeated,
he caned each of their chieftains several hundred times,
with only Zhào Yánshòu exempted.
On the Yǐchǒu day,
the various armies withdrew from Dìngzhōu and returned.
An edict was issued placing Tàizhōu under the jurisdiction of Dìngzhōu.
(Placed under Dìngzhōu's Yìwǔ Army.)
12. In summer,
the fourth month,
on the Xīnsì day,
the Emperor departed from Chánzhōu.
On the Jiǎshēn day,
he returned to Dàliáng.
(Earlier this year in the first month,
an edict was issued for a personal campaign.
In the second month, he reached Chánzhōu.
Now that the various armies were returning victorious,
he therefore returned to Dàliáng.)
13. On the Jǐchǒu day,
Yèdū was again made the Tiānxióng Army.
(In the first year of the Táng Zhuāngzōng's Tóngguāng era,
Wèizhōu was made the Dōngjīng Xīngtáng Prefecture,
and the Tiānxióng military district was abolished.
In the third year,
Dōngjīng was abolished and made Yèdū.
When the Jìn arose,
they followed this,
changing Xīngtáng Prefecture to Guǎngjìn Prefecture.
Now it was again made the Tiānxióng Army.)
14. Mǐn's Zhāng Hànzhēn reached Fúzhōu
and attacked its eastern pass.
Huáng Rénfèng, hearing that his family had been exterminated,
opened the gates and fought with all his strength,
greatly defeating the Mǐn troops.
He captured Zhāng Hànzhēn,
brought him into the city,
and executed him.
Zhuó Yánmíng had no other strategy;
he merely sprayed water and scattered beans in the main hall,
performing various Buddhist rites.
He also sent an envoy to Pútián to welcome his father.
(In the early Wǔdé era of the Táng,
Pútián County was established from part of Nán'ān County,
belonging to Quánzhōu.
In the fourth year of the Sòng's Tàipíng Xīngguó era,
Xīnghuà Army was separately established,
located 160 *lǐ* northeast of Quánzhōu.)
After Lǐ Réndá established Yán Míng,
he personally took charge of the affairs of the Six Armies and various guards.
He stationed Huáng Rénfèng at the West Gate
and Chén Jìxún at the North Gate.
Rénfèng calmly said to Jìxún:
"The reason why one is considered human
is because one possesses loyalty, trustworthiness, benevolence, and righteousness.
I once rendered service to Fùshā,
but later betrayed him—
this is disloyalty.
Someone entrusted their nephew to me, yet I killed him with others—
this is untrustworthiness.
Wáng Jìchāng
was the nephew of the Mǐn ruler Yánzhèng.
From,
pronounced cái yòng fān.
Those I killed were all old acquaintances from my hometown—
this is inhumanity.
Abandoning my wife and children,
leaving them to be trampled upon by others—
this is unrighteousness.
This body of mine has sunk nine times and floated ten;
even death would not absolve my shame!"
He then beat his chest and wept bitterly.
Jìxún said:
"A true man sacrifices himself for fame and achievement;
why care about wife and children!
You should set this matter aside,
lest it bring disaster upon you."
When Réndá heard of this,
he sent someone to accuse Rénfèng and Jìxún of plotting rebellion,
and had them both killed.
From then on, all military authority fell into Réndá's hands.
15 In the fifth month,
on the first day, Bǐngshēn,
a general amnesty was declared.
16 Shùnguó military commissioner Dù Wēi,
who had long been stationed in Héngzhōu,
(Emperor Gāozǔ Tiānfú seventh year,
Dù Wēi first garrisoned Héngzhōu,
see volume 283.)
Héng,
pronounced hù dēng fān.
relied on his status as a royal relative,
(Dù Wēi married Emperor Gāozǔ's younger sister, Princess Sòngguó Cháng.)
and often used border defense as a pretext
to extort money and silk from officials and commoners to fill his private coffers.
If wealthy families possessed rare treasures, famous beauties, or fine horses,
he would seize them by force;
or he would falsely accuse them of crimes and have them killed,
confiscating their family property.
Moreover, he was excessively timid and cowardly.
Whenever several dozen Khitan cavalry crossed the border,
Wēi would already have closed the gates and ascended the ramparts.
Sometimes, a few riders would drive hundreds or thousands of captured Chinese past the city walls,
yet Wēi would only stare wide-eyed and crane his neck to watch,
with no intention of intercepting them.
As a result, the enemy had no fear or restraint,
and many of the subordinate cities were massacred.
Wēi never sent a single soldier to rescue them.
Across a thousand lǐ,
exposed bones lay like thick grass.
("Exposed bones lay like thick grass"
is a phrase from the Zuǒzhuàn.)
"Like thick grass" means
like grass growing wildly across the vast wilderness.
Exposed,
pronounced bù bǔ fān.
Wēi saw that his region was devastated and in ruins,
and that he was resented by the masses.
He also feared the strength of the Khitan,
and repeatedly submitted memorials requesting to return to the court.
The emperor did not permit it.
Without waiting for a reply,
Wēi abruptly abandoned his command and went to the court.
When the court heard of this,
they were shocked and alarmed.
Sāng Wéihàn said to the emperor:
"Wēi deliberately disobeyed the court's orders
and abandoned the border garrison.
Ordinarily, he relies on his past achievements
to demand leniency and indulgence.
Yet when the border regions are troubled,
he shows no intention of defending them.
We should take this opportunity to remove him,
to avoid future troubles."
The emperor was displeased.
Wéihàn said:
"If Your Majesty cannot bear to remove him,
you should assign him a small garrison near the capital,
and not entrust him with a major frontier command again."
The emperor said:
"Wēi
is my close relative;
he certainly harbors no ulterior motives.
(Meaning he has no other intentions.)
Do not doubt him!"
From then on, Wéihàn dared not speak again on state affairs,
and resigned his post citing foot illness.
Dù Wēi could not be removed, yet Sāng Wéihàn sought to leave—
the Jìn dynasty was nearly finished.
Again,
pronounced fú yòu fān.
On Bǐngchén,
Wēi arrived in Dàliáng.
17 On Dīngsì,
Lǐ Réndá conducted a grand review of his troops,
inviting Zhuó Yánmíng to oversee the inspection.
Réndá secretly instructed soldiers to rush forward and ascend the steps,
stabbing Yánmíng to death.
Réndá feigned shock,
fleeing in panic;
the soldiers together seized Réndá,
and made him sit in Yánmíng's seat.
Réndá then proclaimed himself acting military commissioner of Wēiwǔ,
adopting the Bǎodà reign era.
(This year
was the third year of Bǎodà of Southern Táng.)
He also sent envoys to pay tribute to Jìn;
and killed Yánmíng's father as well.
The Táng appointed Réndá as military commissioner of Wēiwǔ and tóngpíngzhāngshì,
bestowing upon him the name Hóngyì,
and enrolled him in the imperial clan register.
(Because he shared the same surname,
he was enrolled in the clan register and given the name Hóngyì,
ranking among the imperial sons.)
This laid the groundwork for Lǐ Réndá's later betrayal of Táng and alignment with Wúyuè.
Good,
pronounced hū dào fān.
18 On Jǐwèi,
Dù Wēi presented 4,000 infantry and cavalry from his personal troops, along with their armor and weapons.
On Gēngshēn,
he also presented 100,000 hú of grain
and 200,000 bundles of fodder,
claiming they were all from his own jurisdiction.
(Meaning they were all from Héngzhōu.)
If he truly possessed these,
they were all extorted from the people.
In his hasty departure from the garrison,
he could not transport them to fill his private stores,
so he presented them instead.)
The infantry were assigned to the Hùguó army,
but Wēi again requested they be made his personal guard,
with provisions and rewards all supplied by the state treasury.
Dù Wēi thus deceived the court in this manner,
yet the emperor could not perceive his treachery,
which later led to the Zhōngdù incident in Héngzhōu.
Again,
pronounced fú yòu fān.
Provisions,
pronounced bǐ jǐn fān,
meaning to supply.
Supplied by,
pronounced niú xiàng fān.
He requested the authority of Tiānxióng military commissioner,
and the emperor granted it.
19 Táng troops besieged Jiànzhōu,
repeatedly defeating Quánzhōu forces.
(The Quánzhōu forces
were those led by Dǒng Sī'ān and Wáng Zhōngshùn to rescue Jiànzhōu.)
They captured their general Shí Hòuqīng.
20 In the sixth month,
on Guǐyǒu,
Dù Wēi was appointed Tiānxióng military commissioner.
21 The Khitan invaded for consecutive years.
(The Khitan invasions
began from the capture of Bèizhōu in the first month of last year.)
Zuǒzhuàn: Shēngōng Wūchén wrote to Zǐ Zhòng and Zǐ Fǎn: "I will surely make you die from exhaustion from constant rushing."
"Rushing" means
when the border is in emergency,
one rushes to rescue it.
The Khitan also lost many people and livestock,
and the people grew weary and distressed.
Empress Dowager Shùlǜ said to the Khitan ruler:
"Would it be acceptable for a Han person to become the ruler of the Hu?"
He said:
"No."
The empress dowager said:
"Then why do you wish to become the ruler of the Han?"
He said:
"The Shí family betrayed our kindness;
it is intolerable."
The empress dowager said:
"Even if you now obtain Han lands,
you cannot hold them.
(Later events indeed matched Empress Dowager Shùlǜ's words.)
What use is regret then?"
She also said to her subordinates:
"How can the Han people sleep so soundly!
When one sleeps restlessly,
one tosses and turns unable to sleep;
sleeping soundly means
one sleeps peacefully.
I have not heard of harmony between the Fan and the Han.
If the Han people truly change their attitude,
why would I begrudge making peace with them!"
Sāng Wéihàn repeatedly advised the Emperor to once again seek peace with the Qìdān to alleviate the state's troubles.
The Emperor appointed the Kāifēng army general Zhāng Huī as a Palace Attendant,
(The Kāifēng army general
refers to a military general of Kāifēng Prefecture.)
and sent humble words to apologize for the offense.
The Qìdān ruler said:
"If Jǐng Yánguǎng and Sāng Wéihàn come themselves,
and in addition cede the two circuits of Zhèn and Dìng to be subordinate to me,
then peace can be made."
The court considered the Qìdān's words angry,
believing they had no intention of making peace,
and thus stopped.
When the Qìdān ruler entered Dàliáng,
he said to Lǐ Sōng and others:
"If the Jìn envoys had come again back then,
then there would have been no war between north and south."
The historian states that the entire Qìdān state, from top to bottom, was originally weary of war.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
someone from Mǐn reported that the relief troops from Fúzhōu were plotting rebellion.
(In the first month of this year,
the ruler of Mǐn dispatched Fúzhōu troops to Jiànzhōu to resist Táng.)
They were sent back,
and ambushes were set up in the narrow passes,
killing them all,
with over eight thousand dead.
Their flesh was dried into jerky and brought back to be eaten.
The Táng general Biān Hào captured Xúnzhōu.
(Xúnzhōu is one hundred and eighty *lǐ* east to Jiànzhōu.)
All eagerly approved of it.
Levies and requisitions for supplies,
depleted the treasuries and storehouses,
and the people of Hóng, Ráo, Fǔ, and Xìn suffered especially.
Yánzhèng sent an envoy to present a memorial declaring himself a subject to Wúyuè,
requesting to become a vassal to seek rescue.
The King of Chǔ, Xī Fàn, suspecting that the Jìngjiāng military governor, concurrently Palace Attendant and administrator of Lǎngzhōu, Xī Gǎo, had gained the people's hearts,
sent people to spy on him.
Xī Gǎo, fearing,
pleaded illness and requested to return,
but was not permitted;
a physician was sent to examine his illness,
and he was poisoned to death.
(Xī Fàn's jealousy of Xī Gǎo began in the 280th scroll, the first year of the Gāozǔ Tiānfú era.)
Zhāng Xīchēn punctuated, Niè Chóngqí proofread.
Sīmǎ Guāng
compiled by imperial command.
Later
The second year of Kāiyùn (Yǐsì, 945)
1 In the eighth month,
on the first day, Jiǎzǐ,
there was a solar eclipse.
2 On Bǐngyín,
the Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs and concurrently Vice Director of the Secretariat and Tongpingzhangshi Hé Níng was dismissed to his substantive post;
the Bureau of Military Affairs Commissioner and Minister of Revenue Féng Yù was appointed Vice Director of the Secretariat and Tongpingzhangshi,
and all matters, great and small,
were entrusted to him.
Since the victory at Yángchéng,
the Emperor believed the empire was without worries,
and became increasingly arrogant and extravagant.
(The victory at Yángchéng is recorded in the previous scroll, last year.)
That victory cannot be relied upon has long been known.
Zhòu of Shāng won a hundred battles but ultimately had no heir;
Fūchāi fought numerous battles and won numerous victories,
yet finally perished his state.
The victory at Sāngtián
was an omen of the destruction of Guó;
the victory at Fāngchéng
was the foundation for the defeat of Yōng.
Xiàng Liáng died at Dìngtáo and the Qín of Yíng was reduced to ruins;
Yǔwén Huàjí was crushed at Líyáng and Lǐ Mì was defeated;
all were disasters caused by relying on victory.
The battle at Yángchéng,
was perilous and only later won.
The Qìdān, with broken wings, returned north,
their accumulated resentment grew even deeper,
and their plans became even more profound.
The Jìn ruler, however, complacently believed there were no worries;
the ancestral temple of the Shí clan,
it is fitting that it received no sacrifices.
All were taken into the inner treasury;
many utensils and curios were made,
palaces and buildings were expanded,
and the rear courtyards were lavishly decorated,
unmatched by recent dynasties;
(Recent dynasties,
refers to recent times,
such as Liáng and Táng.
Dynasty,
pronounced *zhāo*.)
Several hundred weavers were employed,
and it took a full year to complete;
also, actors were rewarded without measure.
Sāng Wéihàn remonstrated, saying:
"Previously, when Your Majesty personally resisted the northern invaders,
(referring to the battle at Chánzhōu in the first year,
the event is recorded in the previous scroll.)
rewards did not exceed a few bolts of silk.
Now, if an actor's single jest or joke pleases Your Majesty,
they are often rewarded with bundles of silk, ten thousand coins, brocade robes, and silver belts.
(Under the Táng system,
ten bolts of silk constituted a bundle.)
Can they not feel aggrieved,
saying: 'We risked the naked blades,
severed sinews and broke bones,
yet our merit is not equal to that of a single jest or joke!'
If it is like this,
then the soldiers will become disheartened,
with whom will Your Majesty defend the altars of soil and grain!"
The Emperor did not listen.
Féng Yù was always adept at catering to the Emperor's wishes,
and because of this, became even more favored.
Once, when he was ill at home,
the Emperor said to the various chief ministers:
"From the prefectural governor level upwards,
appointments must wait until Féng Yù emerges."
Such was the reliance placed upon him.
Dòu Guǎngdé had virtuous conduct;
Emperor Wén of Hàn, because he was the Empress's younger brother,
fearing the world would criticize him for favoritism,
did not dare to make him chief minister.
What kind of man was Féng Yù,
that the Jìn Emperor Chū would openly declare in court to show his intention of personal trust!
A ruler facing disorder,
each considers his own ministers worthy,
is this not what it means!
Bribes and gifts from all quarters
converged at his gate like spokes to a hub.
Because of this, the court administration deteriorated further.
The historian states that the form of Jìn's destruction was already complete.
(Court,
pronounced *cháo*.)
3 The Táng troops had besieged Jiànzhōu for a long time,
(The Táng attack on Jiànzhōu began in the second month of this year,
the event is recorded in the previous scroll.)
Someone said to Dǒng Sī'ān:
(Said,
means to instruct him.)
"You should choose your course early."
Sī'ān said:
"For generations we have served the Wáng family;
to betray them in their peril,
who in the world would accept me!"
The multitude was moved by his words,
and none rebelled.
On Dīnghài,
the Táng vanguard bridge and road commissioner Wáng Jiànfēng of Shàngyuán was the first to ascend,
(Shàngyuán was originally Jiāngníng County,
renamed during the Shàngyuán era of Emperor Sùzōng of Táng,
attached to Jiāngníng Prefecture.)
and the Mǐn ruler Yánzhèng surrendered.
(Mǐn, since Wáng Cháo obtained Fújiàn at the end of the Táng,
passed to Shěnzhī, Yánhàn, Lín, Chǎng, Xī,
and ended with Yánzhèng.)
Dǒng Sī'ān rallied his troops and fled to Quánzhōu.
The historian states that the two generals of Quánzhōu served the Mǐn ruler from beginning to end.
Earlier, when the Táng troops came,
the people of Jiàn suffered from the disorder under the Wáng family and the heavy exactions of Yáng Sīgōng.
(The heavy exactions of Yáng Sīgōng are recorded in the 283rd scroll, the eighth year of Tiānfú.)
(Exaction,
pronounced *liǎn*.)
When they captured Jiànzhōu,
they allowed the soldiers to plunder extensively,
burning palaces and common dwellings until all were gone;
that night,
in the cold rain,
those who froze to death lay piled upon each other,
and the people of Jiàn were disappointed.
The Táng ruler, because they had merit,
did not question any of them.
4 The Hàn ruler killed Prince Shàoyǎ, Hóng Yǎ.
Hóng Yǎ
was the Hàn ruler's younger brother.
5 In the ninth month,
Xǔ Wénzhěn with Tīngzhōu,
Wáng Jìxūn with Quánzhōu,
and Wáng Jìchéng with Zhāngzhōu,
all surrendered to Táng.
Xúnzǐ has a saying:
"To annex is easy,
but to consolidate firmly is difficult."
Táng could seize Mǐn,
but could not ultimately possess Mǐn.
(This sets the stage for the Mǐn people's rebellion against Táng.)
6 On Bǐngshēn,
Jǐng Yánguǎng, the Western Capital留守 and concurrently Palace Attendant, was appointed Deputy Pacification Commissioner of the Northern Front Field Headquarters.
7 The Palace Director Wáng Qīnzuò was appointed as acting administrator of Héngzhōu.
At that time, military supplies were lacking,
so an imperial edict ordered Qīnzuò to requisition grain from the people.
Dù Wēi had over a hundred thousand hu of grain stored in Héngzhōu,
and Qīnzuò reported this by registering it.
Wēi was greatly angered,
and submitted a memorial stating:
"What crime have I committed,
that Qīnzuò seizes and registers my grain!"
The court therefore summoned Qīnzuò to return.
As for Dù Wēi's grain in Héngzhōu,
was it not the very amount he had previously offered in his memorial?
Even if it were beyond what was offered in his memorial,
it was still accumulated through extortion from the soldiers and people.
To report and register it,
what fault was there!
If the laws of the court
are not enforced upon the noble and powerful,
but only oppress the poor and lowly to meet demands,
then the state is no longer a state.
为,
read as wèi.
还,
read as xuán.
8 On Wùshēn,
the Wēixìn Army was established in Cáozhōu.
9 The Imperial Guard Cavalry and Infantry Commander-in-Chief Lǐ Shǒuzhēn was dispatched to garrison Chánzhōu.
10 On Yǐmǎo,
the Zhāngdé Military Commissioner Zhāng Yànzé was dispatched to garrison Héngzhōu.
11 The Hàn ruler executed Liú Sīcháo, Lín Shǎoqiáng, Lín Shǎoliáng, and Hé Chāngtíng.
The Left Vice Director of the Secretariat Wáng Huī
had previously conspired with Gāozǔ to establish Hóngchāng,
as recorded in the 283rd scroll, seventh year of Tiānfú.
Yīngzhōu
was located in the territory of Zhēnyáng County, Guìyáng Commandery of Hàn.
In the Táng dynasty, Zhēnyáng County was placed under Guǎngzhōu.
The Hàn ruler Liú Yǎn divided Zhēnyáng County to establish Yīngzhōu.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì: from Guǎngzhōu north to Yīngzhōu is 420 li.
He was ordered to commit suicide.
Both inside and outside the court, everyone feared for their own safety.
12 In winter,
tenth month,
on Guǐsì,
the Zhèn'ān Army was established in Chénzhōu.
13 The Táng Yuánjìng Empress Dowager Sòng passed away.
14 Wáng Yánzhèng arrived at Jīnlíng,
and the Táng ruler appointed him as Grand General of the Yǔlín Guards.
Yáng Sīgōng was executed to appease the people of Jiàn.
This was because Yáng Sīgōng had imposed heavy taxes.
Chóng Wén governed with leniency and simplicity,
and the people of Jiàn thus became settled.
To pacify and nurture a devastated remnant,
governance should indeed be like this.
Since Gài Gōng imparted this method to Cáo Shēn,
Shēn used it to administer Qí,
and later to administer Hàn,
few later generations have understood this method.
治,
read as zhí.
15 Previously,
the Gāolì king Wáng Jiàn used military force to annex neighboring states,
becoming quite powerful,
as recorded in the 281st scroll, first year of Gāozǔ's Tiānfú.
丽,
read as lí.
"Bóhǎi
is our marriage ally,
its king was captured by the Qìdān,
we request to join the imperial court in attacking and seizing it."
Gāozǔ did not respond.
When the Emperor became enemies with the Qìdān,
Wàluó mentioned it again.
The Emperor wanted Gāolì to harass the Qìdān's eastern border to divide their military strength;
then Jiàn died,
and his son Wǔ declared himself acting administrator of state affairs,
submitting a memorial to report the mourning.
In the eleventh month,
on Wùxū,
Wǔ was appointed as Grand Righteous Army Commissioner and King of Gāolì.
The Interpreter-in-Chief Guō Rényù was sent as envoy to his state,
conveying the instruction to attack the Qìdān.
Fearing the Qìdān would learn of it,
it was not explicitly stated in the imperial edict,
but only conveyed orally through the instruction.
Seeing their troops were extremely weak,
Wàluó's earlier words
were merely Jiàn's exaggeration,
as they truly did not dare to be enemies with the Qìdān.
Sòng Bái said: During the Jìn Tiānfú era,
a Western Regions monk Wàluó came to court,
skilled in fire divination.
Soon he bid farewell to Gāozǔ,
requesting to travel to Gāolì,
where King Jiàn treated him with great courtesy.
At that time, the Qìdān had already annexed Bóhǎi's territory for years,
so Jiàn casually said to Wàluó:
"Bóhǎi was originally our relative state,
its king was captured by the Qìdān,
I wish to attack and seize it for the imperial court,
and also to settle old grievances.
When you return,
speak to the Son of Heaven,
we should coordinate to attack them together."
Wàluó returned,
fully reported this,
but Gāozǔ did not respond.
When the Later Emperor engaged in warfare with the Qìdān,
Wàluó reported it again.
The Emperor sent Guō Rényù with a swift edict instructing Jiàn
to deeply attack their territory to contain them.
Then Jiàn had already died,
Wǔ was administering state affairs,
and was at odds with his father's senior ministers,
they were preying on each other.
Internal troubles were somewhat pacified,
but military power was not yet strong,
and the barbarians were timid and cowardly.
Wàluó's words
were all Jiàn's empty boasts.
Wǔ then used other reasons to explain.
Offering explanations to exonerate himself.
16 On Yǐmǎo,
the Wúyuè king Qián Hóngzuǒ executed the Internal Palace Supervisor Dù Zhāodá.
On Jǐwèi,
he executed the Internal Guard Upper Commander-in-Chief and Míngzhōu Prefect Kàn Fán.
Zhāodá
was the grandson of Dù Jiànhuī,
Dù Jiànhuī assisted the Wúyuè king Qián Liú with achievements.
The wealthy man of Qiántáng, Chéng Zhāoyuè, used bribes to befriend these two,
gaining access to serve by Hóngzuǒ's side.
Zhāoyuè was cunning and flattering,
the king favored him,
treating him with more favor than the old generals,
which Fán could not accept;
Zhāoyuè learned of this,
went to Fán and kowtowed to apologize,
Fán reproached him for a long time,
then said:
"At first I was determined to kill you;
now that you have repented,
I too am relieved."
Zhāoyuè was afraid,
and plotted to remove Fán.
Fán was authoritarian and stubborn,
and many in the state disliked him.
Zhāoyuè wanted to send Fán out to a provincial post,
but feared Fán would realize it,
so privately said to the Right Commander-in-Chief Hú Jìnsī:
"Now we intend to appoint you and Fán each to your home prefectures,
so Fán will not suspect,
is that acceptable?"
Jìnsī agreed,
so Fán was appointed as Míngzhōu Prefect,
and Jìnsī as Húzhōu Prefect.
Kàn Fán
was from Míngzhōu;
Hú Jìnsī,
was from Húzhōu.
"Sending me out to the provinces
is to discard me."
Jìnsī said:
"An old soldier getting a large prefecture,
is fortunate;
why not go!"
Fán thus accepted the appointment.
But then Zhāoyuè used other reasons to keep Jìnsī.
The mother of the Internal and External Cavalry and Infantry Commander-in-Chief Qián Rénjùn
was the aunt of Dù Zhāodá.
Zhāoyuè thus slandered that Fán and Zhāodá were plotting to support Rénjùn in rebellion,
and they were imprisoned and tortured until they confessed.
After Fán and Zhāodá were executed,
Rénjùn was stripped of his office,
and imprisoned in the Eastern Mansion.
Then Zhāoyuè prosecuted the factions of Kàn and Dù,
all those in positions of power
equal to himself,
or whom he suspected,
over a hundred were executed or exiled,
and the people of the state feared him, not daring to look directly.
This sets the stage for Hóngzuǒ later executing Zhāoyuè.
治,
read as zhí.
Zhāoyuè considered him simple-minded,
so he alone was spared.
Hú Jìnsī alone surviving
became the stepping stone to the disaster of the Qián clan's depositions and successions.
Zhāo Yuè arrested Shèn Wēnqí, a former subordinate of Rén Jùn.
Shèn
is a surname;
in ancient times there was Shèn Dào.
Wēnqí
is his given name.
He was subjected to exhaustive torture.
Shèn Wēnqí remained steadfast and unyielding;
Hóng Zuǒ praised him,
and promoted him to a state official position.
"State official"
refers to an official of the Wúyuè Kingdom.
Shèn Wēnqí was promoted from a provincial government clerk to a state official.
He was from Qúzhōu.
On the 17th day of the twelfth month,
Yǐchǒu,
Wúyuè King Hóng Zuǒ was additionally appointed as the Marshal of the Southeastern Military Forces.
On the 18th day, Xīnwèi,
the former Secretariat Drafter Yīn Péng of Guǎngjìn
was appointed as Supervising Secretary and Academician of the Privy Council.
The Táng changed Wèizhōu to Xìngtáng Prefecture,
and Emperor Gāozǔ changed it to Guǎngjìn Prefecture.
He was a partisan of Féng Yù;
whenever the court had appointments or promotions,
Yù would discuss them with Péng.
As a result, requests and bribes
filled his gate.
Earlier,
the Emperor's illness had not yet subsided.
Last winter,
the Emperor fell ill,
as seen in the previous volume.
It was said that on the first day of the first month this year,
a maidservant,
that is, a female slave,
(in the Táng, attending and inquiring about one's health was called "qǐjū,"
and people today still use this term)
asked, "Has the imperial younger brother Ruì been reading lately?"
Ruì
refers to Chóng Ruì;
to avoid the Emperor's personal name,
the character
"Chóng"
was omitted.
This was reported to Féng Yù,
and Yù then slandered Sāng Wéihàn, saying he had intentions to depose and install;
the Emperor became suspicious.
The Emperor had always been wary of Chóng Ruì,
and due to the maidservant's inquiry from Sāng Wéihàn's household,
he was already suspicious of Wéihàn;
Féng Yù further slandered him,
making the suspicion even more unshakable.
Lǐ Shǒuzhēn had long disliked Wéihàn,
and Féng Yù, Lǐ Yàntāo, and Shǒuzhēn conspired to oust him;
considering the Secretariat Director and concurrent Kaifēng Prefect Zhào Yíng to be gentle and easily controlled,
they jointly recommended him to replace Wéihàn.
On Dīnghài,
Wéihàn was removed from his administrative duties
and made Kaifēng Prefect;
Yíng was appointed as Secretariat Director,
and Lǐ Sōng as Privy Councilor and concurrent Palace Attendant.
Wéihàn then claimed to have foot ailments,
hoping to avoid court audiences,
and cut off all guests.
This was also to distance himself from suspicion.
"Fù"
is pronounced fú yòu fān.
"Cháo"
is pronounced zhí yáo fān.
Someone said to Féng Yù:
"Lord Sāng is a senior statesman;
now that he has been relieved of his privy duties,
even if he is not retained in a ministerial position,
he should still be generously granted a major province.
Why make him the capital prefect,
dealing with trivial and miscellaneous affairs?"
"Wěi"
means miscellaneous.
"I fear he might rebel."
This means the reason for not granting Wéihàn a major military command
is the fear that he might raise troops and rebel.
"How could a scholar rebel!"
Yù said:
"Even if he does not rebel himself,
I fear he might incite others to do so."
This refers to Wéihàn's support of the Jìn ancestor's plan to raise troops in Jìnyáng.
Dài Yǎn, a retired scholar of Xiāngyīn in Chǔ,
(Liú Xù said: Xiāngyīn
was Luó County in Hàn,
Sòng established Xiāngyīn County,
which belonged to Yuèzhōu in Táng.
In the fourth year of Chúnhuà of Sòng,
Xiāngyīn County was placed under Tánzhōu.
Jiǔyù Zhì: It is 115 lǐ northeast of the prefecture.)
was imprisoned by King Xī Fàn of Chǔ;
Deputy Commander of the Tiāncè Army Dīng Sījǐn submitted a memorial earnestly remonstrating,
and Xī Fàn stripped him of his offices and titles.
Xiè Zhòngxuān, an official in the household of Prince Jǐngdá of Qí of Táng, said to Jǐngdá:
"Sòng Qíqiū
was a commoner friend of the late Emperor;
now abandoning him in the wilds
does not satisfy public sentiment."
Jǐngdá spoke on his behalf to the Táng sovereign:
"Qíqiū is a figure of longstanding reputation;
if he is not to be employed, that is fine,
but why must he be abandoned to make a name?"
The Táng sovereign then sent Jǐngdá personally to Qīngyáng to summon him.
(Qíqiū was in seclusion in Qīngyáng; see the eighth year of Tiānfú, volume 283.)
In spring,
the first month,
Qíqiū was appointed as Grand Mentor and concurrent Secretariat Director,
but only attended court gatherings,
not participating in government affairs.
He merely attended court gatherings upon summons.
He and the Secretariat Vice-Director Féng Yánjǐ were both made Tongpingzhangshi.
Jiàn Xūn was experienced in administrative affairs,
but was timid and indecisive;
Yánjǐ was skilled in literary composition,
but cunning and flattering,
fond of grand talk,
and formed many cliques.
Ministry of Waterways Director Gāo Yuè
submitted a memorial pointing out the faults and evils of Yánjǐ and his brothers;
the Táng sovereign was angered,
and demoted Yuè to Qízhōu Registrar.
Earlier,
the Táng sovereign established the Xuānzhèng Institute within the palace,
appointing the Hanlin Academician and Supervising Secretary Cháng Mèngxī to lead it,
exclusively handling confidential matters,
and both he and Secretariat Vice-Director Yán Xù were loyal, upright, and selfless.
The Táng sovereign said to Mèngxī:
"Among the high ministers, only Yán Xù remains neutral,
but he lacks talent,
and I fear he cannot withstand the partisans;
you should assist him."
Not long after,
Mèngxī was removed from the Xuānzhèng Institute,
and Xù was also sent out as the Observation Commissioner of Chízhōu.
Mèngxī then feigned illness and indulged in drinking,
no longer participating in court affairs.
The history states that when the upright and the wicked are mixed,
the upright are ultimately overcome by the wicked.
"Fù"
is pronounced fú yòu fān.
He was the son of Kě Qiú.
Yán Kěqiú
was the chief strategist of Xú Wēn.
In the second month,
on Rénxū, the first day,
there was a solar eclipse.
The Jìnchāng Military Commissioner and concurrent Palace Attendant Zhào Zàilǐ,
(Jìn made Jīngzhào Prefecture the Jìnchāng Army.)
was greedy and oppressive wherever he went,
and his family wealth was the greatest among all the commanders.
The Emperor coveted his wealth,
and in the third month,
on Gēngshēn,
arranged for his son, the Zhènníng Military Commissioner Yán Xù, to marry Zàilǐ's daughter.
Zàilǐ himself spent a hundred thousand strings of cash,
and the government's expenses
were several times more.
Yán Xù and his younger brother Yán Bǎo
were both grandsons of Emperor Gāozǔ,
and the Emperor raised them as his own sons.
Wáng Jìxūn, the Prefect of Quánzhōu of Táng, sent a letter to Wǔwēi Military Commissioner Lǐ Hóngyì to establish friendly relations.
Hóngyì, because Quánzhōu was formerly subordinate to the Wǔwēi Army,
was angered by Jìxūn's equal diplomatic protocol,
(Wáng Jìxūn and Lǐ Hóngyì both served Southern Táng;
although Hóngyì held a military commission,
they served the sovereign as equals,
so naturally they could not adopt the protocol of subordinate and superior.
Lǐ Hóngyì used this to start a military conflict.)
In the fourth month,
he sent his younger brother Hóngtōng to lead ten thousand troops to attack him.
Earlier,
when the Shuòfāng Military Commissioner Féng Huī was in Língzhōu,
he detained the Tuòbá tribal chieftain Yánchāo in the prefectural seat,
(see the fourth year of Tiānfú, volume 282.)
"Dǎng"
is pronounced dǐ lǎng fān.
"Qiú"
is pronounced cí yóu fān.
"Zhǎng"
is pronounced zhī liǎng fān.
and when he was about to leave his command, he released him.
The former Military Commissioner of Zhangwu, Wáng Lìngwēn, replaced Huī in governing Shuòfāng.
He did not pacify and care for the Qiāng and Hú tribes,
but instead applied the laws of the Central Plains to restrain them.
In ancient times, when the Zhōu dynasty enfeoffed Wèi,
it demarcated its borders according to Zhōu laws,
because its territory lay within the Central Plains.
When it enfeoffed Jìn,
it demarcated its borders according to Róng laws,
because its territory was near the Róng and Dí tribes.
It has long been understood that the Róng and Dí cannot be restrained by the laws of the Central Plains.
They competed in raiding and plundering.
The three clans of Tuòbá Yànchāo, Shí Cún, and Yěsībāo
jointly attacked Língzhōu,
killing Lìngwēn's younger brother, Lìngzhōu.
On the Wùwǔ day,
Lìngwēn submitted a memorial reporting the emergency.
6 The Military Commander of Quánzhōu, Liú Cóngxiào, said to the Regional Inspector, Wáng Jìxūn:
"Lǐ Hóngtōng's military force is very strong.
The soldiers, because Your Excellency's rewards and punishments are unjust,
are unwilling to fight hard.
Your Excellency should step aside and reflect on yourself!"
He then deposed Jìxūn and sent him back to his private residence.
Liú Cóngxiào established Wáng Jìxūn. See the previous year in the previous scroll.
He led troops to attack Lǐ Hóngtōng,
and heavily defeated him.
He reported this to the Táng court.
The Táng sovereign appointed Cóngxiào as Regional Inspector of Quánzhōu,
summoned Jìxūn back to Jīnlíng,
and sent generals to lead troops to garrison Quánzhōu.
This sets the stage for Liú Cóngxiào later sending the Táng garrison generals back.
The Regional Inspector of Tīngzhōu, Xǔ Wénzhěn, was appointed Regional Inspector of Qízhōu.
7 Two hundred lǐ northwest of Dìngzhōu is Lángshān.
Note on the Xiōngnú: Lángshānzhài is eighty lǐ northeast to Yìzhōu,
and southeast to the border of Guǎngxìn Army.
Within the fort was a Buddhist temple,
where a nun named Sūn Shēnyì resided.
She used sorcery to delude the masses,
and her predictions were quite accurate,
so people near and far believed in and followed her.
A man from Zhōngshān named Sūn Fāngjiǎn
(In the Ouyáng History, it is written
"Sūn Fāngjiàn."
This is because Sūn Fāngjiǎn later avoided the taboo of the imperial father of Zhōu Tàizǔ,
and thus changed his name to Fāngjiàn.)
Examination of discrepancies says: The Veritable Records of Zhōu Shìzōng states
"a man from Qīngyuàn."
Here, we follow the Veritable Records of Hàn Gāozǔ.
He claimed to be the nephew of Shēnyì,
abstained from alcohol and meat,
and served Shēnyì with great reverence.
When Shēnyì died,
Fāngjiǎn succeeded her in practicing her arts.
He claimed that Shēnyì had achieved "sitting in transformation."
(Those who revere and believe in Buddhism,
and study its teachings,
focusing single-mindedly and with stillness,
upon death,
can sit cross-legged upright as if alive,
which is called "sitting in transformation.")
He served her as if she were alive,
and his followers increased daily.
The Old History of the Five Dynasties says: During the Qiándé era of the Sòng dynasty,
her dried bones were moved to the capital,
and burned in the northern suburbs,
after which the sorcerous followers ceased.
At that time, the Jìn dynasty had severed relations with the Qìdān,
and the northern border regions suffered heavy taxes and corvée labor,
with banditry rampant,
so the people could not peacefully pursue their livelihoods.
Fāngjiǎn and Xíngyǒu therefore led the brave and strong men of their village,
and occupied the temple, turning it into a stockade for self-protection.
When the Qìdān invaded,
Fāngjiǎn led his men to intercept and attack them,
capturing a considerable amount of their armor, weapons, cattle, horses, and military supplies.
People bringing their families to rely on him grew increasingly numerous.
After a long time,
they reached over a thousand households,
and thus became bandits.
Fearing suppression by officials,
they submitted to the imperial court.
The court also relied on them to resist invaders,
appointing him as Commander of the Northeastern Recruitment.
Fāngjiǎn often entered Qìdān territory to raid and plunder,
killing and capturing many.
Later, his demands became incessant,
and if the court did not fully meet his wishes,
he would surrender the entire stockade to the Qìdān,
requesting to serve as a guide for their invasions.
On the borders,
treacherous people like this,
were not limited to Sūn Fāngjiǎn alone;
they were what the Táng people called
"two-faced."
pronounced as jiàng.
鄉,
read as xiàng.
道,
read as dǎo.)
People dying of starvation numbered in the tens of thousands everywhere,
and between Yǎnzhōu, Yùnzhōu, Cāngzhōu, and Bèizhōu,
bandits arose,
and officials could not suppress them.
The Military Commissioner of Tiānxióng, Dù Wēi, sent his personal army officer, Liú Yánhàn, to purchase horses at the border.
Fāngjiǎn captured him
and presented him to the Qìdān.
Yánhàn escaped and returned.
In the sixth month,
on the Rénxū day,
he arrived at Dàliáng,
reporting
that "Fāngjiǎn intends to take advantage of the famine in the Central Plains,
to lead the Qìdān in an invasion.
We should prepare for this."
This sets the stage for Sūn Fāngjiǎn taking advantage of the Central Plains being without a ruler,
and the Qìdān returning north,
to enter and occupy Dìngzhōu.
8 Earlier,
when the Military Commissioner of Shuòfāng, Féng Huī, was in Língwǔ,
he won the hearts of the Qiāng and Hú tribes.
Within a year of trading for horses,
he obtained five thousand horses.
The court grew suspicious of him,
transferred him to govern Bīnzhōu and Shǎnzhōu,
and then summoned him to the capital to serve as Commander of the Imperial Guard Infantry and concurrently Military Commissioner of Héyáng.
Huī understood the court's intentions,
regretted leaving Língwǔ,
pronounced as lì.)
and requested to be reappointed to govern Língzhōu.
The court also, because the Qiāng and Hú were causing disturbances,
on the Bǐngyín day,
reappointed Huī as Military Commissioner of Shuòfāng,
to lead troops from Guānxī to attack the Qiāng and Hú;
appointing the Prefect of Wēizhōu, Yào Yuánfú, as Commander of the Campaign Army's Cavalry and Infantry.
(Wēizhōu
was the Ānlèzhōu of the Táng dynasty.
It was lost to Tǔbō in the mid-period,
recovered in the third year of Dàzhōng,
and renamed Wēizhōu.
The Liáng and Táng dynasties abandoned it,
and the Jìn dynasty reestablished it.
Later Zhōu changed it to Huánzhōu,
named for the great river winding around it,
which was also the old name of the prefecture from the early Táng.
Zhào Xún's *Jùmǐ Tújīng* states: Língzhōu is five hundred lǐ south to Huánzhōu.
According to the Old History,
in the fourth year of Tiānfú, a May edict
elevated Língzhōu's Fāngqú Garrison to Wēizhōu,
transferring the two counties of Mùbō and Mǎlǐng from Níngzhōu to it;
Later Zhōu changed it to Huánzhōu,
and in the fourth year of Xiǎndé,
it was downgraded to Tōngyuǎn Army.)
9 On the Yǐchǒu day,
Dìngzhōu reported that the Qìdān had amassed troops pressing on the border.
An edict appointed the Military Commissioner of Tiānpíng and Commander of the Imperial Guard Cavalry and Infantry, Lǐ Shǒuzhēn, as Commander of the Northern Campaign Army,
with the Military Commissioner of Yìchéng, Huángfǔ Yù, as his deputy;
the Military Commissioner of Zhāngdé, Zhāng Yǎnzé, serving as Commander of the Cavalry and concurrently Deputy Commander;
the Military Commissioner of Yìwǔ, Jìrén Lǐ Yīn, serving as Commander of the Infantry and concurrently Formation Commander;
and sending the Imperial Guard Commander, Línqīngrén Wáng Yǎnchāo, and Tàiyuán's Bái Yányù, with ten battalions of their troops to Xíngzhōu.
At that time, the Commander of the Cavalry and Military Commissioner of Zhèn'ān, Lǐ Yǎntāo, was in power.
(At that time, Chénzhōu was established as Zhèn'ān Army.)
Whatever Shǒuzhēn did outside,
whether major or minor,
Yǎntāo would inevitably learn of it.
Shǒuzhēn outwardly respected him but inwardly resented him.
This sets the stage for Lǐ Shǒuzhēn and Dù Wēi surrendering to the Qìdān.
10 Earlier,
after the Táng forces captured Jiànzhōu,
(Last year in August,
Táng captured Jiànzhōu.)
the Táng sovereign did not permit it.
The Privy Councilor, Chén Jué, requested to go personally to persuade Lǐ Hóngyì,
and would certainly make him come to court.
Sòng Qíqiū recommended Jué for his talent and eloquence,
saying he could achieve this without using a single weapon,
and would effortlessly bring Hóngyì.
The Táng sovereign then enfeoffed Hóngyì's mother and wife as Ladies of the State,
promoted his four younger brothers in office,
appointed Jué as Commissioner of Propaganda and Instruction for Fúzhōu,
and bestowed generous gifts of gold and silk upon Hóngyì.
He intended to entice Lǐ Hóngyì with official rank and wealth to lure him.
When Hóngyì met Jué,
his words and demeanor were very arrogant,
and he treated him coldly and with neglect;
Jué did not dare mention the matter of coming to court and returned.
This sets the stage for Chén Jué raising troops to attack Fúzhōu, suffering defeat and returning.
pronounced as xuán,
or also as huán.)
In the autumn of the 11th year,
in the seventh month,
the Yellow River breached at Yángliú,
flowing westward into Shēn County,
spreading forty li wide,
and flowing north from Cháochéng.
Shēn County lies east of Wèi Prefecture,
Cháochéng lies southeast of Wèi Prefecture,
forty li apart.
Guǎng (wide),
is pronounced like gǔ kuàng fān in ancient times.
Someone came from Yōuzhōu,
saying Zhào Yánshòu intended to return to the state;
the Privy Councilors Lǐ Sōng and Féng Yù believed it,
ordering Tiānxióng Military Commissioner Dù Wēi to send a letter to Yánshòu,
fully conveying the court's decree,
enticing him with great benefits.
Luò
Prefecture military officer Zhào Xíngshí had once served Yánshòu,
and was sent to secretly deliver the letter to him.
Yánshòu replied:
"Having long been in a foreign land,
I yearn to return to the Central Kingdom.
I beg for a great army to respond and support,
to pull myself southward."
His words were earnest and intimate.
The court was delighted,
and again sent Xíngshí to Yánshòu,
to set a date for the plan.
From this point, the Jìn people fell into Zhào Yánshòu's scheme.
Fù (again),
is pronounced fú yòu fān.
In the eighth month,
Lǐ Shǒuzhēn reported:
"Encountered over a thousand Khitan cavalry north of the Great Wall,
this is the Great Wall built by Yān during the Warring States period,
located south of Gù'ān County in Zhuō Prefecture.
The Old History of the Five Dynasties states: Lǐ Shǒuzhēn reported the great army reached Wàngdū County,
then successively arrived north of the Great Wall,
where they met the enemy and fought.
Beheaded their chieftain Xièlǐ,
and drove the remaining multitude into the water, where many drowned."
On Dīngmǎo,
an edict ordered Lǐ Shǒuzhēn to return and garrison Chán Prefecture.
The Emperor, having severed relations with the Khitan,
frequently summoned the Tǔyùhún chieftain Bái Chéngfú to court,
feasting and bestowing gifts lavishly.
Chéngfú followed the Emperor to fight the Khitan at Chán Prefecture,
and also garrisoned Huá Prefecture with Zhāng Cóng'ēn.
As the year was extremely hot,
he sent his tribe back to Tàiyuán,
to herd livestock in the regions of Lán and Shí.
The tribe frequently broke the law,
and Liú Zhīyuǎn showed no leniency;
the tribe, knowing the court was weak,
and fearing Zhīyuǎn's strictness,
plotted to flee together back to their homeland.
The Tǔyùhún tribe, knowing the court was weak,
and fearing Liú Zhīyuǎn's strictness;
however, they dared not cause trouble in Tàiyuán,
fearing Liú Zhīyuǎn's authority and strategy,
and having no opportunity to commit misdeeds,
thus wished to flee back to their homeland.
Second in rank to Chéngfú,
led his own tribe to first flee and submit to the Khitan,
who appointed him as Yún Prefecture Surveillance Commissioner,
to entice Chéngfú.
Zhīyuǎn and Guō Wēi plotted:
"Now the realm faces many troubles,
keeping this tribe in Tàiyuán,
is a disease close to the heart,
it is better to remove them."
Chéngfú's household was very wealthy,
feeding horses with silver troughs.
Wēi urged Zhīyuǎn to execute them,
and seize their goods to supply the army.
Zhīyuǎn secretly memorialized:
"The Tǔyùhún are fickle and hard to secure,
I request they be moved inland."
The Emperor sent envoys to mobilize their tribe of 1,900 people,
and distributed them to Héyáng and other prefectures.
Zhīyuǎn sent Wēi to lure Chéngfú and others into residing within Tàiyuán city,
then falsely accused Chéngfú and five clans of plotting rebellion,
surrounded them with troops and killed them,
totaling four hundred people,
and confiscated their family assets.
An edict praised and rewarded him,
and the Tǔyùhún thus declined.
The *Institutes of the Five Dynasties* states: Among the Tǔyùhún chieftains was one Hèlián Duó,
during the Xiántōng era of the Táng,
who followed Tàiyuán Military Commissioner Kāng Chéngxùn to pacify Xúfāng and was meritorious,
and the court appointed him Zhènwǔ Military Commissioner.
He again usurped and occupied Yúnzhōng,
and later Táng Tàizǔ drove him out,
so he submitted to Lǐ Kuāngchóu of Yōuzhōu;
his tribe scattered and lived within the boundaries of Yù Prefecture,
acting as rulers among themselves,
their surnames not constant.
There was Bái Chéngfú,
who since the beginning of the Tóngguāng era served as Commander,
relying on the stone gate north of Zhōngshān as a stockade,
and Zhuāngzong bestowed upon him the titles of Níngshuò and Fènghuà as two prefectures,
making the Commander a Military Commissioner,
and further bestowing upon Chéngfú the surname Lǐ,
named Shàolǔ.
Their herding,
sought good water and grass,
with several thousand able-bodied men.
Sheep and horses multiplied,
entering the markets of the Central Plains,
and the court often cared for and supported them.
In the third year of Lùwáng's Qīngtài era,
Bái Kějiǔ served as Níngshuò and Fènghuà Deputy Military Commissioner,
first appearing in history.
In the first year of Jìn's Tiānfú era,
Gāozǔ, because the Khitan had aided in establishing the dynasty,
ceded the lands north of Yànmén and Yōuzhōu to bribe them,
from then on the Tǔyùhún tribes were all subordinate to the Khitan.
Afterwards, suffering under the Khitan's oppressive rule,
and further enticed by Zhèn Prefecture Military Commissioner Ān Zhòngróng,
they turned against the Khitan,
leading their carts, tents, sheep, and horses via the Wǔtái route to return to the state.
The Khitan were greatly angered,
because the court had recruited and accepted rebels and fugitives,
and sent envoys to reprimand.
In the sixth year, first month,
Gāozǔ ordered Attendant Official Zhāng Chéng and others to lead two thousand troops,
to search the valleys of Bīng, Zhèn, Xīn, and Dài four prefectures for Tǔyùhún,
and return them to their old lands;
however, also because the Khitan's demands were insatiable,
he was discontent,
and ordered Hàn Gāozǔ to go out and govern Tàiyuán,
secretly to comfort and pacify them.
That year in the fifth month,
the great chieftain Bái Chéngfú and his followers came to court;
in the ninth month,
again sent chieftain Bái Kějiǔ to court.
The Young Sovereign succeeded to the throne,
severed relations with the Khitan,
frequently summoned their chieftains to court,
richly bestowing gifts,
and at every great banquet,
always ordered them to be seated in order after the meritorious ministers.
When defending against the enemy at Chán Prefecture during the Kāiyùn era,
summoned Chéngfú and others to lead their tribal followers to accompany the campaign.
As the year was very hot,
many of his followers died,
and again sent them back to Tàiyuán,
moving their tents to Lán and Shí Prefectures.
However, Chéngfú governed his subordinates without method,
often violating military orders.
His clansman Bái Kějiǔ,
second to Chéngfú,
while herding horses,
led his own tents to flee north.
The Khitan bestowed upon him office and rank,
and again sent him to secretly entice Chéngfú.
Chéngfú also thought of rebelling and leaving,
but the matter did not come to fruition.
Hànzǔ knew of it,
and so surrounded their tribe with troops,
captured Chéngfú and his clansmen Bái Tiěkuì, Hèlián Hǎilóng, and five families,
altogether over four hundred people,
executed them,
confiscated their cattle and horses,
and ordered another tribal chief Wáng Yìzōng to govern the remaining members.
Pú Prefecture Prefect Mùróng Yànchāo was implicated for illegally levying taxes,
embezzling five hundred hu of government wheat to make yeast,
and distributing it to the local people.
Lǐ Yàntāo had long held a grudge against Yànchāo,
exposed the matter,
the crime deserving death.
Yàntāo urged Féng Yù to have him killed,
but Liú Zhīyuǎn submitted a memorial arguing for his rescue.
Mùróng Yànchāo,
was Liú Zhīyuǎn's full brother,
hence he rescued him.
Shàng (submit),
is pronounced shí zhǎng fān.
"As for Yànchāo's crime,
all the regional lords in the realm today have committed it.
If the law were fully applied to them,
I fear no one would feel secure."
On Jiǎxū,
an edict pardoned Yànchāo from death,
stripped him of office and rank,
and exiled him to Fáng Prefecture.
15. Táng Chén Jué returned from Fúzhōu,
reaching Jiànzhōu.
Jiànzhōu
was the Tánzhōu established by the Mǐn ruler Wáng Yánzhèng.
After the Southern Tang conquered Jiànzhōu,
they divided it into Yánpíng, Jiànpǔ, and Fùshā counties and established Jiànzhōu.
By the time the Sòng unified the realm,
as Shǔzhōng also had a Jiànzhōu,
they added
the character "Nán"
to make it Nánjiànzhōu.
(Chén Jué) was ashamed of having deceitfully claimed he could persuade Lǐ Hóngyì to come to court but failed to bring him.
Shìwèiguān
refers to those who serve as guards directly by the ruler's side,
similar to the Shìguān of the High Táng.
Chén Jué mobilized troops from Tīng, Jiàn, Fǔ, and Xìnzhōu, along with garrison soldiers,
and ordered Jiànzhōu military supervisor Féng Yánlǔ to lead them,
heading towards Fúzhōu to fetch Hóngyì.
Yánlǔ first sent a letter to Hóngyì,
explaining the consequences of fortune and misfortune.
Hóngyì replied with a letter requesting battle,
and dispatched Lóuchuán Zhǐhuīshǐ Yáng Chóngbǎo to lead the provincial army to resist them.
One version
writes "provincial army"
as
"naval force."
The Jiàn River flows east past Jiànzhōu to Fúzhōu,
all being a great river,
hence the locals also call it a river.
"Fúzhōu is isolated and imperiled,
it can be captured within days."
The Táng ruler was furious at Jué for acting on his own authority;
many ministers said:
"The troops are already arrayed beneath the city walls,
we cannot stop now,
we should send troops to assist them."
On the Dīngchǒu day,
Jué and Yánlǔ defeated Yáng Chóngbǎo at Hòuguān.
The counties of Mǐn and Hòuguān
both had their administrative seats in the outer city of Fúzhōu.
This battle took place within the boundaries of Hòuguān County.
Defeated,
(the character) bǔ is pronounced mài.
On the Wùyín day
they took advantage of the victory to attack the western gate of Fúzhōu.
Hóngyì launched a counterattack,
routing them heavily,
and captured the Táng Left Shénwēi Zhǐhuīshǐ Yáng Kuāngyè.
The Táng ruler appointed Yǒng'ān Jīédùshǐ Wáng Chóngwén as the Dōngnánmiàn Dōuzhāotǎoshǐ,
(recall that) last year in October,
the Táng established the Yǒng'ān Army in Jiànzhōu.
Yánlǔ was made Nánmiàn Jiānjūnshǐ,
and they joined forces to attack Fúzhōu,
capturing its outer walls.
Hóngyì firmly held the second city.
(This refers to) the second ring of walls.
16. Féng Huī led his troops across the Hànhǎi,
reaching Huīdé.
Zhāng Jì said: From Wēizhōu to Língzhōu, the Hànhǎi spans seven hundred lǐ,
a saline, barren marshland
without streams, brooks, rivers, or valleys.
Huīdé
is a place name
south of Língwǔ.
Zhāng Shùnmín said: The present Hànjiāngpíng is the Hànhǎi,
located north of Qīngyuǎnjūn.
Zhào Xún's Jùmǐtújīng states: Between Yán, Xià, and Qīngyuǎnjūn,
it is all sandy desert,
commonly called the Hànhǎi.
From Huánzhōu exiting Qīnggāngchuān,
was originally the main road to Língzhōu.
From here passing Měilìzhài,
one gradually enters Píngxià,
traversing the Hànhǎi,
where water springs are hard to find.
One reaches Yàodé Qīngbiānzhèn and enters Língzhōu.
Tuòbá Yànchāo had tens of thousands of troops,
arrayed in three formations,
blocking the vital road,
and occupying the water springs to await them.
The army was greatly afraid.
Huī sought peace with Yànchāo through bribery,
and Yànchāo agreed.
From dawn until noon,
messengers went back and forth several times,
but the troops did not withdraw.
Yào Yuánfú said:
"The barbarians know we are hungry and thirsty,
they are falsely agreeing to peace to exhaust us;
if it reaches evening,
then we will all be captured.
Although the barbarians are numerous now,
their elite troops are few—
those arrayed against the western mountains are them.
The rest are infantry,
not worth worrying about.
I ask you to maintain a strict formation and wait for me—
'maintain a strict formation' means
keeping the troops disciplined and the formation orderly.
For a minor victory I will raise a yellow flag,
then the main army will join forces and attack them,
we will surely defeat them."
Thereupon he led the cavalry forward first,
fighting fiercely with close-combat weapons.
Yànchāo retreated slightly,
Yuánfú raised the yellow flag,
Huī led his troops to join him,
and Yànchāo was heavily defeated.
Féng Huī had kept Tuòbá Yànchāo confined within the walls of Língwǔ city,
so Yànchāo certainly knew the reason and harbored resentment.
When Huī left his garrison, Yànchāo was able to get out.
Once Yànchāo had gotten out and Huī returned,
a tiger released from its cage,
if it can freely turn and bite back,
will stop at nothing.
If they had not fought hard and subdued him,
Féng Huī's authority and commands could no longer be enforced in Shuòfāng.
Shuaì
is pronounced shuài.
Huī entered Língzhōu.
17. In the ninth month,
the Qìdān invaded HéDōng with thirty thousand troops;
on the Rénchén day,
Liú Zhīyuǎn defeated them at Yángwǔgǔ,
beheading seven thousand.
18. After the death of the Southern Hàn's Liú Sīcháo and others,
Chén Dàoxiáng felt inwardly uneasy.
Chén Dàoxiáng
was one who, along with Liú Sīcháo and others, assassinated the Southern Hán ruler Liú Hóngdù.
(The account of) killing Liú Sīcháo and others is found in the ninth month of last year.
According to Lù Zhèn's Jiǔguózhì,
Chén Dàoxiáng's father Chén Dǎng
was an old acquaintance of Dèng Shēn,
hence this.
Shēn said:
"Foolish bumpkin!
This book contains accounts of the execution of Hán Xìn and the mincing of Péng Yuè,
you should read it carefully!"
The Hàn ruler heard of this,
and exterminated the clans of Dàoxiáng and Shēn.
19. Lǐ Hóngyì proclaimed himself Wǔwēi Liúhòu,
changed his name to Hóngdá,
and submitted a memorial to the Jìn requesting appointment;
Lǐ Hóngyì's original name was Réndá,
Hóngyì was the name bestowed by the Táng;
having rebelled against the Táng,
he then changed his name.
On the Jiǎwǔ day
(the court) appointed Hóngdá as Wǔwēi Jīédùshǐ, Tóngpíngzhāngshì,
in charge of the affairs of the Mǐn state.
20. Zhāng Yànzé reported defeating the Qìdān north of Dìngzhōu,
and again defeating them at Tàizhōu,
beheading two thousand.
21. On the Xīnchǒu day,
Fúzhōu Páizhènshǐ Mǎ Jié
led Táng troops from Mǎmùshān, pulling up stockades and entering,
reaching the Shànhuàmén bridge.
Dōuzhǐhuīshǐ Dīng Yànzhēn resisted them with a hundred soldiers.
Hóngdá retreated to defend Shànhuàmén,
the two outer rings of the city walls were all occupied by Táng troops.
Hóngdá changed his name to Dá.
Hóngdá changed his name to Dá
because the Wúyuè king's personal name included the character Hóng,
so he avoided it.
Chóng
is pronounced zhí lóng fān.
Gēng
is pronounced gōng héng fān.
He requested troops from Wúyuè.
22. The Chǔ king Mǎ Xīfàn knew the Emperor was fond of extravagance and luxury,
and repeatedly presented him with rare treasures and curios,
seeking the position of Dōuyuánshuài.
On the Jiǎchén day,
(the Emperor) appointed Xīfàn as Zhūdào Bīngmǎ Dōuyuánshuài.
23. On the Bǐngchén day,
the Yellow River breached at Línhuáng in Chánzhōu.
Línhuáng
was a town on the Yellow River in the state of Wèi during the Spring and Autumn period.
During the Hàn it was Guān County of Dōngjùn,
where the Xīntái of Duke Xuān of Wèi was located.
The Later Wèi established Línhuáng County,
which belonged to Chánzhōu in the Táng;
in the first year of Duāngǒng of the Sòng,
Línhuáng was abolished and merged into Guānchéng County.
24. The Khitan envoy, Yíngzhōu Prefect Liú Yánzuò, sent a letter to Yuèshòu Military Supervisor Wáng Luán,
requesting to surrender the city and submit to the court.
He further stated:
"The Khitan troops in the city number less than a thousand,
I beg the court to dispatch light troops to launch a surprise attack,
and I will act as an insider.
Moreover,
this autumn has seen heavy rain,
and from the north of Wǎqiáo Pass,
the accumulated water stretches endlessly.
The Khitan ruler has already returned to his headquarters,
and even if he hears of disturbances south of the pass,
Yíngzhōu and Mòzhōu,
which were ceded by the Jìn to the Khitan,
lie south of Wǎqiáo Pass.
He will be unable to rescue them."
Luán and Tiānxióng Military Commissioner and concurrently Zhōngshū Lìng Dù Wēi repeatedly memorialized that Yíngzhōu and Mòzhōu could be seized under these circumstances,
and Shēnzhōu Prefect Mùróng Qiān presented a map of Yíngzhōu and Mòzhōu.
Féng Yù and Lǐ Sōng believed this to be true,
and intended to dispatch a large army to welcome Zhào Yánshòu and Yánzuò.
Previously, Zhào Yánshòu had also deceitfully communicated his willingness to submit.
Earlier,
the Imperial Guard Infantry and Cavalry Commander-in-Chief and Tiānpíng Military Commissioner Lǐ Shǒuzhēn had led troops past Guǎngjìn on several occasions,
and Dù Wēi treated him generously,
bestowing upon him gold, silk, armor, and weapons,
each time amounting to tens of thousands;
Shǒuzhēn thus became close with Wēi.
When Shǒuzhēn came to court,
the Emperor commended him, saying:
"I have heard that as a general,
you often spend your private wealth to reward the soldiers."
He replied:
"All of this is due to Dù Wēi's loyalty to the state,
who provided me with gold and silk;
how dare I claim credit for his virtue!"
He then said:
"If Your Majesty ever wages war in the future,
I wish to join forces with Wēi to pacify the northern deserts."
The Emperor thus also considered him worthy.
When the northern campaign was about to be launched,
the Emperor consulted with Féng Yù and Lǐ Sōng,
appointing Wēi as commander-in-chief,
with Shǒuzhēn as his deputy.
Zhào Yíng privately said to Féng and Lǐ:
"Dù holds imperial kinship,
meaning he is married to a princess.
Yet his desires remain unsatisfied,
and his heart is often discontented.
He holds both military and ministerial positions,
meaning he commands a major garrison and concurrently serves as Zhōngshū Lìng.
Unsatisfied,
meaning his desires are not yet fulfilled.
Discontented,
also meaning dissatisfied.
Qiàn,
pronounced kǔ diǎn fān.
If there is indeed a matter in the north,
it would be better to appoint only Shǒuzhēn."
Dù Wēi's true intentions,
even Zhào Yíng understood them.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on Xīnwèi,
Wēi was appointed as Northern Front Field Commander-in-Chief,
Shǒuzhēn as Military Supervisor,
Tàiníng Military Commissioner Ān Shěnqí as Left and Right Wing Commander-in-Chief,
Wǔníng Military Commissioner Fú Yànqīng as Left Wing Cavalry Commander-in-Chief,
Yìchéng Military Commissioner Huángfǔ Yù as Right Wing Cavalry Commander-in-Chief,
Yǒngqīng Military Commissioner Liáng Hànzhāng as Cavalry Formation Commander,
former Wēishèng Military Commissioner Sòng Yànyún as Left Wing Infantry Commander-in-Chief,
Fèngguó Left Wing Commander-in-Chief Wáng Ráo as Right Wing Infantry Commander-in-Chief,
and Míngzhōu Militia Commissioner Xuē Huáiràng as Vanguard Commander-in-Chief.
An imperial edict was also issued, proclaiming:
"We are specially dispatching a great army,
to go and pacify the cunning barbarians.
First, we shall take Yíngzhōu and Mòzhōu,
securing the region south of the pass;
next, we shall recover Yōuyān,
sweeping clean the northern frontier."
It further stated:
"Whoever captures the barbarian ruler
shall be appointed as a high-ranking military commissioner,
rewarded with ten thousand strings of cash,
ten thousand bolts of silk,
