the Emperor first heard of Dù Wēi's surrender;
that evening,
he also heard that Yànzé had reached Huázhōu.
He summoned Lǐ Sōng, Féng Yù, and Lǐ Yàntāo into the palace to discuss matters,
intending to issue an edict ordering Liú Zhīyuǎn to dispatch troops for aid.
(Tàiyuán is 1,200 lǐ from Luòyáng,
and Luòyáng is another 380 lǐ from Dàliáng.
Even if Liú Zhīyuǎn, upon hearing the order, immediately sprang into action,
it would already be too late.)
On the Guǐyǒu day,
before dawn,
Yànzé broke through the gates and entered from the Fēngqiū Gate.
Lǐ Yàntāo led five hundred imperial guards to confront him,
but could not stop him.
Yànzé stationed his troops outside the Míngdé Gate.
(The Wǔdài Huìyào states: The Míngdé Gate is the southern gate of the imperial city of Dàliáng.
The Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ states: In the tenth month of the third year of Tiānfú,
the gate of the Dàníng Palace was renamed the Míngdé Gate.)
The Emperor started a fire in the palace,
and personally, sword in hand, drove more than ten members of the inner court to throw themselves into the fire,
but was restrained by his personal army commander Xuē Chāo.
Soon after, Yànzé, from the Kuānrén Gate, conveyed a letter from the Khitan ruler and the Empress Dowager offering consolation and reassurance.
(The Wǔdài Huìyào states: The eastern gate of the imperial city of Dàliáng is the Kuānrén Gate.)
The Emperor then ordered the fire extinguished,
and had all the palace city gates opened.
The Emperor sat in the garden,
weeping together with the Empress.
He summoned Hanlin Academician Fàn Zhì to draft a surrender memorial,
calling himself
"Your grandson and subject Chóngguì,
disaster has struck, my spirit is confused,
my fortune exhausted, Heaven has abandoned me.
Now, together with the Empress Dowager and my wife, Lady Féng,
the entire clan, bound, awaits punishment in the open fields.
I dispatch my sons, Zhènníng Military Commissioner Yánxù,
and Wēixìn Military Commissioner Yánbǎo,
to present one state treasure
and three golden seals in welcome."
(The state treasure is the Shòumìng Bǎo created in the third year of Gāozǔ's Tiānfú era.
Xù is pronounced Xūjù.)
"And the new bride, concubine Lǐ shì."
The humiliation of calling oneself subject and concubine,
only the Jìn and Sòng experienced it.
Alas,
how grievous!
Shàng,
is pronounced Shízhǎng.
Fù Zhùér entered to proclaim the Khitan ruler's command.
The Emperor removed his yellow robe,
put on plain garments,
bowed twice and received the proclamation,
while all those around him covered their faces and wept.
The Emperor sent for Zhāng Yànzé,
wishing to discuss matters with him.
Yànzé said:
"This subject has no face to see Your Majesty."
The Emperor summoned him again,
but Yànzé merely smiled faintly and did not respond.
Someone urged Sāng Wéihàn to flee.
Wéihàn said:
"I am a high minister,
where would I flee to!"
He sat and awaited his fate.
Yànzé, on the Emperor's order, summoned Wéihàn.
When Wéihàn reached Tiānjiē,
(The main street outside the southern gate of the palace city is called Tiānjiē, the main thoroughfare.)
he halted his horse, and before he finished speaking,
a military officer in front of his horse gestured for Wéihàn to proceed to the Imperial Guard Department.
(Gesturing him to the Imperial Guard Department indicated he was to be imprisoned.
Another version states: At that time, Zhāng Yànzé was residing in the Imperial Guard Department offices.)
He turned and said to Lǐ Sōng:
"You, Shìzhōng, are in charge of the state,
(Lǐ Sōng held the office of Shìzhōng.)
yet you let Wéihàn die for it.
Why is that?"
Sōng looked ashamed.
Yànzé sat arrogantly to receive Wéihàn.
Wéihàn reproached him, saying:
"Last year, I rescued you from among the criminals,
restored you to a major military governorship,
and entrusted you with military authority."
(It is said that during Gāozǔ's time, both court and populace requested Zhāng Yànzé's execution;
he was recalled from Jīngzhōu to serve in the imperial guard.
Last year, Sāng Wéihàn promoted him to jointly resist the Khitan,
restored him as Zhāngguó Military Commissioner,
and had him lead troops to garrison Chángshān.)
Yànzé had no reply,
and dispatched troops to guard him.
Xuānhūishǐ Mèng Chénghuì,
who had always been favored by the Emperor for his flattery and cunning,
at this time, when the Emperor summoned Chénghuì
wishing to consult with him,
Chénghuì hid and did not come;
Zhāng Yànzé arrested and killed him.
Yán Zé unleashed his soldiers to plunder on a large scale,
and the poor people took advantage of the situation,
also competing to break into the homes of the wealthy,
killing people and taking their goods.
It took two days for this to stop,
leaving the capital city completely empty.
The goods accumulated like mountains at Yán Zé's residence.
He considered himself to have rendered meritorious service to the Khitan,
as Zhāng Yánzé took pride in having swiftly entered Biàn as an achievement.
Whenever he went out or came in, he was accompanied by several hundred horsemen,
and his flags and banners all bore the inscription
"Loyal Heart for the Sovereign."
Those who saw it laughed at him.
When soldiers captured criminals and brought them before him,
Yán Zé would not inquire about their offenses;
he would merely glare and raise three fingers,
and they would immediately be driven out to have their waists or necks severed.
Yán Zé had long been at odds with Gé Ménshǐ Gāo Xūn.
Taking advantage of being drunk, he went to Gāo's home,
killed his uncle and younger brother,
and displayed their corpses at the gate.
The scholars and common people trembled with fear.
Zhōngshū Shèrén Lǐ Tāo said to someone:
"Rather than fleeing to the ditches and still not escaping,
I might as well go and see him."
So he submitted his name card and paid a visit to Yán Zé, saying:
"The person who submitted a memorial requesting the execution of Tàiwèi, Lǐ Tāo,
respectfully comes to request death."
The matter of Lǐ Tāo requesting the execution of Zhāng Yánzé is recorded in the 283rd volume, in the seventh year of Gāozǔ's Tiānfú era.
Yán Zé said to Tāo:
"Are you afraid today, Shèrén?"
Tāo replied:
"The fear I feel today
is just like the fear you felt in years past.
If only Gāozǔ had heeded my words,
how could things have come to this!"
Yán Zé laughed heartily
and ordered wine to be served to him.
Tāo drank a full cup and left,
as if no one else were around.
This Lǐ Tāo
was a great-great-grandson of Lǐ Huí's clan,
clear in argument and courageous,
truly having inherited his lineage.
On the jiǎxū day,
Zhāng Yánzé moved the Emperor to the Kāifēng Prefecture office,
not allowing him to stay even for a moment.
In the palace, there was wailing and lamentation.
The Emperor, along with the Empress Dowager and Empress, rode in palanquins,
followed by more than ten palace attendants and eunuchs on foot.
Those who saw it shed tears.
The shame of a fallen state—
those who speak of it feel heartache,
how much more those who witness it!
This is what Chéng Zhèngshū called true understanding.
Heaven!
Mankind!
Yán Zé sent someone to hint to him, saying:
"The Khitan ruler is arriving;
these things cannot be hidden."
The Emperor returned all of them,
also distributing some to Yán Zé as gifts.
Yán Zé selected the rare treasures for himself
and sealed up the remainder to await the Khitan.
Yán Zé dispatched Kòngquè Zhǐhuīshǐ Lǐ Yún to guard the Emperor with soldiers,
cutting off communication inside and out.
The Emperor's aunt, Princess Wūshì, bribed the gatekeepers,
entered to bid farewell to the Emperor,
returned to her residence, and hanged herself.
The memorials submitted by the Emperor and Empress Dowager to the Khitan ruler
were all first shown to Yán Zé
before they dared to be sent.
The Emperor sent someone to fetch several bolts of silk from the inner treasury,
but the keeper refused to give them,
saying:
"These are not the Emperor's property."
He also requested wine from Lǐ Sōng,
but Sōng also declined, using other reasons not to present it.
He also wished to see Lǐ Yàntāo,
but Yàntāo also declined and did not go.
The Emperor was disheartened for a long time.
At that time,
the ministers of the Jìn court
already regarded the deposed Emperor as a stranger;
even if disheartened, what could be done?
Disheartened,
chǒu jiū fān.
Féng Yù flattered Zhāng Yánzé,
requesting to personally deliver the imperial seal,
hoping the Khitan would reappoint him.
Ministers of a fallen state—
their insight is precisely like this.
Reappoint,
fú yòu fān.
Lady Chǔguó Dīngshì,
mother of Yán Xù,
was of great beauty.
Yán Zé sent someone to fetch her;
the Empress Dowager hesitated and did not hand her over.
Yán Zé cursed and reviled,
immediately taking her away by carriage.
That evening,
Yán Zé killed Sāng Wéihàn.
Textual analysis states: The Old History of the Five Dynasties records:
"The Emperor recalled that while Wéihàn was serving as chancellor,
he repeatedly offered counsel and plans,
urging peace with the barbarians.
Fearing that once the Khitan ruler arrived in the capital, his own faults would be exposed,
he wanted to kill Wéihàn to silence him,
and thus ordered Zhāng Yánzé to kill him."
However, at that time, would Yánzé have been willing to obey the young Emperor's command again?
This account is not adopted here.
He reported to the Khitan ruler
that Wéihàn had hanged himself.
The Khitan ruler said:
"I had no intention of killing Wéihàn;
why did he do this!"
He ordered that his family be generously cared for.
Gāo Xíngzhōu and Fú Yànqīng both went to the Khitan camp to surrender.
The two came from Chánzhōu to surrender.
They were interrogated.
The battle of Yángchéng
is recorded in the previous volume, last year.
Defeated,
bǔ mài fān.
Interrogated,
qù jí fān.
"At that time, we only knew to exert all our strength for the Jìn sovereign;
today, life or death is at your command."
The Khitan ruler laughed and released them.
Fú Yànqīng spoke straightforwardly,
and the Khitan ruler had no grounds to condemn him.
For,
yú wèi fān.
On the jǐmǎo day,
Yán Xù and Yán Bǎo returned from the camp.
The Khitan ruler bestowed a handwritten edict upon the Emperor
and sent Xiè Lǐ to say to the Emperor:
"Grandson, do not worry;
I will certainly ensure you have a place to eat."
The Emperor's heart was somewhat eased,
and he submitted a memorial expressing gratitude.
The Khitans believed the national treasure they offered was poorly crafted,
and did not match the details of previous history records.
They suspected it was not genuine,
and with an imperial decree questioned the emperor,
asking for the genuine one to be presented.
Lǐ Xīnchuán said: The "Qín Seal"
is written in the Chóngyú seal script by Lǐ Sī,
measuring four inches around.
According to "The Diagram of the Jade Seal," this seal was carved from Zhào Jade,
originally a raw jade offered by Biànhé,
and taken by Lín Xiàngrú.
I have examined it based on ritual regulations,
as the jade is five inches with a flaw,
it should not have been recarved into a seal,
this claim is incorrect.
The Qín Seal remained until the Han, referred to as the National Seal,
from then until the Han,
the treasure used by the emperor,
was indeed the Qín Seal;
it was sealed by Zǐ Yīng,
thrown by Empress Yuán,
retrieved by Wáng Xiàn,
returned by Chìméi,
all were the same object.
It was lost during Dǒng Zhuó's uprising.
"The Book of Wú" claims Sūn Jiān found it in a well at the Zhen Official’s residence in Luòyáng,
only to be taken by Yuán Shù,
then recovered by Xú Qiú and presented,
which is unlikely.
If so,
why would the Wèi not treasure it and carve their own seal?
In successive dynasties, they used its name.
It was lost during the chaos of Yǒngjiā to Liú Shí,
and returned to the south in Yǒnghé times
as the Jìn Seal.
During the Wèi dynasty,
the National Seal was carved in the style of the Qín text,
except the Qín Seal read from right,
the Wèi Seal read from left.
When Jìn ruled the world,
they carved their own seal,
with the text:
"Mandated by Heaven,
may the Emperor live long and prosper."
Some books claim it was the Qín Seal passed through to the Han,
which is greatly mistaken.
This seal passed to Liú Cōng and Shí Lè,
and after Shí Zhī's death,
his minister Jiǎng Gàn sought aid from Xiè Shàng,
sending the seal to Jiāngnán,
Wáng Biāozhī disputed this,
stating it was not the Qín Seal.
At the end of Tàiyuán,
obtained from Western Yān,
passed through the Six Dynasties,
to the Suí era,
as the Mùróng Yān Seal.
In the Jìn Xiàowǔ’s nineteenth year of Tàiyuán,
the Western Yān ruler Yǒng sought aid from Xì Huī,
offering a seal six inches square,
four and six-tenths inches high,
inscribed like the Qín Seal,
it passed through the Sòng, Qí, Liáng as a treasure.
After Hóujǐng's death,
Xīn Shù of Northern Qí obtained it in Guǎnglíng,
presenting it to the Gāo family.
Later it passed through Zhōu and Suí,
always mistakenly identified as the Qín Seal,
only after the unification of Jiāngnán,
was it recognized as not genuine,
and thereafter called the Divine Seal.
Liú Yù's northern expedition,
retrieved it from Guānzhōng,
passing through the Jìn and Chén,
before the Suí possessed it,
as the Yáo Qín Seal.
In Jìn's Yìxī thirteen year,
Liú Yù entered Guānzhōng,
obtaining the National Seal and presented it,
measuring four inches,
with inscriptions matching the Qín,
yet subtly raised and not deeply carved.
When Suí destroyed Chén, they obtained this,
declaring it the true seal,
dismissing Yǔwén's transmitted Divine Seal as false.
Scholars say ancient seals were deeply carved,
using seal paste,
later gradually raised,
for imprinting paper,
thus the raised ones are not Qín Seals,
Yáo's merely copied its script.
During the Kāiyùn chaos,
it was lost to Yēlǜ,
acquired by the Jurchens as a great treasure,
as the Shí Jìn Seal.
During the sixteenth year of Zhēnguān of Táng Tàizōng,
a mandate seal was carved,
the inscription reads:
"Emperor's bright mandate,
those with virtue shall prosper,"
later returned to Zhū Quánzhōng,
when Cóngkē immolated himself,
the seal was lost with him.
Dégōng entered Biàn,
Chóngguì presented the seal,
claiming it was "carved by the previous emperor,"
likely referring to Jìngtáng.
During Táng it was mistakenly thought to be the Qín Seal,
but the actual loss of the Qín Seal had occurred long ago.
Now according to this text,
"Shí Zhī's death",
should be read as
"Rǎn Mǐn's death".
Lǐ Xīnchuán's account differs from the "Dà Táng Liù Diǎn",
both texts are preserved here,
awaiting a knowledgeable person.
By the Zhōu dynasty,
two more treasures were made.
The officials submitted their explanations,
based on the "Liù Diǎn",
with detailed notes afterward.
The term "decree,"
read as "jí".
"When Cóngkē immolated himself,
events are recorded in Volume 280, Táng Gāozǔ's Tiānfú first year.
Surely it was burnt with him.
This treasure was made by the previous emperor,
events appear in Volume 281, Tiānfú third year.
Today how can I dare conceal the treasure!"
Thus it ceased.
The emperor heard the Khitan lord was crossing the river,
planning to greet him with the empress dowager beforehand;
Zhāng Yànzé reported it first,
but the Khitan lord did not allow it.
The authorities wanted the emperor to carry jade in his teeth, yoked with a sheep,
with great ministers bearing coffins,
to greet outside the city;
prepared rituals were to be reported to the Khitan lord first,
but he said:
"I send elite troops to take Dàliáng directly,
this is not surrender."
He did not permit it either.
He ordered the Jìn civilian and military officials,
everything usual;
the court's systems,
all conducted with Hàn rites.
Northerners called China the Hàn.
The Khitan lord replied:
"I am fully armored and commanding troops,
there's no time for ceremonial observances yet."
All was refused.
Using Taichang’s rites,
necessitates changing Hu attire to Chinese attire,
hence he said no time.
Earlier when the Khitan lord arrived in Xiàngzhōu,
immediately dispatched troops towards Héyáng to capture Jǐng Yán’guǎng.
Yán’guǎng had no place to hide unexpectedly,
not knowing he would be captured promptly.
Xiàngzhōu,
pronounced like "sīliàng."
Héyáng,
pronounced like "qìyù."
The Nine Domain Records: Fēngqiū County is sixty lĭ north of Dàliáng.
"Your actions caused the two lords to fall out of favor,
all was your doing.
Where is your ten-thousand swords ready?"
Qiáo Róng was summoned,
to debate and confirm,
a total of ten articles.
Initially Yán’guǎng did not admit,
but Róng showed him the written words on paper,
Jǐng Yán’guǎng recorded what he said to give to Qiáo Róng,
detailed in Volume 283, Tiānfú eighth year.
For each admission,
a stick was given.
By the eighth count,
Yán’guǎng could only prostrate and plead for death,
thus he was locked up.
On the thirtieth day of bǐngxū,
all officials lodged at Fēngshàn Temple.
For greeting the Khitan lord.
Fēngshàn Temple is east of Dàliáng city.
Zhāng Xīchén punctuation, Niè Chóngqí overseen proofreading.
